````text
Stage 1 — Lead Source Strategy

Goal of this stage:

Decide where MenuList leads come from,
which source we use first,
what fields we extract,
how we control cost,
and what we explicitly avoid.

My recommendation:

Primary source: Apify Google Maps Scraper
Backup benchmark: Outscraper
Do not use official Google Business Profile APIs for lead generation
Do not integrate 5 data providers in v0
Do not scrape reviews/photos/menus for MenuList content

Use external data only to find who to contact. The MenuList asset begins only when the owner sends or confirms their menu.

1.1 Source strategy decision

Use this source stack:

Tier 1: Apify Google Maps Scraper
Tier 2: Apify/Outscraper contact enrichment
Tier 3: Manual CSV imports
Tier 4: Outscraper benchmark
Tier 5: Customer-demand signals later

Do not start with:

SerpApi
DataForSEO
Google Places API
Google Business Profile API
Zomato/Swiggy scraping
Instagram scraping
multi-provider enrichment

Those can come later if needed.

The first bottleneck will not be “can we get enough restaurants?” The bottleneck will be:

Are they real?
Are they local SMBs?
Do they have a phone/email?
Do they lack a clean digital menu?
Will they respond?
Can we convert them into MenuList links?

So v0 needs source simplicity + strong filtering.

1.2 Primary source: Apify Google Maps Scraper

Use Apify’s Google Maps Scraper as the first source.

Why:

It gives local business data at category + location level.
It returns phone/website/category/location fields.
It can be run programmatically.
It supports export/API workflows.
It is cheap enough for testing.
It is flexible for area-level campaigns.

Apify’s maintained Google Maps Scraper lists pricing from $2.10 per 1,000 scraped places, is categorized for lead generation, and claims it can extract place names, categories, URLs, addresses, coordinates, phone numbers, websites, company contact details, and other lead-enrichment fields.
Apify

Apify also supports custom search areas using GeoJSON polygons, multipolygons, or point-radius searches, which matters because MenuList should acquire by dense local clusters, not by huge city-wide random queries.
Apify

Use this as the initial actor:

apify: compass/crawler-google-places

Potential secondary actor:

apify: lukaskrivka/google-maps-with-contact-details

The second actor is more contact-enrichment-oriented. It lists extraction of emails, social profiles, phone numbers, website, address, and related contact fields, also from $2.10 per 1,000 scraped places.
Apify

My choice:

Start with compass/crawler-google-places.
Use contact-enrichment only when the lead has a website but no email/phone found.

Do not enrich everything by default. Enrichment is where cost and noise can creep in.

1.3 Apify plan recommendation

Start with:

Apify Starter: $29/month

Do not start with Scale or Business.

Apify’s pricing page lists Free at $0 with $5 usage credit, Starter at $29/month, Scale at $199/month, and Business at $999/month, with paid plans including prepaid usage and pay-as-you-go overage.
Apify

For the first campaign, Starter is enough.

Upgrade only when:

You are running campaigns weekly
You have proven qualified lead rate
You know cost per MenuList link created
You need higher concurrency or better support

Do not upgrade because scraping feels exciting.

1.4 Backup benchmark: Outscraper

Outscraper is the cleanest backup/comparison provider.

Why benchmark it later:

Simple pricing
Google Maps-specific
CSV/API export
Good for comparing lead quality and phone/email coverage

Outscraper’s pricing page says Google Maps Scraper is free for the first 500 businesses/places, then $3 per 1,000 records from 501 to 100,000 businesses, and $1 per 1,000 records after 100,000 businesses. It also lists API access, CSV/Excel/Parquet/JSON, advanced filters, and enrichments.
Outscraper

Use Outscraper only after Apify imports the first 1,000–3,000 leads.

The benchmark question should be:

Which source gives cheaper qualified leads?

Not:

Which source gives cheaper raw leads?

Benchmark fields:

raw cost per 1,000
qualified lead rate
phone availability
email availability
duplicate rate
wrong-category rate
closed-business rate
no-menu/no-website signal quality

If Outscraper produces cleaner phone numbers or better qualified lead rate, we can switch or use it as backup.

1.5 Why not DataForSEO / SerpApi in v0

DataForSEO and SerpApi are useful, but not ideal as first lead source.

DataForSEO’s Google Maps SERP API is priced per SERP page, with listed Standard Queue pricing at $0.0006 per SERP page, Priority at $0.0012, and Live Mode at $0.002, and it is positioned more like SERP/local SEO infrastructure than a simple lead scraper.
DataForSEO

SerpApi lists pricing by monthly search volume: Free 250 searches/month, Starter $25 for 1,000 searches/month, Developer $75 for 5,000, Production $150 for 15,000, and Big Data $275 for 30,000 searches/month.
SerpApi

These are better for:

search result monitoring
local SEO tooling
rank tracking
structured SERP access
specific query diagnostics

They are not the cleanest first choice for:

bulk local restaurant/cafe lead acquisition

Use them later only if you need:

Google search result presence checks
"restaurant name menu" SERP checks
MenuList SEO monitoring
competitor visibility tracking

Not for v0 lead acquisition.

1.6 Why not official Google Business Profile APIs

Do not use Google Business Profile APIs for cold lead generation.

Google’s GoogleLocations API guide explicitly says the API is intended for managing locations with existing business relationships and should not be used for lead generation or competitive analysis.
Google for Developers

Also, Google Maps Platform terms prohibit exporting, extracting, scraping, storing, resharing, or rehosting Google Maps Content outside the services, including copying and saving business names, addresses, Places information, and user reviews.
Google Cloud

So the practical operating rule remains:

Google/Maps-derived data = temporary internal lead intelligence.
Owner-submitted menu/info = MenuList truth.

Do not build MenuList pages from scraped Google data.

1.7 Source hierarchy for v0

Use this hierarchy.

Source A — Google Maps via Apify

Purpose:

Find restaurants/cafes/bakeries/cloud kitchens in target areas.

Fields to collect:

business name
category
phone
website
Google Maps URL
address text
area/city
coordinates
closed/open status if available
rating/review count as internal demand signal only

Do not import into MenuList public pages:

reviews
photos
descriptions
menu photos
popular items
owner responses

Use those only, if at all, as temporary internal qualification signals.

Source B — Website contact enrichment

Use only for leads that have a website but no phone/email extracted.

Purpose:

Find email/contact page/menu page from the business’s own website.

Allowed:

crawl public business website
detect contact email
detect WhatsApp/phone
detect menu URL
detect Instagram link
detect whether menu exists

This helps qualify leads:

If website already has a clean menu, lower priority.
If website exists but menu is missing/broken, still good.
If website has contact email, use email outreach.

Do not overdo this in v0. Use it only for promising leads.

Source C — Manual CSV import

This is important.

You should support manual import from day one.

Why:

You may already collect leads from Instagram, field visits, referrals, or personal research.
A human-curated list can outperform scraped lists.
Manual import lets you test the pipeline before full Apify automation.

CSV columns:

business_name
category
city
area
phone
email
website
source_url
notes

This prevents engineering from blocking acquisition.

Source D — Outscraper benchmark

Use after first Apify batch.

Benchmark campaign:

Same city
Same areas
Same categories
Same max lead count
Compare qualified lead yield

Example:

Apify: 1,000 raw leads → 220 qualified
Outscraper: 1,000 raw leads → 260 qualified

Only switch if the difference matters.

Source E — Customer-demand signals later

This is the long-term best source, but not v0.

Later, MenuList should collect signals like:

user searched for "ABC Cafe menu"
user requested menu for a business
user clicked "menu unavailable"
user reported old menu

Then outreach becomes:

Customers are looking for your menu on MenuList. Claim/add it here.

That is much stronger than cold scraping.

But it requires existing MenuList traffic, so it is not Stage 1 default.

1.8 What lead sources to avoid initially
Avoid Zomato/Swiggy scraping

Reason:

Not needed for v0.
High policy/brand risk.
They are platforms, not neutral lead sources.
Delivery-menu data is not the same as canonical business menu.

Also, it pulls MenuList mentally toward food delivery comparison, which is the wrong category.

Avoid Instagram scraping in v0

Instagram can be useful manually, but don’t automate it initially.

Reason:

Often messy.
High false positives.
Harder to extract phone/email cleanly.
Many restaurants use Instagram as a content channel, not a structured truth source.

Use Instagram link as an enrichment field if Apify finds it, but do not make Instagram scraping the first engine.

Avoid public directory cloning

Do not build a scraped restaurant directory.

Reason:

Wrong positioning.
SEO thin-content risk.
Data quality risk.
Legal/policy risk.
Does not create owner-verified MenuList truth.

Your internal tool should generate outreach targets, not public scraped pages.

1.9 First campaign source design

Start narrow.

Recommended first campaign:

City: Bangalore
Areas:
- Koramangala
- Indiranagar
- HSR Layout
- Jayanagar

Categories:
- cafe
- restaurant
- bakery
- dessert shop
- cloud kitchen

Raw target:
500–1,000 leads

Qualified target:
100–250 leads

Contacted target:
50–100 in first batch

Do not scrape 10,000 leads first. That creates noise before you understand conversion.

1.10 Query strategy

Use area + category queries.

Bad query:

restaurants in Bangalore

Good queries:

cafes in Koramangala Bangalore
restaurants in Koramangala Bangalore
bakeries in Koramangala Bangalore
dessert shops in Koramangala Bangalore
cloud kitchens in Koramangala Bangalore

cafes in Indiranagar Bangalore
restaurants in Indiranagar Bangalore
bakeries in Indiranagar Bangalore
dessert shops in Indiranagar Bangalore
cloud kitchens in Indiranagar Bangalore

Reason:

Area-level queries create cleaner local clusters.
Cluster density matters for eventual MenuList authority.
It reduces generic chains and low-relevance results.
It makes manual QA faster.

For each query, cap results.

Suggested initial cap:

max 100–150 places per query

With 4 areas × 5 categories × 100 results:

2,000 max raw leads before dedupe

After dedupe and qualification, expect much less.

For the first test, set lower caps:

50 places per query

That gives approximately:

4 areas × 5 categories × 50 = 1,000 raw max

Good enough.

1.11 Fields to extract

For v0, extract only fields useful for qualification/outreach.

Required fields
TypeScript
type SourceLead = {
  source: "apify_google_maps";
  sourceRunId: string;

  businessName: string;
  category?: string;

  phone?: string;
  website?: string;
  email?: string;

  address?: string;
  area?: string;
  city: string;

  mapsUrl?: string;

  isPermanentlyClosed?: boolean;
  isTemporarilyClosed?: boolean;

  rating?: number;        // internal only
  reviewCount?: number;   // internal only

  rawSourceUrl?: string;
};
Do not store long-term
reviews
review text
reviewer names
Google photos
photo URLs
Google descriptions
popular times
menu images from Google
owner responses

Review count and rating can be used as internal demand proxies if they come in the source data, but do not show them publicly on MenuList from scraped data.

1.12 Lead-source scoring at source level

Each source should be evaluated with these metrics.

raw leads imported
duplicate rate
contactable rate
phone coverage
email coverage
wrong-category rate
closed-business rate
has-website rate
no-website rate
likely-no-menu rate
qualified lead rate
cost per raw lead
cost per qualified lead
cost per contacted lead
cost per menu received

The key number:

cost per menu received

Not cost per scrape.

Example:

Apify cost: $20
Raw leads: 5,000
Qualified leads: 800
Contacted: 300
Replies: 30
Menus received: 12

Cost per raw lead: $0.004
Cost per qualified lead: $0.025
Cost per menu received: $1.67 before outreach labor/cost

This is the right way to think.

1.13 Source risk rating

Assign a source risk level.

TypeScript
type SourceRisk = "low" | "medium" | "high";
Low risk
owner submission
manual referral
your own customer demand data
business’s own website contact page
manual import from known relationship
Medium risk
Apify/Outscraper Google Maps lead discovery
public business website crawling
public directory discovery
High risk
scraped reviews
scraped photos
scraped menus from third-party platforms
Zomato/Swiggy data
Instagram automation
Google Business Profile API for lead generation

For v0, use:

low + medium only

No high-risk source should feed outreach or MenuList content without manual decision.

1.14 Recommended first source configuration

Use this setup:

Provider: Apify
Actor: compass/crawler-google-places
Mode: category + area query
City: Bangalore
Areas: Koramangala, Indiranagar, HSR Layout, Jayanagar
Categories: cafe, restaurant, bakery, dessert shop, cloud kitchen
Max results per query: 50
Total raw cap: ~1,000
Reviews/photos extraction: off or ignored
Contact enrichment: off in first run unless included cheaply

Fields to import:

title/name
category
phone
website
address
maps URL
coordinates
closed status
rating/review count for internal scoring only

Fields to ignore:

reviews
photos
descriptions
popular times
menu images

After first import, inspect:

how many have phone?
how many have website?
how many look like chains?
how many are duplicates?
how many are real SMB restaurants/cafes?
how many have no obvious digital menu?

Then decide whether contact enrichment is needed.

1.15 When to use contact enrichment

Use contact enrichment only for these leads:

score is already high
phone missing
email missing
website exists
business looks local
business likely lacks clean menu

Do not enrich low-score leads.

Enrichment rule:

Only enrich leads with preliminary score >= 60.

Reason:

It is wasteful to pay for email/contact enrichment on junk leads.

Example:

1,000 raw leads
400 pass basic filters
150 have website but no phone/email
Only enrich those 150

This keeps cost disciplined.

1.16 Website/menu detection logic

For businesses with a website, detect:

Does website exist?
Does it load?
Does it have menu page?
Does it have PDF menu?
Does it have image menu?
Does it have WhatsApp link?
Does it have contact email?
Does it have phone?

This is not for building public pages. It is for scoring.

A restaurant with a website can still be a good MenuList lead if:

website exists but menu is missing
menu is PDF/image only
menu is hard to open on mobile
menu is stale-looking
website is slow/broken
no QR/shareable menu page

Do not make “has website” an automatic rejection.

MenuList is not competing with websites. MenuList is offering a clean, current, shareable menu truth layer.

1.17 Source output contract

Every source should normalize into one common object.

TypeScript
type ImportedLead = {
  sourceProvider: "apify" | "outscraper" | "manual";
  sourceType: "google_maps" | "website" | "manual_csv";
  sourceRunId: string;

  businessName: string;
  category?: string;

  city: string;
  area?: string;
  address?: string;

  phone?: string;
  email?: string;
  website?: string;
  mapsUrl?: string;

  internalSignals: {
    hasPhone: boolean;
    hasEmail: boolean;
    hasWebsite: boolean;
    possiblyClosed: boolean;
    rating?: number;
    reviewCount?: number;
    sourceConfidence: number;
  };

  raw: Record<string, unknown>;
};

The lead engine should not care whether the source is Apify or Outscraper later. Everything becomes ImportedLead.

1.18 Source-run object

Each scraping/import run should create a source run record.

TypeScript
type SourceRun = {
  id: string;

  provider: "apify" | "outscraper" | "manual";
  sourceType: "google_maps" | "website_enrichment" | "manual_csv";

  campaignName: string;

  input: {
    city: string;
    areas: string[];
    categories: string[];
    queries: string[];
    maxResultsPerQuery: number;
  };

  cost: {
    estimatedUsd?: number;
    actualUsd?: number;
  };

  results: {
    rawImported: number;
    duplicates: number;
    rejected: number;
    qualified: number;
    contactable: number;
  };

  status: "queued" | "running" | "completed" | "failed";

  startedAt: Date;
  completedAt?: Date;
};

This lets you compare campaigns and vendors.

1.19 First-stage cost expectation

For the first Bangalore test:

Raw leads: 500–1,000
Apify tool cost: likely low
Apify plan: $29 Starter
Contact enrichment: avoid initially or cap tightly
AI previews: 0
Email cost: negligible
WhatsApp: assisted/manual

Given Apify’s listed scraper pricing from $2.10 per 1,000 scraped places and Starter plan at $29/month, source cost should not be the blocker for a 500–1,000 lead test.
Apify
+1

Set a first campaign hard cap:

Max source spend: $50
Max raw leads: 1,000
Max enriched leads: 150
Max contacted leads: 100

If you cannot produce meaningful signal within this, the issue is not scraping budget. The issue is message, qualification, or category focus.

1.20 Source quality decision rule

After first campaign, decide based on this.

Continue with Apify if:

qualified lead rate >= 20%
contactable rate >= 40%
duplicate rate <= 25%
wrong-category rate <= 15%
cost per qualified lead is acceptable

Benchmark Outscraper if:

phone coverage is poor
duplicates are high
closed businesses are common
category quality is bad
Apify output is inconsistent

Stop or change category if:

qualified lead rate < 10%
contactable rate < 25%
wrong-category rate > 30%
most businesses already have clean menus

Do not keep scraping just because it is cheap.

1.21 Final Stage 1 decision

Build source strategy like this:

Use Apify Google Maps Scraper as primary source.
Run small area/category campaigns.
Extract only fields needed for qualification and outreach.
Use scraped data as temporary lead intelligence.
Do not use scraped reviews/photos/menu content.
Use contact enrichment selectively, not globally.
Support manual CSV imports from day one.
Benchmark Outscraper only after first Apify batch.
Avoid DataForSEO/SerpApi/official Google APIs for v0 lead acquisition.

First campaign:

Provider: Apify
Actor: compass/crawler-google-places
City: Bangalore
Areas: Koramangala, Indiranagar, HSR Layout, Jayanagar
Categories: cafe, restaurant, bakery, dessert shop, cloud kitchen
Raw cap: 1,000
Qualified target: 100–250
Contacted target: 50–100
AI previews: 0
Default CTA: send menu → get MenuList link + QR

That is the right source foundation.

Next stage: Stage 2 — Lead definition and qualification logic.
````

````text
Stage 2 — Lead Definition and Qualification Logic

Goal of this stage:

Define exactly what counts as a valid MenuList lead,
what gets rejected,
how leads are scored,
and which leads deserve outreach first.

This is the most important stage. Bad qualification will make the whole system look busy but produce weak results.

2.1 Core definition

A MenuList lead is not simply:

Any restaurant found on Google Maps.

A valid MenuList lead is:

A local food business with reachable contact details and a likely need for a clean digital menu link / QR.

The lead should satisfy three conditions:

1. It is a relevant food business.
2. It is reachable by phone, WhatsApp, or email.
3. It has weak, missing, or inconvenient digital menu presence.

That third condition is the wedge.

MenuList should not just contact restaurants. It should contact restaurants where MenuList can clearly reduce friction.

2.2 The first principle

The system should optimize for:

menu received

Not:

lead scraped
phone number found
message sent

So every qualification rule should answer:

Is this business likely to send us its menu?

That means the best early leads are not always the biggest restaurants. The best early leads are usually:

small/local
owner-operated
reachable
not too digitally sophisticated
has customer demand
likely uses WhatsApp
likely lacks a clean digital menu/QR
2.3 Lead stages

Keep the lead lifecycle simple.

TypeScript
type LeadStatus =
  | "raw_imported"
  | "normalized"
  | "duplicate"
  | "rejected"
  | "scored"
  | "qualified"
  | "ready_to_contact"
  | "contacted_whatsapp"
  | "contacted_email"
  | "replied"
  | "menu_received"
  | "menulist_link_created"
  | "menulist_link_sent"
  | "converted"
  | "not_interested"
  | "do_not_contact";

Do not create sales stages like “demo scheduled,” “proposal sent,” or “deal negotiation.” This is not a SaaS sales CRM. This is a menu acquisition engine.

2.4 Qualification pipeline

Every imported lead should pass through this pipeline:

Raw import
→ Normalize
→ Deduplicate
→ Hard reject gates
→ Score
→ Segment
→ Contact decision

Detailed:

1. Normalize business name, phone, website, city, area, category.
2. Deduplicate against existing leads and existing MenuList businesses.
3. Reject clearly bad leads.
4. Score remaining leads.
5. Segment into A/B/C priority.
6. Contact only A and selected B leads.

This prevents the common mistake:

Scrape 5,000 leads → message everyone → low response → blame channel.

The problem is usually qualification, not the channel.

2.5 Input fields needed for qualification

From Apify or any similar source, collect only what helps qualification and outreach.

Apify’s Google Maps scraper listings state that they can extract place/business data such as addresses, contact details, business leads, websites, opening hours, prices, menus, coordinates, and other fields, and can be run or exported through API workflows. For MenuList, import only the fields needed for qualification and contact, not scraped content for public reuse.
Apify

Minimum fields:

TypeScript
type ImportedLead = {
  sourceProvider: "apify" | "outscraper" | "manual";
  sourceType: "google_maps" | "website" | "manual_csv";
  sourceRunId: string;

  businessName: string;
  category?: string;

  city: string;
  area?: string;
  address?: string;

  phone?: string;
  email?: string;
  website?: string;
  mapsUrl?: string;

  isTemporarilyClosed?: boolean;
  isPermanentlyClosed?: boolean;

  rating?: number;       // internal scoring only
  reviewCount?: number;  // internal scoring only

  raw?: Record<string, unknown>;
};

Important rule:

Ratings/review count can be used as internal demand signals.
Do not display scraped reviews/ratings publicly as MenuList truth.

Google Maps Platform terms restrict scraping, extracting, exporting, caching, storing, resharing, or rehosting Google Maps content outside the services, including Maps content such as business/place information and reviews. So this system should treat scraped source data as temporary lead intelligence, not canonical MenuList content.
Google Cloud

2.6 Hard reject rules

A lead should be rejected before scoring if it fails any hard gate.

Reject Rule 1 — Wrong vertical

Accept only food businesses for now.

Accepted categories:

restaurant
cafe
bakery
dessert shop
ice cream shop
sweet shop
cloud kitchen
fast food
juice shop
tea shop
coffee shop
biryani place
pizza place
burger place
food truck
takeaway food business

Reject categories:

hotel without restaurant relevance
grocery store
supermarket
catering-only business
event planner
food wholesaler
bar-only venue
liquor store
banquet hall
home chef without public business presence
school/college canteen
corporate cafeteria
closed business

Some edge cases should go to manual review:

pub + restaurant
hotel restaurant
resort cafe
food court stall
franchise branch
delivery-only kitchen
Reject Rule 2 — Outside target geography

For first campaign, reject anything outside selected areas.

Example target:

Bangalore:
- Koramangala
- Indiranagar
- HSR Layout
- Jayanagar

Reject if:

city does not match
area does not match
address is ambiguous and cannot be resolved

Reason:

Cluster density matters.
Operating focus matters.
You want local proof, not scattered leads.
Reject Rule 3 — No contact path

Reject if there is no usable contact path.

Valid contact path:

phone
WhatsApp-capable phone
email
website contact form
Instagram DM manually found

For v0:

phone or email should be required

If no phone/email but website exists, send to enrichment queue.

No phone/email + no website = reject
No phone/email + website = enrich once
No contact after enrichment = reject
Reject Rule 4 — Permanently closed

Reject if source indicates:

permanently closed
moved with no clear new location
duplicate ghost listing

Temporarily closed can go to manual review, not automatic reject.

Reject Rule 5 — Duplicate

Reject or merge if same business already exists.

Duplicate signals:

same normalized phone
same website
same maps URL
same business name + same area
same address + similar name
already exists on MenuList

Phone match should be the strongest duplicate signal.

Reject Rule 6 — Large chain / low owner reachability

Do not waste early outreach on large chains.

Reject or low-priority if:

large national chain
mall chain with centralized marketing
franchise brand with many branches
hotel group
enterprise restaurant group

Early MenuList adoption should come from owner-operated SMBs, not brands requiring corporate approvals.

Exception:

local 2–5 outlet chain
popular local cafe group
owner-accessible branch

These can be high-value but should be manual review.

Reject Rule 7 — Strong existing menu presence

Reject or deprioritize if the business already has:

clean mobile menu page
active digital menu QR
well-structured website menu
updated menu link in bio
delivery menu is clearly sufficient for their use case

Do not reject just because they have a website.

A business with a website can still be a good MenuList lead if:

menu is PDF-only
menu is image-only
menu is hard to open on mobile
menu is missing
menu is stale
menu is buried
no QR/shareable menu link
no fast WhatsApp-friendly menu page

MenuList’s wedge is not “you don’t have a website.”
The wedge is:

your menu is not easy enough for customers to access, trust, and share
2.7 Scoring model

After hard rejects, score the remaining leads.

Use a 100-point model.

Lead Score =
  Fit Score
+ Reachability Score
+ Menu Gap Score
+ Demand Score
+ Conversion Ease Score
- Risk Penalty

Recommended weights:

Fit Score:             20
Reachability Score:    25
Menu Gap Score:        25
Demand Score:          15
Conversion Ease Score: 15
Risk Penalty:          -30 max

This keeps the model practical.

2.8 Fit Score — max 20

Purpose:

Is this the right kind of business for MenuList?

Rules:

restaurant/cafe/bakery/dessert shop: +20
cloud kitchen/takeaway: +15
bar + restaurant: +10
hotel restaurant: +8
unclear food category: +5
wrong category: reject

For the first campaign, prefer:

cafes
restaurants
bakeries
dessert shops

Why:

They commonly need shareable menus.
They are owner-reachable.
They use WhatsApp.
They benefit from QR.
They often have messy or image-based menus.
2.9 Reachability Score — max 25

Purpose:

Can we actually contact the owner/team?

Rules:

phone available: +15
email available: +8
website contact form/email available: +5
WhatsApp link detected: +10
Instagram link available: +3
no contact: reject

Cap total at 25.

Priority:

phone > email > website form > Instagram

For v0, phone is the strongest signal because your CTA is simple:

Send menu photo/PDF here.

But be careful: WhatsApp is operationally sensitive. WhatsApp Business policy says business-initiated conversations must use approved message templates, and Meta’s opt-in guidance says businesses must clearly state when a person is opting in to receive WhatsApp communications. So v0 should use assisted/manual WhatsApp opening rather than blind automated blasting.
WhatsApp for Business
+1

2.10 Menu Gap Score — max 25

Purpose:

Does this business likely need MenuList?

Rules:

no website: +10
website exists but no obvious menu page: +10
menu is PDF/image-only: +8
menu link broken: +12
menu buried/hard to access: +6
only Instagram menu/highlights: +8
no clear QR/digital menu: +5
already has clean mobile menu: +0

Cap total at 25.

This is the most strategically important score.

A great MenuList lead is not simply offline. It is a business where customers face friction answering:

What is available?
What does it cost?
Is the menu current?
How do I share it?
2.11 Demand Score — max 15

Purpose:

Is there enough customer demand to justify outreach?

Use proxy signals.

Rules:

review count / public activity high: +5 to +8
rating present and business looks active: +3
located in dense commercial area: +5
category has high menu demand: +5
visible customer photos/activity: +3 internal only

Cap total at 15.

Do not overfit this. Demand score is a prioritization tool, not truth.

For MenuList, a high-demand business with a weak menu presence is better than a random business with no website.

2.12 Conversion Ease Score — max 15

Purpose:

How likely is this business to convert quickly?

Rules:

small/local business: +5
owner-operated likely: +5
single location: +4
uses WhatsApp/phone visibly: +4
has simple menu category: +3
already has existing MenuList-style need: +3

Subtract or reduce for:

large chain
luxury restaurant group
corporate approval likely
unclear ownership
no obvious owner contact

Early goal is not enterprise logos. Early goal is fast menu acquisition.

2.13 Risk Penalty — max -30

Purpose:

Avoid bad contacts, bad data, and bad brand risk.

Penalties:

possible duplicate: -15
possible chain/corporate owner: -10
possibly closed: -20
source confidence low: -10
wrong/ambiguous category: -15
phone seems invalid: -10
source terms/data risk high: -20
already has strong menu infrastructure: -10

If risk penalty exceeds 25, route to manual review or reject.

2.14 Final scoring formula

Simple TypeScript version:

TypeScript
type LeadScores = {
  fit: number;             // 0-20
  reachability: number;    // 0-25
  menuGap: number;         // 0-25
  demand: number;          // 0-15
  conversionEase: number;  // 0-15
  riskPenalty: number;     // 0-30
};

function calculateLeadScore(scores: LeadScores): number {
  const raw =
    scores.fit +
    scores.reachability +
    scores.menuGap +
    scores.demand +
    scores.conversionEase -
    scores.riskPenalty;

  return Math.max(0, Math.min(100, raw));
}

Keep the formula explainable. Do not use ML here.

2.15 Lead segments

After scoring, segment leads.

A Leads — contact first
Score: 75–100

Meaning:

relevant food business
phone/email available
likely weak menu presence
local SMB
good demand signal
low risk

Action:

ready_to_contact

Use:

WhatsApp assisted send if phone exists
email if email exists
manual call for very strong leads
B Leads — review/contact selectively
Score: 55–74

Meaning:

potentially useful but some uncertainty

Action:

manual review
contact if batch needs more volume
maybe enrich

Examples:

has website but menu unclear
phone exists but category ambiguous
good business but possible chain
no phone but email exists
C Leads — do not contact now
Score: 35–54

Meaning:

weak fit or low conversion chance

Action:

hold or reject

Use later only if you need volume.

Reject
Score: <35 or hard reject triggered

Action:

rejected
2.16 Contact decision rules

Use deterministic rules.

TypeScript
function getContactDecision(lead: Lead): ContactDecision {
  if (lead.status === "rejected") return "do_not_contact";
  if (lead.hasDoNotContactFlag) return "do_not_contact";
  if (lead.score >= 75 && lead.phone) return "whatsapp_assisted";
  if (lead.score >= 75 && lead.email) return "email";
  if (lead.score >= 55 && lead.phone && lead.needsManualReview === false) return "whatsapp_assisted";
  if (lead.score >= 55 && lead.email) return "email";
  return "hold";
}

Default:

A leads: contact
B leads: review/contact selectively
C leads: hold
Rejected: no contact
2.17 Website/menu detection rules

For leads with websites, run a lightweight website checker.

Do not scrape entire sites deeply. Just inspect common paths and homepage links.

Check:

/
 /menu
 /menus
 /our-menu
 /food-menu
 /restaurant-menu
 /downloads
 /contact

Detect:

menu page exists
PDF menu exists
image menu exists
contact email exists
phone exists
WhatsApp link exists
Instagram link exists
site loads slowly or fails

Use this only for scoring.

Website menu status
TypeScript
type WebsiteMenuStatus =
  | "no_website"
  | "website_down"
  | "no_menu_found"
  | "menu_pdf"
  | "menu_image"
  | "menu_page_found"
  | "clean_mobile_menu"
  | "unknown";

Scoring:

no_website: +10 menu gap
website_down: +12 menu gap
no_menu_found: +10 menu gap
menu_pdf: +8 menu gap
menu_image: +8 menu gap
menu_page_found: +3 menu gap
clean_mobile_menu: +0 menu gap
unknown: +5 menu gap

This avoids the dumb rule:

has website = bad lead

That rule is wrong. The real question is:

does the business have a clean, current, shareable menu link?
2.18 Deduplication logic

Deduping matters because repeated outreach to the same business damages trust.

Use layered dedupe.

Strong duplicate signals
same phone
same email
same website
same Google Maps URL/source URL
same MenuList business ID

Auto-merge or reject duplicate.

Medium duplicate signals
same normalized name + same area
same normalized name + same address
similar name + close coordinates

Manual review.

Weak duplicate signals
similar name only
same chain name in different areas
same category/address area but no phone match

Do not auto-merge.

Normalized key

Generate:

TypeScript
function createLeadKey(input: {
  businessName: string;
  area?: string;
  city: string;
  phone?: string;
  website?: string;
}) {
  if (input.phone) return `phone:${normalizePhone(input.phone)}`;
  if (input.website) return `website:${normalizeDomain(input.website)}`;

  return `name_area:${slugify(input.businessName)}:${slugify(input.area || "")}:${slugify(input.city)}`;
}

Phone and website should dominate name matching.

2.19 Chain/franchise detection

Do not overbuild this, but add simple rules.

Signals:

same name appears in many areas
brand terms like "outlet", "branch", "franchise"
large known brand list
website domain indicates corporate chain
many locations from same name

Classification:

TypeScript
type BusinessScale =
  | "single_location"
  | "small_local_chain"
  | "large_chain"
  | "unknown";

Scoring:

single_location: +5 conversion ease
small_local_chain: +3 conversion ease, maybe high value
large_chain: -10 risk / manual review
unknown: 0

Local 2–5 outlet chains can be valuable later. But for the first campaign, single-location businesses are cleaner.

2.20 The qualification object

Store score explanation, not just score.

TypeScript
type LeadQualification = {
  leadId: string;

  hardReject: {
    rejected: boolean;
    reasons: string[];
  };

  scores: {
    fit: number;
    reachability: number;
    menuGap: number;
    demand: number;
    conversionEase: number;
    riskPenalty: number;
    total: number;
  };

  detectedSignals: {
    foodBusiness: boolean;
    targetArea: boolean;
    hasPhone: boolean;
    hasEmail: boolean;
    hasWebsite: boolean;
    websiteMenuStatus: WebsiteMenuStatus;
    likelyLocalSMB: boolean;
    possibleChain: boolean;
    possibleDuplicate: boolean;
    possiblyClosed: boolean;
  };

  segment: "A" | "B" | "C" | "REJECT";
  recommendedAction:
    | "contact_whatsapp"
    | "contact_email"
    | "manual_review"
    | "enrich_contact"
    | "hold"
    | "reject";

  explanation: string[];
  createdAt: Date;
};

This is useful in the admin UI. You need to see why a lead is scored high.

2.21 Example scoring
Example 1 — Strong lead
Business: Local cafe in Koramangala
Phone: yes
Email: no
Website: no
Category: cafe
Area: target
Review count: moderate/high
Chain: no

Score:

Fit: 20
Reachability: 15
Menu Gap: 20
Demand: 10
Conversion Ease: 12
Risk Penalty: 0

Total: 77
Segment: A
Action: WhatsApp assisted send

This is the ideal first-batch lead.

Example 2 — Website exists but menu weak
Business: Bakery in Indiranagar
Phone: yes
Website: yes
Menu: PDF/image only
Category: bakery
Local SMB: yes

Score:

Fit: 20
Reachability: 20
Menu Gap: 13
Demand: 8
Conversion Ease: 12
Risk Penalty: 0

Total: 73
Segment: B / near A
Action: contact if batch needs volume

This is still a good MenuList lead. Website does not kill it.

Example 3 — Large chain
Business: National pizza chain branch
Phone: yes
Website: yes
Menu: clean website/app
Category: restaurant

Score:

Fit: 20
Reachability: 15
Menu Gap: 0
Demand: 15
Conversion Ease: 2
Risk Penalty: 20

Total: 32
Segment: Reject / hold
Action: do not contact in v0

High demand, low conversion. Not useful now.

Example 4 — No contact
Business: Small food stall
Phone: no
Email: no
Website: no
Category: food
Area: target

Result:

Hard reject: no contact path

Even if it needs MenuList, you cannot reach them efficiently.

2.22 First campaign thresholds

For the first Bangalore test, use strict thresholds.

Raw imported: 500–1,000
Reject aggressively
Contact only:
- A leads score >= 75
- selected B leads score >= 65 if they have phone

Initial targets:

Qualified rate: 20–35%
Contactable rate: 40%+
A-lead rate: 10–20%
Manual review queue: max 100
Contacted first batch: 50–100

If you import 1,000 raw leads and only 20 are A leads, your source/query is too broad or your categories are wrong.

If you import 1,000 raw leads and 800 are A leads, your scoring is too loose.

2.23 Recommended qualification defaults for v0

Use these exact defaults initially:

Hard reject:
- wrong vertical
- outside target area
- permanently closed
- no phone and no email after enrichment
- duplicate
- large chain with clean menu

Score thresholds:

A: 75+
B: 55–74
C: 35–54
Reject: <35

Contact rules:

A + phone → WhatsApp assisted
A + email → email
B + phone + no manual concern → WhatsApp assisted
B + email → email
C → hold
Reject → no contact

Enrichment rules:

Only enrich if preliminary score >= 60
Only enrich if website exists
Only enrich if phone/email missing
Do not enrich rejected leads

Preview rules:

No AI preview during qualification.
No AI preview before outreach.
AI preview only after reply/click/high-value manual selection.
2.24 Admin filters needed

The lead dashboard should support these filters:

city
area
category
score range
segment A/B/C
has phone
has email
has website
website menu status
possible chain
possible duplicate
status
source run
contact decision

Default view:

Qualified A leads with phone, not contacted, sorted by score desc

That is the operator’s daily work queue.

2.25 Stage 2 final spec

The qualification engine should do this:

1. Import raw leads from Apify/manual CSV.
2. Normalize fields.
3. Deduplicate against leads and existing MenuList businesses.
4. Reject wrong, unreachable, closed, duplicate, and poor-fit leads.
5. Score remaining leads from 0–100.
6. Segment into A/B/C/Reject.
7. Recommend outreach channel.
8. Store score explanation for operator review.

The most important strategic rule:

Prioritize businesses with menu friction, not just businesses without websites.

The best v0 lead is:

local restaurant/cafe
single-location or small SMB
phone available
no clean menu link
no strong website menu
in target area
likely owner-reachable

That is who MenuList should contact first.
````

````text
Stage 3 — Minimal Lead Database and Schema

Goal of this stage:

Create the smallest database model needed to:
1. import leads,
2. dedupe them,
3. score them,
4. contact them,
5. track replies,
6. collect menus,
7. connect converted leads to existing MenuList menu/business records.

This should live inside the existing MenuList app/admin. Do not create a separate CRM.

3.1 Core database decision

Use existing MenuList storage. If you are already on Firebase/Firestore, use Firestore collections.

Firestore is suitable for this because it is document-oriented, stores data as documents inside collections, and is optimized for large collections of small documents. That matches lead records well. Keep each lead document small because Firestore documents have a 1 MiB size limit.
Firebase
+1

Core rule:

Lead Engine data should reference MenuList data.
It should not duplicate MenuList product data.

Example:

Lead has menuList.businessId
Lead has menuList.menuId
Lead has menuList.menuUrl

But the actual menu remains in the existing MenuList menu system.

3.2 Collections we need

Use only these collections for v0:

leadCampaigns
leadSourceRuns
leads
leadDedupeKeys
leadOutreachEvents
leadOnboardingLinks
leadSuppressions
leadRawItems   optional, TTL/debug only

That is enough.

Do not add:

deals
pipelines
salesStages
organizations
contacts
tasks
notes as separate CRM module
previewPages
AIAssets
proposalRecords

This is not HubSpot. It is a lead intake machine.

3.3 Collection overview
Required
Collection	Purpose
leadCampaigns	Defines a campaign: city, areas, categories, source, caps
leadSourceRuns	Tracks each Apify/import run
leads	Main lead record
leadDedupeKeys	Prevents duplicate leads and duplicate outreach
leadOutreachEvents	Tracks WhatsApp/email/open/click/reply/manual events
leadOnboardingLinks	Tracks /start/{token} links
leadSuppressions	Do-not-contact and global suppression list
Optional
Collection	Purpose
leadRawItems	Temporary raw Apify/debug payloads, deleted later

Use TTL for leadRawItems. Firestore TTL policies can automatically delete stale documents based on an expiration field, typically within 24 hours after expiry, though TTL deletes are billable document deletes.
Firebase

3.4 Main principle: lead document stays small

The leads document should contain only current operational state.

Do not put full Apify payloads, reviews, photos, menus, or long scrape results inside the lead document.

Good:

business name
phone
email
website
score
status
campaignId
sourceRunId
onboarding link
MenuList menu ID
last contacted time

Bad:

all Google reviews
all photos
full website HTML
raw Apify JSON
generated AI page HTML
large menu extraction payload

Firestore documents support nested objects, but they are still lightweight records and have size/depth/index limits. Keep nested maps shallow and predictable.
Firebase
+1

3.5 leadCampaigns

A campaign defines a batch.

Example:

Bangalore Cafes — Koramangala, Indiranagar, HSR, Jayanagar

Schema:

TypeScript
type LeadCampaign = {
  id: string;

  name: string;

  status:
    | "draft"
    | "active"
    | "paused"
    | "completed"
    | "archived";

  target: {
    country: "IN";
    city: string;
    areas: string[];
    categories: string[];
    keywords: string[];
  };

  source: {
    provider: "apify" | "outscraper" | "manual_csv";
    actorId?: string;
    sourceType: "google_maps" | "manual_import" | "website_enrichment";
  };

  caps: {
    maxRawLeads: number;
    maxResultsPerQuery: number;
    maxQualifiedLeads: number;
    maxContactedPerDay: number;
    maxEnrichedLeads: number;
    maxAiPreviews: number; // default 0
  };

  filters: {
    minScoreToContact: number; // default 75
    minScoreForManualReview: number; // default 55
    requirePhoneOrEmail: boolean;
    excludeLargeChains: boolean;
    excludeClosedBusinesses: boolean;
  };

  stats: {
    rawImported: number;
    duplicates: number;
    rejected: number;
    qualified: number;
    readyToContact: number;
    contacted: number;
    replied: number;
    menuReceived: number;
    menuLinksCreated: number;
    converted: number;
  };

  cost: {
    estimatedSourceCostUsd?: number;
    actualSourceCostUsd?: number;
    costPerQualifiedLeadUsd?: number;
    costPerMenuReceivedUsd?: number;
    costPerMenuLinkCreatedUsd?: number;
  };

  createdBy: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
};

Recommended defaults:

TypeScript
const defaultCampaignCaps = {
  maxRawLeads: 1000,
  maxResultsPerQuery: 50,
  maxQualifiedLeads: 250,
  maxContactedPerDay: 100,
  maxEnrichedLeads: 150,
  maxAiPreviews: 0,
};

Important:

maxAiPreviews = 0 by default.

Preview generation should not happen unless we explicitly run an experiment.

3.6 leadSourceRuns

Every Apify run or CSV import creates one source-run record.

This lets you measure source quality.

Schema:

TypeScript
type LeadSourceRun = {
  id: string;

  campaignId: string;

  provider: "apify" | "outscraper" | "manual_csv";
  sourceType: "google_maps" | "website_enrichment" | "manual_import";

  status:
    | "queued"
    | "running"
    | "completed"
    | "failed"
    | "cancelled";

  apify?: {
    actorId: string;
    runId?: string;
    datasetId?: string;
    input?: Record<string, unknown>;
  };

  manualCsv?: {
    fileName: string;
    uploadedBy: string;
    rowCount: number;
  };

  input: {
    city?: string;
    areas?: string[];
    categories?: string[];
    queries?: string[];
    maxResultsPerQuery?: number;
  };

  results: {
    rawImported: number;
    normalized: number;
    duplicates: number;
    rejected: number;
    qualified: number;
    contactable: number;
    errors: number;
  };

  cost: {
    estimatedUsd?: number;
    actualUsd?: number;
    currency: "USD" | "INR";
  };

  error?: {
    code: string;
    message: string;
  };

  startedAt?: Date;
  completedAt?: Date;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
};

Decision:

Source runs measure source quality.
Leads measure business-level acquisition.
Keep them separate.

3.8 leadDedupeKeys

This is the most important anti-noise collection.

Purpose:

Prevent duplicate lead creation.
Prevent duplicate outreach.
Map every normalized phone/domain/source/name-area key to one canonical lead.

Document ID:

sha256(dedupeKey)

Example raw dedupe keys:

phone:+919876543210
email:owner@example.com
domain:abccafe.com
maps:place-url-hash
name_area_city:abc-cafe:koramangala:bangalore

Schema:

TypeScript
type LeadDedupeKey = {
  id: string; // sha256(key)
  key: string;

  leadId: string;
  campaignIds: string[];

  keyType:
    | "phone"
    | "email"
    | "domain"
    | "maps_url"
    | "name_area_city";

  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
};

Import logic:

For each imported lead:
1. Generate dedupe keys.
2. Check if any key exists in leadDedupeKeys.
3. If yes, attach sourceRunId to existing lead or mark duplicate.
4. If no, create lead and create dedupe-key docs.

Use transaction/batch write so the lead and dedupe keys are created together.

This is what stops the system from messaging the same restaurant three times because it appeared under “cafe,” “restaurant,” and “bakery.”

3.9 Dedupe key generation

Use deterministic normalization.

TypeScript
type DedupeInput = {
  businessName: string;
  city: string;
  area?: string;
  phone?: string;
  email?: string;
  website?: string;
  mapsUrl?: string;
};

function generateDedupeKeys(input: DedupeInput): string[] {
  const keys: string[] = [];

  if (input.phone) {
    keys.push(`phone:${normalizePhone(input.phone)}`);
  }

  if (input.email) {
    keys.push(`email:${normalizeEmail(input.email)}`);
  }

  if (input.website) {
    keys.push(`domain:${normalizeDomain(input.website)}`);
  }

  if (input.mapsUrl) {
    keys.push(`maps:${stableHash(input.mapsUrl)}`);
  }

  keys.push(
    `name_area_city:${slugify(input.businessName)}:${slugify(input.area || "")}:${slugify(input.city)}`
  );

  return keys;
}

Priority:

phone > email > domain > mapsUrl > name_area_city

Do not rely on business name alone. Restaurant names are messy.

3.10 leadOutreachEvents

Do not put every event directly inside the lead document. Keep lead document as current state. Store event history separately.

Schema:

TypeScript
type LeadOutreachEvent = {
  id: string;

  leadId: string;
  campaignId: string;

  type:
    | "whatsapp_opened"
    | "whatsapp_sent_manual"
    | "email_sent"

    | "email_opened"
    | "email_clicked"

3.11 leadOnboardingLinks

This powers the cheap link strategy:

menulist.com/start/{token}

This is not an AI preview. It is a lightweight upload/start page.

Do not expose leadId directly in the URL. Use a random token.

Schema:

TypeScript
type LeadOnboardingLink = {
  id: string; // random ID or token hash

  leadId: string;
  campaignId: string;

  tokenHash: string;

  status:
    | "active"

};

Recommended URL:

/start/{token}

When owner opens it:

1. Server hashes token.
2. Looks up leadOnboardingLinks by tokenHash.
3. Loads minimal lead display data.
4. Shows upload/send-menu flow.
5. Increments click count.

The public page should show:

Create MenuList link for {Business Name}
Upload menu photo/PDF
Confirm WhatsApp number
Get menu link + QR

No scraped data. No fake preview.

3.12 leadSuppressions

This collection prevents future mistakes.

Purpose:

Do-not-contact list across all campaigns.

Suppression keys:

phone:+919876543210
email:owner@example.com
domain:brand.com
lead:{leadId}

Schema:

TypeScript
type LeadSuppression = {
  id: string; // sha256(suppressionKey)

  key: string;

  keyType:
    | "phone"
    | "email"
    | "domain"
    | "lead"
    | "business";

  reason:
    | "do_not_contact"
    | "not_interested"
    | "wrong_business"
    | "complaint"
    | "duplicate"
    | "converted"
    | "manual_block";

  leadId?: string;
  businessId?: string;

  notes?: string;

  createdBy: "system" | "operator";
  createdAt: Date;
};

Before any outreach, check suppression keys.

If a lead is do_not_contact, create suppressions for:

phone
email
domain
leadId

This is non-negotiable.

3.13 Optional leadRawItems

Use only for debugging imports.

Do not store these forever.

Schema:

TypeScript
type LeadRawItem = {
  id: string;

  sourceRunId: string;
  campaignId: string;

  provider: "apify" | "outscraper" | "manual_csv";

  raw: Record<string, unknown>;

  normalizedLeadId?: string;
  importStatus:
    | "pending"
    | "imported"
    | "duplicate"
    | "rejected"
    | "error";

  error?: {
    code: string;
    message: string;
  };

  expiresAt: Date; // TTL field

  createdAt: Date;
};

Retention:

7–30 days

Reason:

Enough time to debug import quality.
Not long enough to become a copied third-party database.

Use Firestore TTL on expiresAt for this collection.

3.14 Status transition map

Allowed transitions:

raw_imported
→ normalized
→ duplicate / rejected / scored

scored
→ qualified / rejected

qualified
→ ready_to_contact / hold

ready_to_contact
→ contacted_whatsapp / contacted_email

contacted_whatsapp
→ replied / not_interested / do_not_contact / follow_up_due

contacted_email
→ replied / not_interested / do_not_contact / follow_up_due

replied
→ menu_requested / menu_received / not_interested

menu_requested
→ menu_received

menu_received
→ menulist_link_created

menulist_link_created
→ menulist_link_sent

menulist_link_sent
→ converted

Do not allow:

do_not_contact → ready_to_contact
converted → contacted
rejected → contacted
duplicate → contacted

Unless manually reopened by admin.

Use a helper:

TypeScript
const allowedTransitions: Record<Lead["status"], Lead["status"][]> = {
  raw_imported: ["normalized", "duplicate", "rejected"],
  normalized: ["scored", "duplicate", "rejected"],
  duplicate: [],
  rejected: [],
  scored: ["qualified", "rejected"],
  qualified: ["ready_to_contact", "rejected"],
  ready_to_contact: ["contacted_whatsapp", "contacted_email", "rejected"],
  contacted_whatsapp: ["contacted", "replied", "not_interested", "do_not_contact"],
  contacted_email: ["contacted", "replied", "not_interested", "do_not_contact"],
  contacted: ["replied", "not_interested", "do_not_contact"],
  replied: ["menu_requested", "menu_received", "not_interested", "do_not_contact"],
  menu_requested: ["menu_received", "not_interested", "do_not_contact"],
  menu_received: ["menulist_link_created"],
  menulist_link_created: ["menulist_link_sent"],
  menulist_link_sent: ["converted"],
  converted: [],
  not_interested: [],
  do_not_contact: [],
};

This protects data quality.

3.15 Lead ID strategy

Use random Firestore document IDs for leads.

Do not use phone number or business name as document ID.

Why:

phone can change
business names collide
document IDs should not leak personal/contact data
dedupe keys handle uniqueness separately

Pattern:

leads/{autoId}
leadDedupeKeys/{sha256(key)}
leadOnboardingLinks/{randomId}
3.16 Minimal admin query requirements

The admin dashboard needs only a few fast queries.

Default work queue
A leads
ready to contact
phone exists
not contacted
sorted by score descending

Query shape:

TypeScript
where("status", "==", "ready_to_contact")
where("segment", "==", "A")
where("contact.hasPhone", "==", true)
orderBy("qualification.scores.total", "desc")
limit(50)
Email queue
TypeScript
where("status", "==", "ready_to_contact")
where("contact.hasEmail", "==", true)
orderBy("qualification.scores.total", "desc")
limit(100)
Follow-up queue
TypeScript
where("outreach.nextFollowUpAt", "<=", now)
where("status", "in", ["contacted_whatsapp", "contacted_email", "contacted"])
orderBy("outreach.nextFollowUpAt", "asc")
limit(100)
Campaign dashboard
TypeScript
where("campaignId", "==", campaignId)
orderBy("qualification.scores.total", "desc")
limit(100)
Duplicate review
TypeScript
where("qualification.detectedSignals.possibleDuplicate", "==", true)
where("status", "==", "normalized")
limit(100)

Use cursor-based pagination for admin lists rather than loading thousands of leads at once. Firestore supports query cursors such as startAt() and startAfter() for paginated reads.
Firebase

3.17 Indexes to create

Create indexes only for real dashboard queries.

Recommended composite indexes:

leads:
- status ASC, segment ASC, contact.hasPhone ASC, qualification.scores.total DESC
- status ASC, contact.hasEmail ASC, qualification.scores.total DESC
- campaignId ASC, status ASC, qualification.scores.total DESC
- outreach.nextFollowUpAt ASC, status ASC
- campaignId ASC, segment ASC, qualification.scores.total DESC
- qualification.detectedSignals.possibleDuplicate ASC, status ASC

leadOutreachEvents:
- leadId ASC, createdAt DESC
- campaignId ASC, createdAt DESC

leadSourceRuns:
- campaignId ASC, createdAt DESC
- status ASC, createdAt DESC

Do not index large raw payload fields.

If using Firestore, be conscious that indexes are not free from a complexity standpoint: Firestore has limits on index counts and index entries per document, and oversized indexed field values can be truncated. Keep query fields explicit and avoid indexing unnecessary raw/source fields.
Firebase

3.18 What gets copied into existing MenuList product data

Only after owner sends or confirms the menu.

Flow:

lead.menu_received
→ existing MenuList menu creation flow
→ create/update MenuList business
→ create menu
→ generate public menu URL
→ generate QR
→ write references back to lead

Lead document update:

TypeScript
menuList: {
  businessId: "mlbiz_123",
  menuId: "menu_456",
  menuUrl: "https://menulist.com/...",
  qrUrl: "https://menulist.com/...",
  createdAt: new Date(),
  sentAt: undefined
}

Then status:

menu_received → menulist_link_created

After sending:

menulist_link_created → menulist_link_sent

After owner acknowledges/uses it:

menulist_link_sent → converted
3.19 Normalization rules

Normalize before scoring/deduping.

Phone
TypeScript
normalizePhone("+91 98765 43210") => "+919876543210"

Rules:

strip spaces
strip hyphens
convert India local 10-digit numbers to +91
reject obviously invalid numbers
Email
TypeScript
normalizeEmail(" Owner@Cafe.com ") => "owner@cafe.com"

Rules:

lowercase
trim
basic validation
Domain
TypeScript
normalizeDomain("https://www.abccafe.com/menu") => "abccafe.com"

Rules:

remove protocol
remove www
remove path
lowercase
Business name
TypeScript
normalizeName("ABC Café & Restaurant!") => "abc cafe restaurant"

Rules:

lowercase
remove punctuation
normalize accents where possible
remove repeated whitespace
Area/city
TypeScript
normalizeArea("HSR Layout") => "hsr-layout"
normalizeCity("Bengaluru") => "bangalore"

Use one canonical city spelling internally.

3.20 Minimal TypeScript module structure

Inside existing MenuList codebase:

/lib/lead-engine
  types.ts
  normalize.ts
  dedupe.ts
  score.ts
  status.ts
  source-runs.ts
  outreach.ts
  onboarding.ts
  menulist-link.ts

Admin routes:

/admin/leads
/admin/leads/[leadId]
/admin/leads/campaigns
/admin/leads/import
/start/[token]

Do not create a separate app unless the existing MenuList admin is already too messy.

3.23 Security posture

Keep lead data admin-only.

Rules:

Public users cannot read leads.
Owners cannot directly read lead records.
The /start/{token} page should use a server route to fetch only safe display data.
Operators/admins can access the lead dashboard.

The public onboarding page should expose only:

business name
city/area
upload/start flow

It should not expose:

source data
score
Google Maps URL
internal notes
campaign details
other leads

This protects the system from becoming a public scraped directory.

3.24 What to avoid in Stage 3

Do not add these yet:

multi-user sales assignments
complex task management
deal value
pipeline forecasting
AI preview records
proposal records
call recordings
full message inbox
review import
photo import
restaurant profile pages for unclaimed leads

Add only when the operating process proves the need.

The v0 dashboard can be simple:

Lead list
Lead detail
Campaign list
Import run list
One-click WhatsApp
Send email
Mark menu received
Create MenuList link

That is enough.

3.25 Stage 3 final schema

Minimum viable database:

leadCampaigns
leadSourceRuns
leads
leadDedupeKeys
leadOutreachEvents
leadOnboardingLinks
leadSuppressions
leadRawItems optional with TTL

Core relationships:

leadCampaigns/{campaignId}
  ↓
leadSourceRuns/{sourceRunId}
  ↓
leads/{leadId}
  ↓
leadOnboardingLinks/{linkId}
  ↓
existing MenuList business/menu records

Anti-duplicate structure:

leadDedupeKeys/{sha256(phone/domain/email/maps/name_area_city)}
  → leadId

Conversion structure:

leads/{leadId}.menuList.businessId
leads/{leadId}.menuList.menuId
leads/{leadId}.menuList.menuUrl
leads/{leadId}.menuList.qrUrl

This is the correct level of system: enough to run acquisition seriously, not enough to become a bloated parallel product.
````

````text
Stage 4 — Apify Ingestion Pipeline

Goal of this stage:

Run Apify campaigns
→ import raw business candidates
→ normalize them
→ dedupe them
→ score them
→ store qualified leads in MenuList admin

This stage should be boring and reliable. No AI preview generation. No outreach yet. No menu generation yet.

4.1 Core decision

Use this pattern:

MenuList controls the campaign.
Apify runs the scrape.
MenuList imports the result.
MenuList dedupes and scores.

Do not let Apify become the source of truth. Apify is just a lead collection worker.

The official Apify JavaScript client supports Actors, runs, datasets, key-value stores, request queues, webhooks, and related platform resources, and its basic flow is: call an Actor, then fetch items from the run’s default dataset.
Apify Documentation

4.2 High-level ingestion flow
Admin clicks “Run Campaign”
→ MenuList creates leadSourceRun
→ MenuList builds Apify input
→ MenuList starts Apify Actor
→ Apify runs Google Maps scraper
→ Apify webhook calls MenuList when run succeeds/fails
→ MenuList fetches dataset items
→ MenuList normalizes each item
→ MenuList dedupes against existing leads
→ MenuList scores each lead
→ MenuList stores qualified/rejected/duplicate leads
→ MenuList updates campaign stats

This is the full pipeline.

4.3 Synchronous vs asynchronous Apify runs

Use asynchronous runs for real campaigns.

Apify’s own API guidance says synchronous runs are suitable when a run typically finishes within 5 minutes; longer jobs should use the asynchronous flow: run the Actor, wait for completion, then collect the data. It also lists webhooks and polling as ways to wait for the run to finish.
Apify Documentation

For MenuList:

Tiny local test: synchronous is okay.
Real campaign: asynchronous + webhook.

Why:

Google Maps scraping can take longer than expected.
You do not want a Next.js request waiting for the scrape.
You need cost tracking, retry logic, and partial failure handling.
4.4 First campaign run structure

Do one Apify run per area, not one run per keyword.

Example campaign:

City: Bangalore
Areas:
- Koramangala
- Indiranagar
- HSR Layout
- Jayanagar

Search terms:
- cafe
- restaurant
- bakery
- dessert shop
- cloud kitchen

This becomes:

Run 1: locationQuery = "Koramangala, Bangalore, India"
       searchStringsArray = ["cafe", "restaurant", "bakery", "dessert shop", "cloud kitchen"]

Run 2: locationQuery = "Indiranagar, Bangalore, India"
       searchStringsArray = ["cafe", "restaurant", "bakery", "dessert shop", "cloud kitchen"]

Run 3: HSR Layout
Run 4: Jayanagar

Apify’s Google Maps Scraper input supports searchStringsArray, locationQuery, and maxCrawledPlacesPerSearch; its docs also note that locationQuery is one location per run.
Apify

This keeps the system clean:

campaign = one acquisition batch
sourceRun = one area-level Apify run
lead = one imported business
4.5 Recommended Apify input for v0

Use conservative settings.

TypeScript
const apifyInput = {
  searchStringsArray: [
    "cafe",
    "restaurant",
    "bakery",
    "dessert shop",
    "cloud kitchen",
  ],

  locationQuery: "Koramangala, Bangalore, India",

  maxCrawledPlacesPerSearch: 50,

  language: "en",

  website: "allPlaces",

  skipClosedPlaces: true,

  scrapePlaceDetailPage: false,

  includeWebResults: false,

  maximumLeadsEnrichmentRecords: 0,
};

Important choices:

website = allPlaces

Because “has website” does not mean “has clean menu.” Some restaurants have websites but still need MenuList.

maximumLeadsEnrichmentRecords = 0

Because contact enrichment can multiply cost. Apify’s input docs say this setting enriches results with contact/company/person-level data, defaults to 0, and warns that requesting multiple leads per place can multiply total leads attempted.
Apify

scrapePlaceDetailPage = false

Because v0 does not need rich place details, reviews, popular times, owner updates, questions, or reservation/order widgets. The input docs say enabling detail-page scraping slows the actor and unlocks extra fields such as review distributions, popular times, opening hours, owner updates, and related data.
Apify

For v0, we need:

name
category
phone
website
address/area
maps URL
closed/open signal
rating/review count if available

We do not need:

reviews
photos
popular times
owner updates
questions and answers
order widgets
reservation widgets
4.6 Why not use withoutWebsite only?

Apify supports filtering places by website status with options like allPlaces, withWebsite, and withoutWebsite.
Apify

Do not start with withoutWebsite.

Use:

website = allPlaces

Reason:

MenuList is not selling websites.
MenuList is acquiring digital menu links.

A restaurant with a website can still be a strong lead if:

menu is missing
menu is PDF-only
menu is image-only
menu is hard to open on mobile
menu is not shareable on WhatsApp
menu is not QR-friendly

Later, you can run an experiment:

Campaign A: allPlaces
Campaign B: withoutWebsite

Then compare:

menu received rate
reply rate
cost per MenuList link created

Do not assume no-website leads are the best leads.

4.7 Collections touched in Stage 4

Stage 4 writes to:

leadCampaigns
leadSourceRuns
leads
leadDedupeKeys
leadRawItems optional
leadOutreachEvents optional only for system events

It should not write to:

MenuList business records
MenuList menus
outreach messages
AI preview records

MenuList business/menu records should be created only after the owner sends or confirms the menu.

4.8 Source run lifecycle

Each Apify area run gets one leadSourceRuns document.

TypeScript
type LeadSourceRunStatus =
  | "queued"
  | "starting"
  | "running"
  | "succeeded"
  | "failed"
  | "importing"
  | "imported"
  | "partially_imported"
  | "cancelled";

Lifecycle:

queued
→ starting
→ running
→ succeeded
→ importing
→ imported

Failure lifecycle:

queued
→ starting
→ running
→ failed

Partial lifecycle:

succeeded
→ importing
→ partially_imported

4.10 Backend functions needed

Keep the function surface small.

startLeadCampaign(campaignId)
startApifySourceRun(sourceRunId)
handleApifyWebhook(request)
importApifyDataset(sourceRunId)
normalizeApifyItem(item)
upsertLeadFromImportedItem(importedLead)
scoreLead(lead)
updateCampaignStats(campaignId)

That is enough.

Do not build:

generic provider orchestration
multi-provider bidding
AI enrichment
automatic outreach
public page creation
4.11 Start campaign function

Admin clicks:

Run Campaign

MenuList does:

1. Load campaign.
2. Validate caps.
3. Generate one sourceRun per area.
4. Start Apify run for each area.
5. Store actor run IDs.

Pseudo-code:

TypeScript
async function startLeadCampaign(campaignId: string) {
  const campaign = await getCampaign(campaignId);

  assertCampaignCanRun(campaign);

  for (const area of campaign.target.areas) {
    const sourceRun = await createLeadSourceRun({
      campaignId,
      provider: "apify",
      actorId: campaign.source.actorId,
      input: buildAreaInput(campaign, area),
      status: "queued",
    });

    await startApifySourceRun(sourceRun.id);
  }
}
4.12 Build Apify input
TypeScript
function buildAreaInput(campaign: LeadCampaign, area: string) {
  return {
    searchStringsArray: campaign.target.categories,

    locationQuery: `${area}, ${campaign.target.city}, India`,

    maxCrawledPlacesPerSearch: campaign.caps.maxResultsPerQuery,

    language: "en",

    website: "allPlaces",

    skipClosedPlaces: true,

    scrapePlaceDetailPage: false,

    includeWebResults: false,

    maximumLeadsEnrichmentRecords: 0,
  };
}

Do not let operators manually enter raw Apify JSON in v0.

The UI should expose only:

city
areas
categories
max results per search

The backend should produce the Apify input.

4.13 Start Apify source run

Use Apify from server-side code only.

TypeScript
import { ApifyClient } from "apify-client";

const client = new ApifyClient({
  token: process.env.APIFY_TOKEN!,
});

async function startApifySourceRun(sourceRunId: string) {
  const sourceRun = await getSourceRun(sourceRunId);

  await updateSourceRun(sourceRunId, {
    status: "starting",
    updatedAt: new Date(),
  });

  const run = await client
    .actor(sourceRun.actorId)
    .start(sourceRun.input.rawApifyInput);

  await updateSourceRun(sourceRunId, {
    status: "running",
    apify: {
      runId: run.id,
      defaultDatasetId: run.defaultDatasetId,
      status: run.status,
      startedAt: new Date(),
    },
    updatedAt: new Date(),
  });
}

Do not expose APIFY_TOKEN to the browser. Keep it in server environment variables or secret storage.

4.14 Webhook handling

Configure Apify webhook events for:

ACTOR.RUN.SUCCEEDED
ACTOR.RUN.FAILED
ACTOR.RUN.ABORTED
ACTOR.RUN.TIMED_OUT

Apify’s webhook docs list those Actor run events and show that Actor run webhooks include actorId, actorTaskId, and actorRunId; they also show that dataset items can be fetched using the actorRunId.
Apify Documentation

Webhook endpoint:

POST /api/internal/apify/webhook

Webhook flow:

1. Validate shared secret.
2. Parse actorRunId and event type.
3. Find leadSourceRun by apify.runId.
4. Idempotency check.
5. Update sourceRun status.
6. If succeeded, enqueue/import dataset.
7. If failed/aborted/timed out, mark failed.
8. Return 200 quickly.

Pseudo-code:

TypeScript
async function handleApifyWebhook(req: Request) {
  validateWebhookSecret(req);

  const body = await req.json();

  const actorRunId = body.eventData?.actorRunId;
  const eventType = body.eventType;

  const sourceRun = await findSourceRunByApifyRunId(actorRunId);
  if (!sourceRun) return ok();

  if (await webhookAlreadyProcessed(actorRunId, eventType)) {
    return ok();
  }

  await markWebhookProcessed(actorRunId, eventType);

  if (eventType === "ACTOR.RUN.SUCCEEDED") {
    await updateSourceRun(sourceRun.id, { status: "succeeded" });
    await importApifyDataset(sourceRun.id);
  }

  if (
    eventType === "ACTOR.RUN.FAILED" ||
    eventType === "ACTOR.RUN.ABORTED" ||
    eventType === "ACTOR.RUN.TIMED_OUT"
  ) {
    await updateSourceRun(sourceRun.id, {
      status: "failed",
      error: {
        code: eventType,
        message: "Apify actor run did not complete successfully",
      },
    });
  }

  return ok();
}

For v0, importing directly after webhook is acceptable if dataset sizes are small. If imports get slow, put importApifyDataset(sourceRunId) behind a task queue. Firebase task queue functions support retry and rate-limiting configuration, which is useful once imports become larger.
Firebase

4.15 Polling fallback

Do not depend only on webhooks.

Add a simple admin/manual fallback:

Button: Sync Apify Status

And a scheduled fallback later:

Every 15–30 minutes:
find sourceRuns where status = running and updatedAt older than X
poll Apify run status
import if succeeded
mark failed if failed/timed out

Why:

webhook delivery can fail
your endpoint can be temporarily down
sourceRun state can become stale

Keep it simple. This is not a distributed systems project.

4.16 Dataset import

Apify stores Actor results in a default dataset, and their docs show fetching dataset items after an Actor call using client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems().
Apify Documentation

Import process:

1. Load sourceRun.
2. Ensure status is succeeded/importing.
3. Get datasetId.
4. Fetch items in pages.
5. Normalize each item.
6. Upsert lead with dedupe.
7. Score lead.
8. Update import stats.
9. Mark sourceRun imported/partially_imported.

Pseudo-code:

TypeScript
async function importApifyDataset(sourceRunId: string) {
  const sourceRun = await getSourceRun(sourceRunId);

  if (!sourceRun.apify.defaultDatasetId) {
    throw new Error("Missing defaultDatasetId");
  }

  await updateSourceRun(sourceRunId, { status: "importing" });

  let offset = 0;
  const limit = 100;
  let stats = createEmptyImportStats();

  while (true) {
    const { items } = await client
      .dataset(sourceRun.apify.defaultDatasetId)
      .listItems({ offset, limit, clean: true });

    if (!items.length) break;

    for (const item of items) {
      const result = await importOneApifyItem({
        sourceRun,
        rawItem: item,
      });

      stats = incrementStats(stats, result);
    }

    offset += items.length;

    if (offset >= sourceRun.campaignCaps?.maxRawLeadsPerRun) {
      break;
    }
  }

  await updateSourceRun(sourceRunId, {
    status: stats.errors > 0 ? "partially_imported" : "imported",
    importStats: stats,
    updatedAt: new Date(),
  });

  await updateCampaignStats(sourceRun.campaignId);
}

Use page size 100–250. Do not load thousands of items into memory at once.

4.17 Raw item storage

Default:

Do not store full raw Apify items permanently.

For debugging, store raw items temporarily in leadRawItems.

TypeScript
type LeadRawItem = {
  id: string;
  campaignId: string;
  sourceRunId: string;
  provider: "apify";
  raw: Record<string, unknown>;
  importStatus: "imported" | "duplicate" | "rejected" | "error";
  normalizedLeadId?: string;
  error?: {
    code: string;
    message: string;
  };
  expiresAt: Date;
  createdAt: Date;
};

Retention:

7 days for normal runs
30 days for debugging problematic runs

Do not store:

reviews
review text
reviewer details
photo URLs
large scraped content

Google Maps Platform terms prohibit scraping/exporting/storing/resharing Maps content outside the services, including examples such as copying and saving business names, addresses, Places information, and user reviews.
Google Cloud

Practical interpretation for MenuList:

Use Apify output to decide who to contact.
Do not build MenuList public pages from scraped Google content.
Do not keep rich scraped data longer than operationally needed.
4.18 Normalization adapter

Create a source-specific adapter.

/lib/lead-engine/sources/apify-google-maps.ts

Purpose:

Convert Apify item shape into MenuList ImportedLead shape.

Do not let Apify fields leak everywhere in the codebase.

TypeScript
type ImportedLead = {
  sourceProvider: "apify";
  sourceType: "google_maps";
  sourceRunId: string;

  businessName: string;
  category?: string;
  categories?: string[];

  city: string;
  area?: string;
  address?: string;

  phone?: string;
  email?: string;
  website?: string;
  mapsUrl?: string;

  isTemporarilyClosed?: boolean;
  isPermanentlyClosed?: boolean;

  rating?: number;
  reviewCount?: number;

  rawSourceUrl?: string;
};

Example adapter:

TypeScript
function normalizeApifyGoogleMapsItem(
  item: Record<string, any>,
  sourceRun: LeadSourceRun
): ImportedLead | null {
  const businessName =
    item.title ||
    item.name ||
    item.placeName ||
    item.businessName;

  if (!businessName) return null;

  const phone =
    item.phone ||
    item.phoneNumber ||
    item.contactPhone;

  const website =
    item.website ||
    item.url ||
    item.websiteUrl;

  const mapsUrl =
    item.url ||
    item.googleMapsUrl ||
    item.placeUrl;

  return {
    sourceProvider: "apify",
    sourceType: "google_maps",
    sourceRunId: sourceRun.id,

    businessName: String(businessName).trim(),

    category: item.categoryName || item.category || undefined,
    categories: item.categories || undefined,

    city: sourceRun.input.city,
    area: sourceRun.input.area,
    address: item.address || item.street || undefined,

    phone: phone ? String(phone) : undefined,
    website: website ? String(website) : undefined,
    mapsUrl: mapsUrl ? String(mapsUrl) : undefined,

    isTemporarilyClosed: Boolean(item.temporarilyClosed),
    isPermanentlyClosed: Boolean(item.permanentlyClosed),

    rating: typeof item.rating === "number" ? item.rating : undefined,
    reviewCount:
      typeof item.reviewsCount === "number"
        ? item.reviewsCount
        : typeof item.reviewCount === "number"
          ? item.reviewCount
          : undefined,

    rawSourceUrl: mapsUrl ? String(mapsUrl) : undefined,
  };
}

Field names can differ across actors, so the adapter should be tolerant.

4.19 Import one item
TypeScript
async function importOneApifyItem({
  sourceRun,
  rawItem,
}: {
  sourceRun: LeadSourceRun;
  rawItem: Record<string, unknown>;
}) {
  const imported = normalizeApifyGoogleMapsItem(rawItem, sourceRun);

  if (!imported) {
    return { type: "rejected", reason: "normalization_failed" };
  }

  const normalized = normalizeImportedLead(imported);

  const hardReject = getHardRejectReason(normalized);
  if (hardReject) {
    await maybeStoreRawDebugItem(sourceRun, rawItem, "rejected", hardReject);
    return { type: "rejected", reason: hardReject };
  }

  const dedupeResult = await upsertLeadWithDedupe({
    campaignId: sourceRun.campaignId,
    sourceRunId: sourceRun.id,
    importedLead: normalized,
  });

  if (dedupeResult.type === "duplicate") {
    return { type: "duplicate", leadId: dedupeResult.leadId };
  }

  const scoredLead = scoreLead(dedupeResult.lead);

  await saveLeadScore(scoredLead);

  return {
    type: scoredLead.segment === "REJECT" ? "rejected" : "created",
    leadId: scoredLead.id,
    segment: scoredLead.segment,
  };
}
4.20 Dedupe inside import

Dedupe must run before scoring.

Process:

1. Normalize phone, email, domain, name, area, city.
2. Generate dedupe keys.
3. Check leadSuppressions.
4. Check leadDedupeKeys.
5. If match exists, mark duplicate or attach sourceRunId to existing lead.
6. If no match, create lead and dedupe key records.

Use these keys:

phone:+919876543210
email:owner@example.com
domain:abccafe.com
maps:hash
name_area_city:abc-cafe:koramangala:bangalore

Strong keys:

phone
email
domain
maps URL

Weak key:

name + area + city

Do not use name alone.

4.21 Idempotency rules

The pipeline must be safe to rerun.

Idempotency keys:

sourceRun.apify.runId
webhook event: actorRunId + eventType
raw item key: sourceRunId + stableHash(businessName + phone + website + address)
dedupe key: phone/email/domain/maps/name_area_city

Why this matters:

Apify webhook can be retried.
Import can fail halfway.
Admin may click retry.
Dataset pagination may restart.

Rerunning import should not create duplicate leads.

4.22 Write strategy

For v0, individual writes are fine for 500–1,000 raw leads.

If you import larger batches, use bulk/batched writes carefully. Firestore’s own guidance says batched writes with hundreds of documents can hit transaction-size/index-update limits, and for large numbers of documents you should reduce batch size or use bulk/parallelized writes.
Firebase

Practical v0 rule:

Process one item at a time.
Use transactions only around dedupe key creation.
Do not prematurely optimize.

For dedupe creation, use a transaction:

read dedupe keys
if none exist:
  create lead
  create dedupe key docs
else:
  mark duplicate / update existing lead source history

Every source run should end with clear stats.

TypeScript
type ImportStats = {

If you only look at raw scraped count, you will fool yourself.

Webhook received but sourceRun missing

do not crash
Dataset item schema changed
normalization_failed
store raw debug item with TTL
increment error count
continue import
Too many duplicates
continue import

Too many errors
if errors > 20% of raw items:
  status = partially_imported
  show warning in admin
Budget cap hit
stop creating new sourceRuns
do not start more Apify runs

4.28 Source adapter interface

Define this now.

TypeScript
type SourceAdapter<TInput, TRawItem> = {
  provider: "apify" | "outscraper" | "manual_csv";
  sourceType: "google_maps" | "manual_import";

  buildInput: (campaign: LeadCampaign, area: string) => TInput;

  startRun: (params: {
    sourceRunId: string;
    input: TInput;
  }) => Promise<{
    providerRunId: string;
    datasetId?: string;
  }>;

  importDataset: (params: {
    sourceRun: LeadSourceRun;
  }) => Promise<ImportStats>;

  normalizeItem: (
    item: TRawItem,
    sourceRun: LeadSourceRun
  ) => ImportedLead | null;
};

Only one adapter in v0:

apifyGoogleMapsAdapter

But this interface prevents lock-in.

Build Stage 4 in this order:

Click:

Store:

defaultDatasetId

Step 3 — Manual import button

Do this before webhooks.

Step 4 — Add webhook

Once manual import works, add:

ACTOR.RUN.SUCCEEDED → auto import
ACTOR.RUN.FAILED → mark failed
Step 5 — Campaign-level batch run

Click:

Creates one sourceRun per area and starts each.

This order is important. Build control first, then automation.

4.31 What not to do in Stage 4

Do not:

send WhatsApp messages
send emails
generate AI previews
create MenuList business pages

scrape reviews/photos for public use

run unlimited Apify jobs
````
