````text
Stage 4 ends when leads are imported, deduped, scored, and visible in admin.

4.32 Stage 4 final spec

The ingestion pipeline should work like this:

Admin creates campaign
→ MenuList creates one Apify sourceRun per area
→ Apify runs Google Maps scrape with conservative settings
→ Apify webhook reports success/failure
→ MenuList imports dataset items page by page
→ source adapter normalizes each item
→ hard rejects bad leads
→ dedupe keys prevent duplicates
→ scoring segments leads into A/B/C/Reject
→ leads become visible in admin work queue
→ campaign/source-run stats update

Default v0 Apify settings:

TypeScript
{
  searchStringsArray: ["cafe", "restaurant", "bakery", "dessert shop", "cloud kitchen"],
  locationQuery: "{area}, {city}, India",
  maxCrawledPlacesPerSearch: 50,
  language: "en",
  website: "allPlaces",
  skipClosedPlaces: true,
  scrapePlaceDetailPage: false,
  includeWebResults: false,
  maximumLeadsEnrichmentRecords: 0
}

My hard recommendation:

Build manual import first.
Then add webhook automation.
Then add campaign-level batch runs.
Do not add outreach until ingestion quality is proven.

Next stage: Stage 5 — Internal lead dashboard.
````

````text
Stage 5 — Internal Lead Dashboard

Goal:

Give you/operator one clean place to review leads, contact them, collect menus, and move them into the existing MenuList flow.

This dashboard should be operational, not CRM-like.

It should answer:

Who should we contact today?
What should we send?
Did they reply?
Did we receive menu?
Did we create/send MenuList link?
What is the cost/conversion quality by campaign?
5.1 Core product decision

Build this inside the existing MenuList admin.

Do not create:

separate CRM
separate sales app
complex kanban pipeline
deal tracking
sales forecasting
AI preview dashboard

Create:

/admin/leads

The dashboard exists to move leads through this flow:

qualified lead
→ contacted
→ replied
→ menu received
→ MenuList link created
→ MenuList link sent
→ converted

That is all.

5.2 Primary user

Assume two user types only.

TypeScript
type LeadAdminRole = "admin" | "operator";
Admin

Can:

create campaigns
run Apify imports
change scoring thresholds
send outreach
mark statuses
delete/reject leads
manage suppressions
view cost/conversion metrics
Operator

Can:

review leads
send one-click WhatsApp/email
mark replies
upload received menu
create MenuList link through existing flow
add notes
mark do-not-contact

Do not add complicated permission layers yet.

5.3 Dashboard route map

Use these routes:

/admin/leads
/admin/leads/campaigns
/admin/leads/campaigns/[campaignId]
/admin/leads/source-runs/[sourceRunId]
/admin/leads/[leadId]
/admin/leads/menu-intake
/admin/leads/follow-ups
/admin/leads/suppressions
/admin/leads/settings

MVP can start with only:

/admin/leads
/admin/leads/[leadId]
/admin/leads/campaigns/[campaignId]
/admin/leads/menu-intake

Everything else can come after.

5.4 Dashboard mental model

Use queues, not CRM stages.

Queues are better because the operator needs to know what to do now.

Recommended queues:

Ready to Contact
Needs Review
Contacted
Replied
Menu Received
MenuList Link Created
Converted
Rejected / Do Not Contact

Each queue maps to a clear action.

Queue	Meaning	Primary action
Ready to Contact	Qualified A/B leads	Send WhatsApp/email
Needs Review	Duplicate/ambiguous/risky leads	Approve/reject/edit
Contacted	Message sent/opened	Wait or follow up
Replied	Business responded	Ask/collect menu
Menu Received	Menu file/text received	Create MenuList link
MenuList Link Created	Link exists but not sent	Send link + QR
Converted	MenuList link sent/accepted	Done
Rejected / DNC	Bad or blocked leads	Do nothing

This is simpler than a pipeline and easier to operate daily.

5.5 Main dashboard: /admin/leads

This is the daily work screen.

Top metrics bar

Show these at the top:

Imported
Qualified
Ready to Contact
Contacted
Replies
Menus Received
MenuList Links Created
Converted
Cost / Menu Received
Cost / Link Created

For the selected campaign/date range.

Example:

Campaign: Bangalore Cafes — Test 01

Raw Imported: 842
Qualified: 188
Ready to Contact: 73
Contacted: 61
Replies: 11
Menus Received: 5
MenuList Links Created: 4
Converted: 3

This keeps the system honest.

5.6 Default work queue

Default view should be:

Ready to Contact
Segment A
Has phone
Not contacted
Sorted by score descending

Because the most common daily task will be:

open lead
review quickly
send WhatsApp/email
move to contacted

Default Firestore-style query shape:

TypeScript
where("status", "==", "ready_to_contact")
where("segment", "==", "A")
where("contact.hasPhone", "==", true)
orderBy("qualification.scores.total", "desc")
limit(50)

Use cursor pagination, not infinite full-table loading. Firestore officially supports query cursors such as startAt() and startAfter() to split query results into batches and paginate results. (Firebase
)

Keep the table dense but readable.

Website

Status

Column	Example	Notes
Score	82	Color-coded A/B/C

Area	Koramangala	Important for local campaigns
Category	Cafe	Normalized category
Phone	Yes / number	Show icon or masked number
Email	Yes / missing	Useful for fallback
Website	No / yes	Not a rejection by itself
Menu Status	No website / no menu / PDF / clean menu	Core MenuList signal
Segment	A	A/B/C/Reject
Status	Ready to Contact	Operational status
Source	Apify	Campaign/source run
Last Contacted	Never / 2d ago	Follow-up control

Avoid too many columns. Put detail in the lead page/drawer.

Upload Menu Asset
Mark Link Created
For link created leads
Send MenuList Link
Copy Link
Copy QR
Mark Sent
Mark Converted

5.21 Data mutation rules

All status-changing actions should go through server-side functions/actions.

Examples:

markLeadContacted()
markLeadReplied()
markMenuReceived()
createOnboardingLink()
markMenuListLinkCreated()
markDoNotContact()
rejectLead()
mergeDuplicateLead()

Because this is admin-only data, do not rely only on client-side checks. Next.js authentication guidance separates authentication from authorization, and sensitive mutations should verify who the user is and what they are allowed to do before changing data. (Next.js
)

Also remember: Firestore server client libraries bypass Firestore Security Rules and authenticate via Google Application Default Credentials, so backend code must enforce its own authorization and IAM must be configured properly. (Firebase
)

Practical rule:

Every server mutation checks:
- is user logged in?
- is user admin/operator?
- is action allowed for current lead status?
- is lead suppressed?
- is transition valid?
5.22 Status transition enforcement

Do not let UI freely edit status.

Use explicit functions.

Example:

TypeScript
async function markWhatsAppSent({
  leadId,
  operatorId,
  templateId,
  messagePreview,
}: {
  leadId: string;
  operatorId: string;
  templateId: string;
  messagePreview: string;
}) {
  const lead = await getLead(leadId);

  assertOperator(operatorId);
  assertStatusIn(lead.status, ["ready_to_contact", "qualified"]);
  assertNotSuppressed(lead);

  await updateLead(leadId, {
    status: "contacted_whatsapp",
    "outreach.firstContactedAt": lead.outreach.firstContactedAt ?? new Date(),
    "outreach.lastContactedAt": new Date(),
    "outreach.lastTemplateId": templateId,
    "outreach.lastMessagePreview": messagePreview,
    "outreach.followUpCount": 0,
  });

  await createOutreachEvent({
    leadId,
    campaignId: lead.campaignId,
    type: "whatsapp_sent_manual",
    channel: "whatsapp",
    templateId,
    message: { bodyPreview: messagePreview },
    createdBy: "operator",
    operatorId,
  });
}

This keeps records clean.

Do not put preview generation in the main queue. It will distract the operator and increase cost.

5.26 Required indexes

Since this dashboard will query combinations of status, segment, campaign, phone/email, and score, Firestore composite indexes will be needed. Firestore automatically creates indexes for basic queries, but compound queries may require manually managed composite indexes; Firestore provides error messages with direct index-creation links when an index is missing. (Firebase
)

Create indexes for the queries you actually use.

Recommended indexes:

leads:
- status ASC, segment ASC, contact.hasPhone ASC, qualification.scores.total DESC
- status ASC, segment ASC, contact.hasEmail ASC, qualification.scores.total DESC
- campaignId ASC, status ASC, qualification.scores.total DESC
- campaignId ASC, segment ASC, qualification.scores.total DESC
- status ASC, outreach.nextFollowUpAt ASC
- status ASC, menuIntake.menuReceivedAt DESC
- qualification.detectedSignals.possibleDuplicate ASC, status ASC

leadOutreachEvents:
- leadId ASC, createdAt DESC
- campaignId ASC, createdAt DESC

leadSourceRuns:
- campaignId ASC, createdAt DESC

Do not index raw payloads or large strings.

5.27 Pagination and loading

Do not load all leads.

Use:

limit 50
cursor pagination
server-side filters

Firestore lets you order and limit results with orderBy() and limit(), and an orderBy() clause also filters for documents where that field exists, so make sure all queried leads have the fields used for ordering. (Firebase
)

Practical rule:

Every lead should always have qualification.scores.total.
Every lead should always have status.
Every lead should always have segment.

This avoids missing rows in ordered queries.
````

````text
Stage 6 — Outreach Templates and Channel Rules

Goal:

Turn qualified leads into menu submissions with the lowest possible friction, cost, and brand risk.

This stage defines:

which channel to use
when to use it
what message to send
how many follow-ups
what gets logged
what must never be automated in v0

Core decision:

WhatsApp = assisted/manual in v0
Email = can be automated earlier
Preview links = not default
Onboarding link = default optional link
CTA = send menu photo/PDF → get MenuList link + QR
6.1 Channel strategy

Use three channels only in v0:

1. WhatsApp assisted send
2. Email
3. Manual call for selected high-value leads

Do not use:

bulk WhatsApp blasting
SMS campaigns
robocalls
Instagram automation
LinkedIn-style cold automation
multi-touch sales sequences

This is not a sales engagement platform. It is a focused menu acquisition workflow.

6.2 Channel priority

Use this rule:

If phone exists → WhatsApp assisted
If email exists and no phone → Email
If both exist → WhatsApp first, email as fallback
If high-value lead and no reply → manual call

Recommended routing:

Lead type	First channel	Backup
A lead + phone	WhatsApp assisted	Email after 2–3 days if email exists
A lead + email only	Email	Manual research/call only if high-value
B lead + phone	WhatsApp assisted after review	Email
B lead + email only	Email	Hold
C lead	Hold	No outreach
No phone/email	Reject/enrich	No outreach
Chain/corporate	Hold/manual only	No automation

The strongest first channel for Indian SMB restaurants is likely WhatsApp, but the safest v0 implementation is assisted send, not API blasting.

6.3 WhatsApp doctrine

There are two different WhatsApp paths.

Path A — Assisted WhatsApp via Click to Chat

This is what I recommend for v0.

Flow:

Dashboard button
→ opens WhatsApp with prefilled message
→ operator reviews
→ operator presses send manually
→ dashboard logs “WhatsApp opened”
→ operator confirms “sent”

WhatsApp’s Click to Chat supports links that open a chat with a pre-filled message in the text field, using the wa.me format. This is useful for one-click assisted outreach without building WhatsApp API automation immediately.
WhatsApp Help Center

Example:

https://wa.me/919876543210?text=Hi%20ABC%20Cafe...

Important:

Opening WhatsApp is not the same as sending.

Your dashboard must have two separate events:

whatsapp_opened
whatsapp_sent_manual
Path B — WhatsApp Business Platform API

Do not start here for cold outbound.

WhatsApp Business Platform charges per delivered message, based on the recipient’s market and message category. WhatsApp lists four categories: marketing, utility, authentication, and service. A cold outbound MenuList acquisition message will usually behave like marketing, not utility.
WhatsApp for Business

WhatsApp also requires opt-in before businesses message people through the Business Platform, and business-initiated messages must use approved templates.
Facebook Developers

So the v0 rule is:

No WhatsApp API cold blasting.
Use assisted WhatsApp first.
Consider API only after reply quality, opt-in flow, and message economics are proven.
6.4 India outreach caution

India has an active regulatory framework around unsolicited commercial communication. TRAI’s TCCCPR framework was created to curb unsolicited commercial communication, and TRAI issued a 2026 draft third amendment after the 2025 second amendment to make the framework more effective.
Press Information Bureau

Practical operating rule:

Keep volume low initially.
Use business contact details only for relevant B2B outreach.
Respect do-not-contact immediately.
Do not repeatedly message non-responders.
Do not automate WhatsApp blasting.

This is not legal advice, but it is the correct risk posture.

6.5 Email doctrine

Email is cheaper and easier to automate than WhatsApp.

Amazon SES lists outbound email at $0.10 per 1,000 emails, plus data/attachment and optional add-on charges.
Amazon Web Services, Inc.
 Resend lists a free tier of 3,000 emails/month and a Pro plan at $20/month for 50,000 emails, with extra paid-plan emails at $0.90 per 1,000.
Resend

Recommendation:

Use Resend first if you want simple developer experience.
Use Amazon SES if cost at scale becomes important.

For v0:

Resend is probably enough.

Email rules:

Use one clear subject.
Use plain text or very light HTML.
Include identity: MenuList + sender name.
Include opt-out line.
Stop after two follow-ups.
Do not use fake personalization.
Do not send attachments in cold email.
Ask them to reply or use the onboarding link.

If you ever send to U.S. recipients, note that the FTC says CAN-SPAM applies to commercial email, including B2B email; it requires accurate headers, non-deceptive subject lines, ad disclosure, a physical address, and a way for recipients to stop future emails.
Federal Trade Commission
 Even for India-focused outreach, use these as baseline hygiene.

6.6 Primary CTA

The CTA should be:

Send your current menu photo/PDF and we will create your MenuList link + QR.

Do not lead with:

We built you a preview.
We found your Google listing.
Your online presence is broken.
We use AI.
We are a business truth layer.

Those are internally true or technically interesting, but they are not the right first message.

Owner-facing wedge:

clean digital menu link + QR

Internal strategic asset:

owner-provided menu truth
6.7 Link strategy inside outreach

Use these three variants for testing.

Variant A — No link

Message asks them to reply with the menu.

Use for early WhatsApp tests.

Why:

Lowest friction.
Feels like a direct human request.
No page load required.
Good for local SMBs.
Variant B — Lightweight onboarding link

Default recommended variant.

menulist.com/start/{token}

The link should show:

Create MenuList link for {Business Name}
Upload menu photo/PDF
Confirm WhatsApp number
Get menu link + QR

No AI preview. No fake menu.

Use for:

email
WhatsApp if message length is acceptable
follow-ups
businesses that prefer upload over chat
Variant C — Preview link

Not default.

Use only for:

manually selected high-value leads
leads that clicked but did not submit
leads that replied
leads that sent menu
small experiment group

Rule:

Preview links must earn their place by improving menu_received_rate.
6.8 Outreach sequence

Keep it tight.

Day 0: first message
Day 2 or 3: one follow-up
Day 7: final follow-up
Then stop

No more than:

1 initial + 2 follow-ups

Stop immediately if:

they reply
they send menu
they say not interested
they ask not to contact
phone/email invalid
negative response
DNC exists

For v0, do not run indefinite drip campaigns.

6.12 Template variable system

Templates should support only safe variables.

Allowed variables:

TypeScript
type OutreachTemplateVariables = {
  business_name: string;
  city?: string;
  area?: string;
  onboarding_link?: string;
  menu_url?: string;
  qr_url?: string;

Do not use risky variables like:

6.13 Template object

Store templates in code or Firestore.

For v0, code is fine.

    | "initial"

    | "link_ready";

};

Example:

TypeScript
const whatsappInitialWithLink: OutreachTemplate = {

  name: "WhatsApp Initial With Onboarding Link",
  channel: "whatsapp",

  version: 1,
  body: `Hi {{business_name}}, this is {{sender_name}} from MenuList.

We help restaurants create a clean digital menu link + QR that customers can open instantly from WhatsApp, Instagram, or in-store.

You can send your menu photo/PDF here, or upload it here:
{{onboarding_link}}

We’ll create your MenuList link and share it back.`,
};
6.14 Message rendering rules

Before rendering:

business_name must exist
sender_name must exist
onboarding_link must exist if template requires it
phone/email must pass validation
lead must not be suppressed
lead status must allow outreach

Render function:

TypeScript
function renderTemplate(
  template: OutreachTemplate,
  variables: OutreachTemplateVariables
): {
  subject?: string;
  body: string;
} {
  let subject = template.subject;
  let body = template.body;

  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(variables)) {
    const token = `{{${key}}}`;
    subject = subject?.replaceAll(token, value ?? "");
    body = body.replaceAll(token, value ?? "");
  }

  if (body.includes("{{") || subject?.includes("{{")) {
    throw new Error("Missing template variable");
  }

  return { subject, body };
}

Store lastMessagePreview on the lead for quick debugging.

6.15 WhatsApp link generation
TypeScript
function createWhatsAppClickToChatUrl(phoneE164: string, message: string) {
  const digits = phoneE164.replace(/\D/g, "");
  const encoded = encodeURIComponent(message);
  return `https://wa.me/${digits}?text=${encoded}`;
}

Rules:

phone must be E.164 normalized
India 10-digit phone becomes +91XXXXXXXXXX
never include plus sign in wa.me number
URL-encode message

Dashboard flow:

1. Operator clicks “Open WhatsApp”.
2. Server renders template.
3. System creates wa.me link.
4. Browser opens link.
5. Event logged: whatsapp_opened.
6. UI shows “Mark sent”.
7. Operator clicks after sending.
8. Event logged: whatsapp_sent_manual.
9. Lead status becomes contacted_whatsapp.
6.16 Email sending rule

For v0, use one provider.

Recommendation:

Use Resend first for speed.
Move to SES if volume/cost demands it.

Email event fields:

TypeScript
type EmailOutreachMetadata = {
  provider: "resend" | "ses";
  providerMessageId?: string;
  templateId: string;
  subject: string;
  bodyPreview: string;
  sentTo: string;
};

Email send flow:

1. Operator clicks “Send Email”.
2. Modal previews subject/body.
3. Operator confirms.
4. Server checks suppression + status.
5. Server sends email.
6. Event logged: email_sent.
7. Lead status becomes contacted_email.
8. Follow-up date set.

Do not send from a personal Gmail account at scale.

Use:

danny@menulist.com
or
hello@menulist.com

Set up:

SPF
DKIM
DMARC
custom return-path if provider supports it

This is not optional if you care about deliverability.

6.17 Follow-up scheduling

Use simple deterministic scheduling.

TypeScript
type FollowUpPolicy = {
  maxFollowUps: 2;
  followUp1AfterDays: 3;
  followUp2AfterDays: 7;
};

After first contact:

nextFollowUpAt = now + 3 days
followUpCount = 0

After follow-up 1:

nextFollowUpAt = firstContactedAt + 7 days
followUpCount = 1

After follow-up 2:

nextFollowUpAt = null
followUpCount = 2
status stays contacted unless manually changed

Stop follow-ups if:

lead.status in replied/menu_received/menulist_link_created/converted/not_interested/do_not_contact/rejected/duplicate
6.18 Outreach state changes

Use explicit mutations.

WhatsApp opened
ready_to_contact → ready_to_contact
event: whatsapp_opened

Why no status change?

Because the operator may open WhatsApp and not send.

WhatsApp sent
ready_to_contact → contacted_whatsapp
event: whatsapp_sent_manual
Email sent
ready_to_contact → contacted_email
event: email_sent
Reply received
contacted_whatsapp/contacted_email → replied
event: reply_received
Menu received
replied/menu_requested → menu_received
event: menu_received
Link created
menu_received → menulist_link_created
event: menulist_link_created
Link sent
menulist_link_created → menulist_link_sent
event: menulist_link_sent
Converted
menulist_link_sent → converted
event: converted
6.19 Suppression rules

Before any outreach, check suppression.

Suppression keys:

phone:+91...
email:...
domain:...
lead:{leadId}
business:{businessId}

Create suppression immediately when:

they ask not to be contacted
they complain
wrong person
invalid contact
clear not interested
operator manually blocks

For “not interested,” I would suppress for at least the current campaign and avoid future contact unless they later opt in.

For “do not contact,” suppress globally.

6.20 Negative response handling

Add quick buttons:

Not interested
Wrong number
Already have menu
Do not contact
Abusive/complaint
Invalid phone
Invalid email

Each maps to action.

Response	Action
Not interested	status = not_interested; suppress lead/campaign
Wrong number	clear phone; suppress phone
Do not contact	status = do_not_contact; suppress phone/email/domain
Already have menu	status = not_interested or hold; note reason
Complaint	do_not_contact; suppress globally
Invalid phone	mark invalid; try email if available
Invalid email	mark invalid; try phone if available

Never argue with negative replies.

6.21 Outreach caps

Use conservative daily caps.

For v0:

WhatsApp assisted: 50/day max
Email: 100/day max
Follow-ups: 50/day max
Manual calls: 10/day max

Campaign caps:

First campaign contacted leads: 100–200 max

Increase only after:

reply rate is known
negative rate is low
menu received rate is acceptable
operator workflow is clean

Suggested thresholds before scaling:

negative response rate < 3%
do-not-contact rate < 1%
menu received rate > 5–10%
cost per menu received acceptable
6.22 Message experiments

Do not over-test initially.

Run three variants:

A: WhatsApp no link
B: WhatsApp with onboarding link
C: Email with onboarding link

Later:

D: WhatsApp with example MenuList link
E: WhatsApp with preview link for high-value leads

Measure:

reply rate
onboarding click rate
menu received rate
negative rate
time to menu received
MenuList link created rate

Primary metric:

menu_received_rate

Not open rate.

6.23 Recommended first experiment

Use 150 qualified leads.

50 WhatsApp no link
50 WhatsApp + onboarding link
50 email + onboarding link

Only use leads with similar quality:

same city
same areas
same category mix
similar score range

Decision rule:

If WhatsApp no-link gets more direct menu replies, use it for local SMBs.
If onboarding link gets more submissions, make it default.
If email has weak response but low cost, keep it as fallback.

Do not test AI preview yet. That belongs after baseline conversion is known.

6.24 Onboarding link behavior in messages

The onboarding link should not feel like a sales page.

It should say:

Create your MenuList menu link

Not:

Start free trial
Book demo
Register now

The page should include:

Business name prefilled
Upload menu photo/PDF
Enter/confirm WhatsApp

After submission:

That is all.

6.26 Lead-specific message selection

Use deterministic selection.

TypeScript
function selectInitialTemplate(lead: Lead): string {
  if (lead.contact.hasPhone && lead.segment === "A") {
    return "wa_initial_with_onboarding_v1";
  }

  if (!lead.contact.hasPhone && lead.contact.hasEmail) {
    return "email_initial_with_onboarding_v1";
  }

  if (lead.contact.hasPhone && lead.digitalPresence.websiteMenuStatus === "no_website") {
    return "wa_initial_short_v1";
  }

  return "wa_initial_with_onboarding_v1";
}

Do not over-personalize. Bad personalization is worse than generic clarity.
````

````text
Stage 7 — Onboarding Link, Not AI Preview Link

Goal:

Give every qualified lead a cheap, trackable, low-friction way to send their menu.

This is the replacement for expensive AI preview links.

The onboarding link is not a website preview. It is not a public profile. It is not a claim page. It is a conversion bridge.

7.1 Core decision

Use this as the default outbound link:

menulist.com/start/{token}

Purpose:

Owner opens link
→ sees their business name
→ uploads/sends menu photo/PDF
→ confirms phone/WhatsApp
→ submits
→ MenuList team creates menu link using existing flow
→ MenuList sends final link + QR

Do not generate an AI preview before the business shows intent.

The logic:

Cold lead + AI preview = cost before intent
Cold lead + onboarding link = intent capture
Menu received + AI structuring = useful automation

So the system should spend AI cost only after the owner sends a real menu.

7.2 What this page is

The onboarding page is:

A lightweight menu submission page for one lead.

It should help the business do one thing:

Send us the current menu.

It should not explain the full MenuList vision.

Owner-facing promise:

Send your menu → get a clean MenuList link + QR.

Internal objective:

Convert lead into owner-provided menu data.
7.3 What this page is not

Do not make this:

AI-generated website
restaurant landing page
public MenuList profile
business claim page
full signup flow
account creation flow
pricing page
dashboard
lead audit page

Those add friction.

A restaurant owner receiving a WhatsApp message should not need to understand MenuList as infrastructure. They only need to understand:

Upload menu. Get link.
7.4 Recommended URL structure

Use tokenized URLs:

/start/{token}

Example:

menulist.com/start/x7Kp92LmQ

Do not use:

/start/abc-cafe-koramangala
/start?leadId=lead_123

Reason:

Business slugs leak lead identity.
Lead IDs should not be public.
Random tokens are safer and easier to revoke.

The token should map to:

leadOnboardingLinks/{linkId}

with:

tokenHash
leadId
campaignId
status
clickCount
submittedAt
expiresAt

Never store the raw token. Store a hash.

7.5 Token behavior

Token rules:

random
unguessable
single-lead scoped
revocable
optionally expiring
not tied to login

Recommended token length:

128-bit random minimum

Implementation idea:

TypeScript
crypto.randomBytes(24).toString("base64url")

Store:

TypeScript
tokenHash = sha256(token)

URL contains:

token

Database stores:

tokenHash

Flow:

User opens /start/{token}
→ server hashes token
→ finds leadOnboardingLink by tokenHash
→ checks status/expiry
→ loads safe lead display data
→ records click
→ renders form
7.6 Expiry rule

For v0:

Do not expire too aggressively.

Recommended:

expiresAt = 30 days after creation

Reason:

Restaurant owners may reply late.
The link is low-risk because it only allows menu submission.

Expire immediately if:

lead marked do_not_contact
lead rejected
lead converted
lead linked to another business manually
token suspected abused

Statuses:

TypeScript
type OnboardingLinkStatus =
  | "active"
  | "clicked"
  | "submitted"
  | "expired"
  | "revoked";
7.7 Page states

The /start/{token} page needs only these states.

State 1 — Valid active link

Show menu upload form.

Create MenuList link for ABC Cafe
Upload your current menu photo or PDF.
We’ll create a clean MenuList link and QR for customers.
State 2 — Already submitted

Show:

Menu received.
We’ll send your MenuList link once it is ready.

Optionally allow another upload:

Upload another file
State 3 — Expired/revoked

Show:

This link is no longer active.
Contact MenuList if you need help.

Do not show internal lead details.

State 4 — Invalid token

Show generic error:

Invalid or expired link.

Do not reveal whether a lead exists.

7.8 Page UX

The page should be extremely simple.

Header
MenuList
Main title
Create your digital menu link
Business context
For: {{business_name}}
{{area}}, {{city}}

Use only safe data:

business name
area
city

Do not show:

source URL
score
Google Maps URL
rating
review count
scraped address unless needed
internal notes
Main CTA

7.12 File upload rules

Accept only:

image/jpeg
image/png
image/webp
application/pdf

Recommended limits:

max file size: 10 MB
max files per submission: 5
max total upload: 25 MB

Reason:

Restaurant menus are often multiple photos.
But unbounded upload creates abuse/cost risk.

Firebase Cloud Storage supports web uploads by creating a storage reference and uploading files; Firebase Storage Security Rules can also restrict uploads by authorization, file size, and content type, so enforce these limits server-side and in Storage Rules.
Firebase
+1

7.13 Upload path

Use deterministic storage paths.

lead-menu-submissions/{leadId}/{submissionId}/{fileName}

Example:

lead-menu-submissions/lead_abc123/sub_789/menu-1.jpg

Do not put raw business names or phone numbers in file paths.

Good:

leadId/submissionId/file

Bad:

abc-cafe-koramangala-owner-phone/menu.jpg
7.14 Upload security

The onboarding page is token-based, not login-based. That means upload security matters.

Recommended implementation:

1. User opens /start/{token}
2. Server validates token
3. Server creates upload session
4. Client uploads files to controlled path
5. Server finalizes submission

For v0, you can simplify:

Submit form → server receives file → server uploads to storage

But if file uploads go directly from browser to Firebase Storage, Storage Rules must validate path, file size, and content type. Firebase Storage Security Rules are path-based and can restrict access based on request properties, including upload size and content type.
Firebase

Use App Check on public upload-related endpoints where practical. Firebase App Check is designed to help protect Firebase and custom backend resources from unauthorized clients and abuse, but it should complement—not replace—token validation, rate limits, and server-side checks.
Firebase
+1

7.15 Server-side submission flow

Use a server-side mutation for final submission.

Next.js Server Actions can handle form submissions and mutations, but Next.js notes Server Functions can be reached through direct POST requests, so authentication/authorization or equivalent validation must happen inside the Server Function. For this tokenized public page, “authorization” means validating the onboarding token, link status, expiry, and rate limits inside the server mutation.
Next.js
+1

Flow:

submitOnboardingForm(formData)
→ validate token
→ validate link active
→ validate file count/type/size
→ create lead submission record
→ upload/store files
→ update lead.status = menu_received
→ update lead.menuIntake
→ update onboarding link status = submitted
→ create leadOutreachEvent(menu_received)
→ show success page

7.28 Route structure

Use:

/app/start/[token]/page.tsx

/app/start/[token]/success/page.tsx

Or:

/app/start/[token]/page.tsx
/app/api/start/[token]/submit/route.ts

My recommendation:

Use a route handler for file upload if files are large.
Use Server Actions for smaller metadata-only mutations.

Reason:

Next.js Server Actions have request body size limits that may need configuration, and file uploads can become awkward through actions. Next.js documents a default Server Actions body size limit of 1 MB unless configured, so direct upload or route-handler upload is cleaner for menu files. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}

7.41 Template integration

When outreach template includes:

{{onboarding_link}}

the system should:

check existing active link
if none, create one
render full URL
store linkId on lead

Pseudo-code:

TypeScript
async function getOrCreateOnboardingLinkForLead(leadId: string) {
  const existing = await findActiveOnboardingLink(leadId);

  if (existing) return existing;

  const token = generateSecureToken();
  const tokenHash = sha256(token);
  const shortCode = generateShortCode();

  const link = await createLeadOnboardingLink({
    leadId,
    tokenHash,
    shortCode,
    status: "active",
    expiresAt: addDays(new Date(), 30),
  });

  return {
    ...link,
    rawToken: token,
    publicUrl: `${BASE_URL}/start/${token}`,
  };
}

Important:

Only return raw token at creation time.
Do not store raw token.

If link already exists, you need the public URL. Since you do not store raw token, either:

store encrypted token

or:

store publicUrl generated at creation

Simpler v0:

store publicPath with token in leadOnboardingLinks

Security trade-off:

The token is still stored, but admin-only.

Better:

store token encrypted with server secret.

For v0, storing publicPath admin-only is acceptable if Firestore rules/admin access are strict. But do not expose it publicly except in the message.

7.42 Storage of token: practical recommendation

Use:

TypeScript
type LeadOnboardingLink = {
  tokenHash: string;
  encryptedToken: string;
  publicPath: string; // optional convenience
}

encryptedToken allows regenerating the URL for admin copy.

Avoid storing raw token directly.

If this feels too much for v0, store public URL only in admin-protected Firestore and revisit later. The risk is moderate because the link is not privileged enough to edit public business truth; it only submits a menu.

This is near-zero compared to AI previews.

No AI required.

Most cost happens only when a lead submits files:

That is good because file submission equals intent.

This is exactly what you want:

AI preview does the opposite:

Then maybe generate a lightweight preview.

Even then, preview should be based on:

not invented menu
not scraped photos/reviews

But this belongs to Stage 10, not Stage 7.
````

````text
Stage 8 — Menu Intake and Existing MenuList Generation

Goal:

Convert owner-submitted menus into live MenuList links + QR codes.

This is where the lead engine becomes valuable.

Everything before this is just acquisition. This stage creates the actual MenuList asset.

8.1 Core decision

Use the existing MenuList menu creation flow.

Do not build a separate menu builder inside the lead engine.

The lead engine should only do this:

receive menu
→ queue it
→ help operator process it
→ pass it into existing MenuList creation flow
→ store final MenuList link + QR back on the lead

So the boundary is:

Lead Engine = acquisition + intake
MenuList Core = menu creation + public link + QR

This prevents the internal tool from becoming another product.

8.2 Correct flow

The full flow should be:

Owner submits menu
→ lead becomes menu_received
→ submission enters menu-intake queue
→ operator reviews menu quality
→ operator creates/attaches MenuList business
→ menu is structured using existing flow
→ operator reviews final menu
→ MenuList link + QR are generated
→ final link is sent back to owner
→ lead becomes converted

Important:

Do not auto-publish owner-submitted menu without review in v0.

Menus are messy. Photos are blurry. Prices may be unclear. Sections may be split across multiple pages. One human quality gate is worth it.

8.3 Inputs into menu intake

Menu can arrive from four places:

1. Onboarding upload page
2. WhatsApp message
3. Email attachment
4. Manual/operator upload

Each input should become the same internal object:

leadMenuSubmission

That keeps the rest of the process consistent.

8.4 Menu intake statuses

Use a small status machine.

TypeScript
type MenuSubmissionStatus =
  | "received"
  | "needs_review"
  | "needs_better_file"
  | "ready_to_process"
  | "processing"
  | "processed"
  | "qa_failed"
  | "ready_to_publish"
  | "published"
  | "link_sent"
  | "converted"
  | "rejected";

Recommended state flow:

received
→ needs_review
→ ready_to_process
→ processing
→ processed
→ ready_to_publish
→ published
→ link_sent
→ converted

Exception states:

needs_better_file
qa_failed
rejected

Keep this separate from lead status, but sync key states back to the lead.

Example:

submission.status = published
lead.status = menulist_link_created
8.5 Lead status sync

When menu arrives:

lead.status = menu_received

When MenuList link is created:

lead.status = menulist_link_created

When link is sent:

lead.status = menulist_link_sent

When owner confirms or starts using it:

lead.status = converted

This gives you a clean funnel:

contacted
→ replied
→ menu_received
→ menulist_link_created
→ menulist_link_sent
→ converted
8.6 Menu intake queue

Route:

/admin/leads/menu-intake

Default view:

submissions where status in ["received", "needs_review", "ready_to_process"]

Table columns:

Business
Area
Source
Files
Received at
Lead status
Submission status
Assigned to
Action

Example:

Business	Source	Files	Status	Action
ABC Cafe	Upload	3 images	Needs review	Review
Green Bowl	WhatsApp	1 PDF	Ready to process	Process
Chai House	Email	2 images	Needs better file	Request clearer menu

The queue should prioritize by:

oldest received first
A-segment leads first
manual high-priority flag
8.7 Submission detail page

Route:

/admin/leads/menu-intake/[submissionId]

Panels:

1. Lead summary
2. Submitted files
3. Business matching
4. Extraction workspace
5. QA checklist
6. Publish/send actions
Panel 1 — Lead summary

Show:

business name
area/city
phone/email
lead score
campaign
source
outreach history

Buttons:

Open lead
Open WhatsApp
Send email
Mark DNC
Panel 2 — Submitted files

Show:

file thumbnails
PDF viewer
download/open original
file type
file size
upload source
submitted at

Actions:

rotate image
mark blurry
mark duplicate
delete bad file
request clearer file

Do not overbuild image editing. Rotation + mark blurry is enough.

Panel 3 — Business matching

Before creating a new MenuList business, check if it already exists.

Actions:

Attach to existing MenuList business
Create new MenuList business
Mark duplicate
Reject submission

Matching fields:

business name
phone
area
city
website
existing MenuList businesses

Rules:

If existing business found → attach.
If not → create new MenuList business draft.

Do not create duplicate MenuList businesses.

Panel 4 — Extraction workspace

This is where menu data is created.

Three processing modes:

Manual
OCR-assisted
AI-assisted structured extraction

Use them in this order.

8.8 Processing mode 1 — Manual entry

This is the simplest v0.

Operator reads menu file and enters:

sections
item names
prices
descriptions if visible
availability notes

Use manual entry for the first 20–50 menus.

Reason:

You need to understand menu messiness before automating extraction.

Manual processing teaches:

common menu formats
price ambiguity
multi-page issues
language mix
veg/non-veg symbols
item variants
add-ons
combos
tax/service charge notes

Do not skip this learning.

8.9 Processing mode 2 — OCR-assisted

After manual processing is understood, add OCR.

Use OCR to convert menu images/PDF pages into text.

Google Cloud Vision supports OCR through TEXT_DETECTION and DOCUMENT_TEXT_DETECTION; Document Text Detection is optimized for dense text/documents. Google’s pricing page says Text Detection and Document Text Detection have the first 1,000 units/month free, then $1.50 per 1,000 units from 1,001 to 5,000,000 units, with lower pricing beyond that. For PDF-like OCR, Google Document AI’s Enterprise Document OCR Processor is listed at $1.50 per 1,000 pages for the first 1–5,000,000 pages/month.
Google Cloud Documentation

Google Cloud

Google Cloud

Cost implication:

OCR cost is not the scary part.
Bad automation and QA mistakes are the scary part.

Example:

500 menus/month
average 3 pages/images each
= 1,500 OCR units

First 1,000 free
next 500 at roughly $1.50 / 1,000
≈ $0.75 OCR cost, before other processing

So yes, you can afford OCR after menu submission.

8.10 Processing mode 3 — AI-assisted structured extraction

After OCR text exists, use an LLM to structure it into MenuList’s menu schema.

This is where AI makes sense.

Input:

OCR text
file/page order
business name
optional operator notes

Output:

JSON matching MenuList menu schema

Use schema-enforced output. OpenAI’s Structured Outputs feature is designed to make model responses adhere to a supplied JSON Schema, which is exactly what you want for turning messy OCR text into structured menu objects.
OpenAI Developers

Important rule:

AI can structure owner-provided menu data.
AI cannot invent missing items, prices, claims, or photos.

If price is unclear:

price = null
needsReview = true

If item name is unclear:

name = best guess
confidence = low
needsReview = true

If section is unclear:

section = "Uncategorized"
needsReview = true

Never hallucinate completeness.

8.11 Recommended processing maturity

Build in this order:

v0: manual processing
v1: OCR-assisted text extraction
v2: AI-assisted JSON structuring
v3: semi-automated QA warnings
v4: owner self-confirmation

Do not start with full automation.

First prove:

Can we get owners to send menus?
Can we turn them into links quickly?
Do owners like the result?
Do they share/use the link?

Only then optimize processing speed.

8.12 Menu schema

Use your existing MenuList schema. If you need a clean internal shape, use something like this:

TypeScript
type Menu = {
  businessId: string;

  status:
    | "draft"
    | "needs_review"
    | "published"
    | "needs_owner_confirmation";

  source: {
    type:
      | "owner_upload"
      | "whatsapp"
      | "email"
      | "manual_operator";
    leadId?: string;
    submissionId?: string;
    originalFileIds: string[];
  };

  sections: MenuSection[];

  metadata: {
    currency: "INR";
    language?: "en" | "hi" | "mixed";
    extractedBy?: "manual" | "ocr" | "ai_assisted";
    reviewedBy?: string;
    ownerConfirmedAt?: Date;
    publishedAt?: Date;
  };
};

type MenuSection = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  sortOrder: number;
  items: MenuItem[];
};

type MenuItem = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  description?: string;
  price?: number;
  priceText?: string;
  variants?: MenuItemVariant[];
  tags?: string[];
  isVeg?: boolean;
  isAvailable?: boolean;
  confidence?: "high" | "medium" | "low";
  needsReview?: boolean;
};

type MenuItemVariant = {
  name: string;
  price?: number;
  priceText?: string;
};

Keep it simple.

Do not model every possible restaurant nuance in v0.

8.13 Extraction JSON schema

For AI-assisted extraction, require strict structure.

Example:

TypeScript
type ExtractedMenuDraft = {
  currency: "INR";
  language: "en" | "hi" | "mixed" | "unknown";

  sections: {
    name: string;
    items: {
      name: string;
      description?: string;
      price?: number;
      priceText?: string;
      variants?: {
        name: string;
        price?: number;
        priceText?: string;
      }[];
      tags?: string[];
      confidence: "high" | "medium" | "low";
      needsReview: boolean;
      reviewReason?: string;
    }[];
  }[];

  extractionWarnings: string[];
};

Warnings should include:

unclear prices
missing prices
possible duplicate items
blurred text
language uncertainty
multi-page order uncertainty
tax/charge ambiguity

This helps operator review quickly.

8.14 Quality rules

Before publishing, require these checks.

Required
business attached or created
at least one menu section
at least one menu item
no obviously fake/invented items
currency confirmed
source files retained
operator reviewed
public link generated
Recommended
prices reviewed
section order reviewed
duplicates removed
business name checked
phone/WhatsApp checked
owner number available for sending link
Optional
opening hours
Instagram link
logo/photo
veg/non-veg tags
item descriptions

Do not block publishing on optional fields.

The goal is a useful menu link, not a perfect business profile.

8.15 QA checklist

Every menu should pass a simple checklist.

[ ] Business matched correctly
[ ] Menu files readable
[ ] Sections look correct
[ ] Item names look correct
[ ] Prices look correct or unclear prices marked
[ ] No AI-invented items
[ ] Public MenuList link opens
[ ] QR code opens correct link
[ ] Ready to send to owner

If any critical item fails:

submission.status = qa_failed

If file is unclear:

submission.status = needs_better_file

Then send owner a clearer-file request.

8.16 Request clearer menu message

WhatsApp:

Thanks. The menu image is a bit unclear, so we may not capture the items/prices correctly.

Can you send a clearer photo or PDF of the menu?

Email:

Hi {{business_name}} team,

Thanks for sharing the menu.

The file is not clear enough for us to create an accurate MenuList link. Could you send a clearer photo or PDF?

Thanks,
Danny
MenuList

Do not guess. Accuracy matters more than speed.

8.17 Menu creation flow

The operator action should be:

Create MenuList Link

Behind that button:

1. Check existing MenuList business.
2. Create business draft if needed.
3. Create menu draft.
4. Attach source files.
5. Fill menu data manually/OCR/AI-assisted.
6. Review.
7. Publish.
8. Generate QR.
9. Update lead and submission.

This can open the existing MenuList admin.

Example:

/admin/businesses/new?fromLead=lead_123&submission=sub_456

or:

/admin/businesses/{businessId}/menus/new?fromLead=lead_123

Do not duplicate menu editing UI inside the lead engine if the existing MenuList admin already has it.

8.18 Business creation rules

If no existing MenuList business exists, create a minimum business record.

Required:

business name
city
area
source = lead_engine
leadId
submissionId
owner contact phone/email if provided
status = draft or active

Optional:

address
hours
Instagram
website

Do not fill business description from AI.

Do not import Google reviews/photos/descriptions.

8.19 Source/provenance

Every menu created from lead intake should remember where it came from.

Store:

TypeScript
source: {
  type: "lead_engine";
  leadId: string;
  submissionId: string;
  receivedVia: "onboarding_upload" | "whatsapp" | "email" | "manual";
  sourceFileIds: string[];
  processedBy: string;

}

This matters later when owner asks:

Where did this menu come from?

Answer:

8.20 Owner confirmation

For v0, do not require owner login before sending the link.

But after sending final MenuList link, ask for confirmation.

{{menu_url}}

Please check once. If anything needs correction, reply here and we’ll update it.

If owner requests correction:

Later, you can add:

But do not block v0 conversion on account creation.

8.22 Conversion definition

Do not mark converted when the menu is received.

Use stricter conversion:

Converted = MenuList link created and sent to owner.

Optional stronger conversion:

Strong converted = owner confirms link or starts using QR/link.

Track both.

TypeScript
type ConversionState = {
  menuReceivedAt?: Date;
  linkCreatedAt?: Date;
  linkSentAt?: Date;
  ownerConfirmedAt?: Date;
  firstPublicViewAt?: Date;
  qrFirstScannedAt?: Date;
};

Primary metric:

MenuList links created per contacted lead

Stronger metric:

Owner-confirmed MenuList links per contacted lead
8.23 QR generation

If MenuList already generates QR codes, use that.

If not, add a simple QR generation step after public menu URL exists.

QR should point to:

public MenuList menu URL

Not to:

lead onboarding link
internal admin URL
temporary preview URL

Store:

TypeScript
menuList: {
  businessId,
  menuId,
  menuUrl,
  qrUrl,
  createdAt,
  sentAt
}

The QR is important because it moves MenuList from “link sent once” to “customer-facing surface.”

8.26 Storage structure

Use Cloud Storage for files.

Firebase Cloud Storage supports browser uploads by creating a reference to a full path and uploading a File/Blob. Firebase Storage Security Rules can restrict access by path, user/auth conditions, file size, and content type; Firebase also recommends robust security rules for production storage.
Firebase

Firebase

Recommended paths:

lead-menu-submissions/{leadId}/{submissionId}/original/{fileId}
lead-menu-submissions/{leadId}/{submissionId}/processed/ocr.txt
lead-menu-submissions/{leadId}/{submissionId}/processed/extracted-menu.json
lead-menu-submissions/{leadId}/{submissionId}/processed/qa.json

Do not use:

business names
phone numbers
owner names

in paths.

8.27 File retention

Keep original menu files, but define retention clearly.

Recommended:

keep original files after conversion
because they are evidence/source for the menu

But do not expose them publicly by default.

Access:

admin/operator only
owner access later if account exists

If lead is rejected or DNC before conversion:

delete files after 30–90 days

If converted:

retain as menu source history
8.28 Manual WhatsApp intake

For WhatsApp submissions, operator needs a simple path.

Flow:

Owner sends menu on WhatsApp
→ operator downloads/saves image/PDF
→ opens lead
→ clicks Add Menu Submission
→ uploads file
→ receivedVia = whatsapp
→ status = received

If owner included short code:

search shortCode → lead found

If no short code:

search phone/business name

Admin needs search by:

phone
business name
short code
campaign

This is practical and enough.

Do not build WhatsApp inbox sync in v0.

8.29 Email intake

For email attachments:

operator opens email
downloads attachment
opens lead
adds menu submission
uploads file
receivedVia = email

Later, you can automate via inbound email parsing.

Not needed in v0.

8.30 What AI should flag

If using AI-assisted structuring, ask it to produce warnings.

Warnings:

missing prices
unclear price
possible duplicate item
possible combo item
variants detected
section ambiguous
blurred text likely
multi-language text
unreadable page
tax/service charge note
owner confirmation recommended

Operator should see warnings before publishing.

8.31 What AI must not do

Hard rule:

No invented menu truth.

AI must not:

invent missing prices
invent menu items
invent descriptions
infer cuisine claims from category
add “popular” labels
add fake images
create offers
correct prices without evidence
translate item names unless asked

If uncertain:

mark low confidence

This protects MenuList’s trust layer.

8.32 Publishing rule

Publish only after human QA in v0.

Minimum publish criteria:

menu has at least one section
menu has at least one item
prices are either present or intentionally blank
business is matched/created
public link opens
QR opens correct URL

If a menu has no prices but the owner sent it that way, it can still be published if the UI handles price-less items.

Do not block on perfection.

Once menu is published, update both:

leadMenuSubmission
leads

submission.menuList = {

via WhatsApp if phone exists

Converted if any of these happens:

8.37 SLA targets

Set internal targets.

For v0:

Menu received → link created: within 24 hours
Link created → link sent: same day
Correction request → corrected link: within 24 hours

For early founder-led operations, even faster is better:

same-day link creation

Speed matters because owner attention decays quickly.

8.38 Operator SOP

Daily workflow:

1. Open /admin/leads/menu-intake.
2. Process oldest/highest-value menu submissions first.
3. Check file quality.
4. Attach/create MenuList business.
5. Create menu in existing MenuList flow.
6. Review against original file.
7. Publish link.
8. Generate/check QR.
9. Send link to owner.
10. Mark link sent.
11. Follow owner corrections if any.

This should be written as an internal SOP.

8.39 When to add OCR/AI

Add OCR/AI only after:

at least 30–50 menus processed manually
you understand common formatting issues
operator time per menu is known
menu_received volume is high enough

Decision rule:

If manual processing is under 5–10 minutes/menu and volume is low, keep manual.
If volume grows or menus are complex, add OCR.
If OCR text cleanup is the bottleneck, add AI structuring.

Do not automate because it is interesting. Automate when it removes a measured bottleneck.

8.40 Cost position

This stage is where AI/OCR spend is justified.

Because:

lead has shown intent
owner has sent source material
MenuList asset will be created

So the spending sequence should be:

No AI before outreach
No AI before click/reply
OCR/AI after menu received

This makes the economics clean:

cost follows conversion intent

That is the right rule.

8.41 What not to build in Stage 8

Do not build:

new standalone menu builder

These are distractions.

Build only:

conversion tracking

8.43 Final Stage 8 spec

The Menu Intake system should do this:

Owner sends/uploads menu
→ system creates leadMenuSubmission
→ lead enters menu_received
→ operator reviews file quality
→ operator attaches/creates MenuList business
→ existing MenuList flow creates structured menu
→ operator QA checks against source file
→ MenuList public menu link + QR are generated
→ link/QR are sent to owner
→ lead marked converted

Hard rules:

Use existing MenuList menu creation.
Do not build a separate product.
Do not auto-publish without human review in v0.
Use AI only after owner sends actual menu.
Do not invent menu items/prices.
Keep original source files as evidence.
Measure link created and owner confirmed, not just menu received.

Best implementation posture:

Manual first.
OCR second.
AI structuring third.
Owner self-serve later.

This stage is the core conversion engine. If it works, the lead engine is not just generating leads — it is producing actual MenuList supply.
````

````text
1. Main verdict

The design is directionally correct.

The best decision we made was:

No AI preview by default.

That protects cost, trust, and simplicity.

The second-best decision was:

MenuList truth starts only after owner submits/confirms menu.

Apify and Google Maps should only find possible leads. They should not become MenuList’s business truth source. Google Maps Platform terms restrict scraping/exporting/storing/resharing Maps content, and Google Business Profile’s GoogleLocations API explicitly says it is not for lead generation or competitive analysis. So the safest operating rule is still: source data = lead intelligence; owner submission = MenuList truth.
Google Cloud

Correct:

Lead Engine, not another product.

The system should exist only to acquire MenuList supply.

Good:

Find food businesses
→ get owner/menu input
→ create MenuList menu link

Danger:

Find businesses
→ generate pages
→ act like a directory

That second path creates legal risk, data-quality risk, and product-positioning drift.

Final rule:

The lead engine exists to produce owner-submitted menus.

Not leads. Not pages. Not demos.

3.2 Source strategy review

Apify is still a good first source.

Apify’s platform plan currently lists Starter at $29/month with usage credit, and multiple Google Maps-related actors list per-1,000-result/place pricing in the low-dollar range, though actor pricing varies by actor and enrichment level.
Apify
+2
Apify
+2

So cost is not the scary part.

The real risks are:

bad leads
duplicates
wrong category
unreachable phone numbers
WhatsApp account risk
low reply rate
poor menu processing speed

Good rule from previous stages:

Start with Apify only.
Benchmark Outscraper later.
Do not integrate five lead vendors.

I would keep this.

3.3 Qualification review

The scoring model is useful, but do not over-trust it initially.

The system should score, but humans should still review the first batches.

Good scoring dimensions:

fit
reachability
menu gap
demand
conversion ease
risk

Correct reject rules:

wrong vertical
outside target area
no phone/email
duplicate
closed
large chain
already has strong clean menu

Important correction:

Do not over-prioritize “no website.”

MenuList is not a website replacement. The real signal is:

no clean, shareable, current digital menu link

A restaurant with a website can still be a strong MenuList lead if the menu is PDF-only, image-only, buried, slow, stale, or not WhatsApp/QR-friendly.

3.4 Database review

The proposed database is okay, but for MVP I would cut it further.

Minimum collections:

leadCampaigns
leadSourceRuns
leads
leadDedupeKeys
leadOutreachEvents
leadOnboardingLinks
leadMenuSubmissions
leadSuppressions

Optional:

leadRawItems

Use leadRawItems only for short-term debugging. Firestore TTL policies can delete documents based on an expiration timestamp, so raw/debug data can expire automatically instead of staying forever.
Firebase

Do not build:

previewPages
auditReports
deals
contacts
tasks
sales pipeline objects
AI asset records

Not needed.

3.5 Apify ingestion review

The ingestion design is good.

Correct flow:

create campaign
→ run Apify
→ import dataset
→ normalize
→ dedupe
→ score
→ show in dashboard

Do not connect ingestion directly to outreach yet.

There must be a review boundary:

imported/scored leads
→ dashboard review
→ outreach

Otherwise the system can start contacting junk.

Important operational rule:

First test should be tiny.

Not 5,000 leads.

Start with:

1 area
2 categories
20–50 results each

Then inspect field quality manually.

3.6 Dashboard review

The dashboard should be queue-based, not CRM-based.

Correct queues:

Ready to Contact
Needs Review
Contacted
Replied
Menu Received
Link Created
Converted
Rejected / DNC

Do not build Kanban, deal stages, revenue forecasting, account pages, or notes infrastructure.

The most important dashboard button is:

Open WhatsApp

The second most important:

Mark Menu Received

The third:

Create MenuList Link

Everything else is secondary.

3.7 Outreach review

The outreach strategy is correct, but this is the highest-risk area.

Do not start with WhatsApp API blasting.

WhatsApp Business Platform charges per delivered message, with rates varying by country and category; it uses categories such as marketing, utility, authentication, and service. Cold outbound would likely fall into marketing/commercial messaging.
WhatsApp for Business

Meta also states that businesses must clearly obtain opt-in to message people on WhatsApp, and WhatsApp’s policy says outside the 24-hour customer-service window, approved message templates are required.
Facebook Developers
+1

So the correct v0 is:

assisted WhatsApp

Meaning:

dashboard opens WhatsApp with prefilled message
human presses send
system logs the action

That gives you 80% of the productivity gain with much lower platform risk.

Email can be automated earlier.

3.8 Onboarding link review

This is one of the strongest parts of the design.

Default link:

menulist.com/start/{token}

Purpose:

upload/send menu

Not:

claim profile
view preview
start trial
book demo

This is the correct replacement for AI previews.

The page should ask only:

name
WhatsApp number
menu photo/PDF
optional note

Do not ask for:

password
account creation
GST
full address
pricing plan
full profile

The first conversion is:

menu_received

Nothing else.

3.9 Menu intake review

The menu-intake design is correct, but the MVP should start manual.

Do not build OCR/AI first.

Correct maturity path:

manual processing
→ OCR-assisted
→ AI-assisted structuring
→ owner self-editing later

AI becomes justified only after the owner submits real menu material.

Good AI use:

extract menu sections/items/prices from owner-uploaded menu

Bad AI use:

invent missing prices
invent items
generate fake food photos
write restaurant claims

Firebase Storage can validate uploads by path, content type, and size through Storage Security Rules, so the upload flow should enforce file type and size limits.
Firebase

4. The biggest missing piece: offer framing

This is the most important thing not yet fully decided.

Your outreach says:

Send your menu and we’ll create your MenuList link + QR.

But the owner may ask:

Is this free?
Why are you doing this?
What do I have to pay?
Who are you?
Can I update it later?

You need a clear offer before sending messages.

My recommendation for v0:

First MenuList menu link + QR setup is free.
No account required.
No payment required.
We send the link back for review.
If they want ongoing updates/control later, that becomes the paid/claim/owner layer.

The first goal is supply acquisition, not immediate monetization.

Owner-facing answer:

For early restaurants, we’re creating the first MenuList menu link free. You can use it on WhatsApp, Instagram, or in-store QR. If you want changes later, reply here and we’ll update it.

Do not hide pricing if there is pricing. But if you want this engine to work, make the first action free.

Reason:

Cold owner + paid ask = low response.
Cold owner + send menu, get useful link = much higher response.

The monetization point should come after value is delivered.

5. Second missing piece: consent language on onboarding page

The onboarding form should include one simple checkbox:

I confirm I represent this business and allow MenuList to create a menu link using the menu I submit.

This protects you.

Do not make it legal-heavy, but add it.

Recommended text:

By submitting, you confirm that you represent this business and allow MenuList to create a digital menu link from the menu files you provide.

This matters because after submission you are creating a public or shareable page.

6. Third missing piece: response handling SOP

Because WhatsApp is assisted/manual, the system will not automatically know replies happened.

You need a manual response protocol.

When a reply arrives, operator marks one of:

positive
menu sent
asked question
not interested
wrong number
do not contact
needs follow-up

For each case:

positive → ask for menu
menu sent → create menu submission
asked question → answer with approved response
not interested → mark not_interested
wrong number → suppress phone
do not contact → suppress globally

Without this SOP, your dashboard data will become inaccurate.

7. Fourth missing piece: standard replies to common objections

Add canned replies.

“Is this free?”
Yes, for early restaurants we’re creating the first MenuList menu link + QR free. Send your current menu photo/PDF and we’ll share the link back for review.
“What is MenuList?”
MenuList helps restaurants create a clean digital menu link and QR that customers can open from WhatsApp, Instagram, or in-store.
“We already have a menu.”
Great. You can send the same menu photo/PDF and we’ll turn it into a clean shareable MenuList link + QR.
“We already have a website.”
That’s fine. MenuList is mainly for a fast menu link + QR that is easy to share with customers on WhatsApp, Instagram, and in-store.
“How much?”
The first setup is free for early restaurants. We’ll create the link and send it back for review.
“Remove us / don’t message again.”
Understood. We won’t contact you again.

Then immediately mark DNC.

These replies should be in the dashboard.

8. Fifth missing piece: email deliverability setup

Before sending email, configure:

SPF
DKIM
DMARC
reply-to inbox
unsubscribe handling
bounce handling

Do not send from Gmail manually at volume.

Use:

hello@menulist.com
or
danny@menulist.com

Email is cheap, but bad deliverability can burn the domain.

9. Sixth missing piece: suppression discipline

This must exist from day one.

Before outreach, check:

phone suppression
email suppression
domain suppression
lead suppression
business suppression

Suppress globally if:

do not contact
complaint
wrong number
invalid contact

Suppress campaign-level if:

not interested
already handled
bad fit

This prevents the system from becoming spammy as campaigns repeat.

10. Seventh missing piece: campaign kill criteria

You need explicit stop rules.

For each campaign, stop or review if:

qualified lead rate < 15%
duplicate rate > 30%
wrong-category rate > 20%
contactable rate < 35%
negative response rate > 5%
menu received rate < 3%
cost per menu received exceeds target
operator time per menu is too high

Do not keep scraping because scraping is cheap.

The main question is:

Can this campaign create MenuList links efficiently?
11. Eighth missing piece: exact definition of conversion

Use three conversion levels.

Soft conversion:
menu received

Real conversion:
MenuList link created and sent

Strong conversion:
owner confirms link or starts using/sharing it

Do not call a lead converted just because they replied.

Primary metric:

MenuList links created per 100 contacted leads

Secondary:

Owner-confirmed links per 100 contacted leads
12. Ninth missing piece: current system integration point

Before coding, define exactly where the lead engine hands off to existing MenuList.

You need one clean internal function or route:

createMenuFromLeadSubmission(submissionId)

It should return:

TypeScript
{
  businessId: string;
  menuId: string;
  menuUrl: string;
  qrUrl: string;
}

If your current MenuList flow cannot expose this yet, build a manual bridge first:

operator opens existing MenuList admin
creates menu manually
pastes menuUrl/qrUrl back into lead

Do not block the lead engine on deep integration.

13. Tenth missing piece: the example link

The outreach should include either:

onboarding link

or sometimes:

example MenuList link

But not a business-specific AI preview.

You need one high-quality sample page:

menulist.com/example

or:

menulist.com/sample-menu

Use that in outreach if needed.

Example message:

Example of what you’ll receive:
{{sample_menu_link}}

This gives clarity without generating costly previews per lead.

14. What I would cut from the earlier design

To keep it lean, cut or defer these:

AI previews
public unclaimed pages
audit reports
owner accounts
self-serve dashboard
WhatsApp API
inbound WhatsApp sync
email parsing
OCR
AI extraction
multi-source vendor system
advanced scoring ML
complex role permissions
multi-operator assignment
sales CRM features

All of those can wait.

The MVP should be painfully simple.

15. The actual MVP scope

Build only this:

Admin
/admin/leads
/admin/leads/[leadId]
/admin/leads/campaigns
/admin/leads/source-runs
/admin/leads/menu-intake
Public
/start/{token}
Backend
Apify import
lead normalization
dedupe
scoring
onboarding link creation
WhatsApp click-to-chat generation
email send
menu submission upload
MenuList link writeback
event logging
suppression
Data
leadCampaigns
leadSourceRuns
leads
leadDedupeKeys
leadOutreachEvents
leadOnboardingLinks
leadMenuSubmissions
leadSuppressions

That is enough.

16. Remaining stages
Stage 9 — Follow-up automation

Purpose:

simple follow-up queue, max 2 follow-ups, stop on reply/DNC

Do not build sequences like a sales tool.

Need define:

Day 0 initial
Day 3 follow-up
Day 7 final
then stop
Stage 10 — Preview-link experiment

Purpose:

test whether AI previews improve conversion enough to justify cost

Preview should not be default.

Test only after baseline exists.

Groups:

A: message only
B: onboarding link
C: AI preview

Decision rule:

AI preview must improve menu_received or link_created rate by at least 2x to justify complexity.
Stage 11 — Metrics and cost control

Purpose:

know whether this replaces paid lead gen / marketing labor

Track:

cost per raw lead
cost per qualified lead
cost per contacted lead
cost per menu received
cost per MenuList link created
cost per owner-confirmed link

This is where you decide whether to scale.

Stage 12 — Scale playbook

Purpose:

how to expand from one area/category to multiple clusters

Scale only after one campaign works.

Recommended expansion:

one area
→ one city cluster
→ one city
→ nearby city
→ category variants

Not India-wide first.

Stage 13 — Implementation backlog

Purpose:

turn this into build tasks

This should be the next practical planning stage after Stage 9–12.

17. Final reviewed architecture

This is the clean version:

1. Campaign
   city + area + category + cap

2. Apify source run
   import raw food businesses

3. Normalization
   clean phone/email/domain/category/area

4. Dedupe
   phone/email/domain/maps/name-area-city keys

5. Scoring
   fit + reachability + menu gap + demand + risk

6. Dashboard
   ready-to-contact queue

7. Outreach
   assisted WhatsApp or email

8. Onboarding
   /start/{token}
   upload menu / WhatsApp fallback

9. Menu intake
   submission queue

10. Existing MenuList generation
   create menu link + QR

11. Send back
   WhatsApp/email final link

12. Conversion tracking
   link sent / owner confirmed / usage

That is the system.

18. My strongest recommendation now

Do not continue designing more abstractions yet.

The next useful spec should be:

Stage 9 — Follow-up automation
Stage 10 — Preview experiment
Stage 11 — Metrics/cost dashboard
Stage 12 — Scale playbook
Stage 13 — MVP implementation backlog

After those, freeze the design and build v0.

The key operating principle remains:

Spend automation before outreach.
Spend human judgment at outreach.
Spend AI only after menu intent.

That is the right cost/risk/quality balance for MenuList.
````

````text
Yes. If you are ready to use AI heavily, I would upgrade the system from a lead dashboard to an AI-operated lead engine.

The earlier version was intentionally conservative:

Apify finds leads
→ human reviews
→ human sends
→ owner sends menu
→ human creates MenuList link

The AI-heavy version should become:

Apify finds leads
→ AI cleans, dedupes, scores, enriches, classifies
→ AI drafts outreach
→ human approves / system sends depending on risk
→ AI reads replies
→ AI extracts menu from image/PDF
→ AI builds structured MenuList draft
→ AI QA-checks against source file
→ human only reviews exceptions
→ final link + QR sent automatically

The goal is not “AI everywhere.” The goal is:

AI handles repetitive judgment.
Human handles irreversible / risky decisions.
My revised recommendation

Use AI aggressively in four places:

1. Lead quality
2. Outreach
3. Reply handling
4. Menu creation + QA

Do not waste AI on:

AI websites
fake previews
AI-generated food photos
public pages before owner input

That still stands.

The best use of AI is not making demos. The best use of AI is removing your operational labor.

Recommended Google AI stack

Use this stack:

Next.js + Firebase/Firestore + Cloud Functions
Apify for scraping
Gemini API / Vertex AI Gemini API for AI work
Genkit for AI workflows
Firebase Storage for menu files

For model access, use Google’s Gemini models server-side from Cloud Functions or Cloud Run. Firebase AI Logic is useful when you need client-side mobile/web Gemini calls with Firebase integrations, App Check protection, and configurable per-user rate limits, but this internal lead engine should mostly call Gemini from the backend, not directly from the browser. Firebase AI Logic also supports both the Gemini Developer API and Vertex AI Gemini API providers, so the provider can be switched without rebuilding the whole app.
Firebase

Use Genkit for AI workflows, not raw scattered model calls. Genkit flows give you type-safe input/output schemas, visual debugging, deployment to Cloud Functions, and a clean way to wrap multi-step AI logic. That fits this system because every AI action should produce structured outputs, not loose text.
genkit.dev

Do not hardcode one model permanently. Firebase’s model docs currently warn that older Gemini 1.0/1.5 are already shut down and Gemini 2.0 Flash / Flash-Lite shut down on June 1, 2026; Firebase recommends using Remote Config so model/version can be changed without shipping a new app.
Firebase

Model routing

Use different Gemini models by task.

Task	Recommended model type	Reason
Lead cleanup, category classification, dedupe hints	Flash-Lite / low-cost model	High-volume, low-risk
Lead scoring explanation	Flash-Lite or Flash	Needs judgment, not deep reasoning
Website/menu presence detection	Flash	Needs web/content interpretation
Outreach personalization	Flash-Lite	Cheap, repeatable
Reply classification	Flash-Lite	Short text classification
Menu image/PDF understanding	Flash or Pro for hard cases	Vision + structured extraction
Menu QA against source file	Flash / Pro for low-confidence cases	Accuracy matters
Daily campaign analysis	Pro or Flash	Reasoning over metrics
Large batch scoring	Gemini Batch API	Lower-cost async processing

Google’s Gemini 3 docs list Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite as the cost-efficient high-volume model, Gemini 3 Flash as speed/pricing with strong intelligence, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview for more complex reasoning; the same page also shows pricing by model and says Gemini 3 supports the Batch API.
Google AI for Developers

For high-volume, non-urgent jobs, use Gemini Batch API. Google says the Batch API is designed for large asynchronous workloads at 50% of standard cost, with a target turnaround of 24 hours. That is ideal for overnight lead scoring, enrichment, duplicate checks, and campaign audits.
Google AI for Developers

Revised AI-first system
1. AI Campaign Planner

Instead of manually deciding queries, let AI generate the Apify campaign plan.

Input:

Areas: Koramangala, Indiranagar, HSR, Jayanagar

JSON

Human work reduced:

campaign setup thinking
query generation
area/category combinations
source-run planning

Build as:

Use Gemini structured outputs so the model returns valid JSON. Gemini supports response schemas/structured outputs, which are designed for extraction, classification, and agentic workflows.

4. AI Menu Gap Detector

Build the AI-heavy version, but not as a freeform “agent that does everything.”

Build it as small deterministic AI flows:

Use Google Gemini models, Genkit flows, structured outputs, function calling, and Batch API.
````

````text
Correct. Stop thinking in “stages” or “MVP.” Long-term, this should be an AI-operated acquisition system where humans mostly supervise exceptions.

The target system is:

MenuList Acquisition OS

Apify / sources find businesses
→ AI cleans, dedupes, enriches, scores, and prioritizes
→ AI decides best channel and drafts outreach
→ AI monitors replies and updates lead state
→ AI collects menu files
→ AI extracts structured menu data
→ AI QA-checks extracted menu against source files
→ MenuList generates link + QR
→ AI sends final message

The dashboard becomes a control room, not the operating layer.

1. Core architecture

Use this architecture long-term:

Sources
  Apify, manual lists, website crawlers, customer demand signals

Data Layer
  Firestore, Storage, existing MenuList business/menu records

AI Control Plane
  Genkit flows + Gemini models + tool/function calls

Execution Layer
  Cloud Functions, Cloud Tasks, scheduled jobs, webhooks

Human Console
  Approvals, exceptions, disputes, QA overrides

Learning Layer
  Campaign results, message performance, source quality, AI error logs

The important mental model:

Every lead is an object.
Every AI decision is an event.
Every AI action has confidence, cost, and rollback path.

Do not build one free-roaming “agent.” Build many narrow AI workers with strict contracts.

Google’s Gemini API supports structured outputs where model responses follow a JSON Schema, which is exactly what you need for reliable classification, extraction, scoring, and tool inputs. Gemini function calling lets the model call external tools/APIs by returning structured parameters instead of free text. Genkit flows are also a good fit because they give type-safe inputs/outputs, developer UI tracing, and deployment to Cloud Functions/Firebase.

4. Model routing

Use different Gemini models for different jobs.

Do not use the strongest model for everything.

Cheap/high-volume model:
- lead normalization
- category classification
- reject reasons
- outreach template selection
- reply classification
- simple scoring

Stronger model:
- fuzzy duplicate resolution
- website/menu inspection
- campaign analysis
- complex reply handling

Multimodal model:
- menu image/PDF understanding
- menu extraction
- menu QA

Batch processing:
- overnight scoring
- bulk normalization
- campaign analysis
- source quality analysis

Gemini Batch API is specifically designed for large asynchronous workloads at 50% of standard cost, which is useful for overnight lead scoring, source quality review, and batch enrichment. Google also supports grounding with Google Search for real-time web content, and Firebase recommends Remote Config so model names/config can be changed without shipping app updates.
Firebase

    | "reply_classification"
    | "menu_extraction"
    | "menu_qa"
    | "campaign_optimization";

  defaultModel: string;
  fallbackModel?: string;

  mode: "realtime" | "batch";

  maxCostUsdPerRun: number;
  maxLatencyMs?: number;

  humanReviewBelowConfidence: number;
};

};

Use Remote Config or an internal config table for model routing. Hardcoding model names everywhere is brittle.

7. AI worker 3 — Duplicate Resolver

Deterministic dedupe remains first:

phone
email
domain
maps URL
name + area + city

AI handles fuzzy cases.

Input:

TypeScript
type DuplicateResolverInput = {
  candidateLead: LeadSummary;
  possibleMatches: LeadSummary[];
};

Output:

TypeScript
type DuplicateResolverOutput = {
  matches: {
    leadId: string;
    isDuplicate: boolean;
    confidence: number;
    reason: string;
    recommendedAction: "merge" | "keep_separate" | "human_review";
  }[];
};

Auto-action rule:

Auto-merge only if:
- strong key match exists, or
- AI confidence >= 0.97 and name/area/address are highly similar

Human review:

confidence 0.75–0.97

Never auto-merge:

same chain name but different branch
same name but different area
conflicting phone numbers
conflicting websites

This prevents duplicate outreach without damaging data integrity.

8. AI worker 4 — Website/Menu Inspector

This is one of the highest-value AI workers.

It answers:

Not:

Tools:

Use function calling here. Gemini function calling is designed for workflows where the model decides when to call tools/APIs and returns structured parameters for those calls.

Input:

This is where AI improves quality massively.

Examples:

Website exists but menu is a PDF → good lead.
Website exists and menu is clean/mobile/shareable → lower priority.
No website + phone available → good lead.
Instagram-only menu → good lead.
Delivery-only menu → possible lead.

Do not manually inspect websites. Let AI do it.

  confidence: number;
};

Hard rules:

No invented prices.
No invented items.
No generated descriptions unless source contains them.
No “popular” labels unless owner/source explicitly says so.
No food photos.

If uncertain:

needsReview = true

The extraction output must be schema-validated. Gemini structured outputs are designed for exactly this kind of predictable JSON extraction.
Google AI for Developers

15. AI worker 11 — Menu QA Agent

This is non-negotiable.

Any AI-extracted menu must be checked by a second AI pass.

Input:

TypeScript
type MenuQaInput = {
  originalFiles: MenuFile[];
  extractedMenu: MenuExtractionOutput;
};

Output:

TypeScript
type MenuQaOutput = {
  safeToPublish: boolean;

  qaScore: number; // 0-100

  issues: {
    severity: "low" | "medium" | "high" | "critical";
    type:
      | "missing_item"
      | "extra_item_not_in_source"
      | "wrong_price"
      | "unclear_price"
      | "wrong_section"
      | "duplicate_item"
      | "source_unreadable";
    itemName?: string;
    explanation: string;
    suggestedFix?: string;
  }[];

  humanReviewRequired: boolean;
  confidence: number;
};

Auto-publish rule:

Only safe if:
qaScore >= 95
no critical issues
no high issues
confidence >= 0.92

Otherwise:

human review

This is how AI improves speed without lowering quality.
````
