18. Automation permission levels

Every AI worker needs an action level.

Level 0 — Suggest only

AI gives recommendation. Human must act.

Use for:

new flows
legal/compliance edge cases
large campaign changes
first-time source types
high-value restaurant groups
Level 1 — Draft and queue

AI prepares action. Human approves in dashboard.

Use for:

first WhatsApp message
duplicate merge
message changes
menu publish
negative replies
Level 2 — Act with guardrails

AI can act if confidence and rules pass.

Use for:

lead normalization
lead scoring
bad lead rejection
email follow-ups
menu file quality checks
creating menu draft
standard replies
Level 3 — Fully autonomous

AI acts without human review.

Use for:

daily reports
score recalculation
campaign anomaly detection
onboarding link creation
event classification
low-risk status updates

This permission model is more important than the model choice.

19. Long-term AI control table

Add this:

TypeScript
type AiPolicy = {
  flowName: string;

  enabled: boolean;

  autonomyLevel: 0 | 1 | 2 | 3;

  confidenceThresholds: {
    autoApprove: number;
    humanReview: number;
    rejectBelow: number;
  };

  maxDailyRuns: number;
  maxDailyCostUsd: number;

  allowedActions: string[];
  blockedActions: string[];

  modelRoute: string;

  evalRequired: boolean;
  lastEvalScore?: number;

  updatedAt: Date;
};

Example:

TypeScript
{
  flowName: "menuExtraction",
  autonomyLevel: 2,
  confidenceThresholds: {
    autoApprove: 0.95,
    humanReview: 0.80,
    rejectBelow: 0.50
  },
  maxDailyRuns: 500,
  maxDailyCostUsd: 30,
  allowedActions: ["create_menu_draft", "flag_review_items"],
  blockedActions: ["publish_menu", "send_to_owner_without_qa"],
  modelRoute: "menu_extraction_v1",
  evalRequired: true
}

This lets you increase autonomy safely over time.

20. AI evaluation system

If AI is doing heavy work, you need evals.

Create test sets:

100 historical leads with correct A/B/C labels
100 duplicate pairs with correct merge/no-merge labels
100 replies with correct classification
100 menu files with human-verified extracted menus
100 QA cases with known errors

For each AI worker, measure:

accuracy
false positive rate
false negative rate
human override rate
cost per successful action
latency
confidence calibration

Add:

aiEvalResults

Schema:

TypeScript
type AiEvalResult = {
  id: string;
  flowName: string;
  model: string;
  datasetName: string;

  metrics: {
    accuracy?: number;
    precision?: number;
    recall?: number;
    falsePositiveRate?: number;
    falseNegativeRate?: number;
    humanOverrideRate?: number;
    avgCostUsd?: number;
    avgLatencyMs?: number;
  };

  passed: boolean;
  createdAt: Date;
};

Rule:

No AI worker gets more autonomy unless evals pass.

This is how you avoid “AI chaos.”

Heavy AI is fine, but cost must follow value.

Cheap AI before intent

Use for:

This improves lead quality.

Expensive AI after intent

Use for:

menu image/PDF extraction
menu QA
owner reply understanding

This creates MenuList assets.

Batch AI where possible

Use for:

overnight lead scoring
bulk duplicate review
source quality analysis
campaign reports

Gemini Batch API is suitable for non-urgent large-scale tasks and offers 50% of standard cost.

Cache repeated context

22. WhatsApp automation boundary

Even in the AI-heavy version, do not let AI blindly blast WhatsApp.

Long-term channel model:

Email:
AI can automate more aggressively.

WhatsApp:
AI can draft, classify, and prepare.
Human or compliant API layer sends, depending on consent and policy.

Replies:
AI can classify and draft responses.

DNC:
AI can detect, system suppresses immediately.

WhatsApp Business Platform pricing is per delivered message and varies by market and category; Meta lists marketing, utility, authentication, and service categories. Templates must also be approved before being sent as template messages.
WhatsApp for Business
+1

So the AI-heavy version should be:

AI prepares WhatsApp.
Human/compliant sending layer controls WhatsApp.

Do not let lead volume burn the WhatsApp channel.

This is not a lead-gen tool anymore.

I searched across four relevant markets: AI outbound platforms, Google Maps/local lead tools, personalized landing-page outbound, and restaurant growth/menu platforms. The main finding is clear:

Everyone is moving toward AI-operated acquisition loops, but most are optimizing for meetings or sales calls. MenuList should optimize for owner-submitted menu truth.

That gives us a sharper system than generic AI SDR tools.

1. AI SDR platforms are becoming autonomous GTM workers

→ personalize outreach
→ run multi-channel sequences
→ classify replies
→ optimize based on results

Artisan’s Ava claims to source leads, track intent signals, write/send personalized multi-channel campaigns, handle objections, and optimize copy. Regie.ai frames itself as an AI sales engagement platform where AI agents handle prospecting work and prioritize leads for reps.

My corrected final recommendation

Build:

another onboarding system

The Growth Engine’s job:

Yes. Adding WhatsApp + Instagram DM + Messenger + Email changes the system materially.

The Growth Engine should now be designed as an omnichannel acquisition engine, not just a lead scraper + outreach dashboard.

The core job remains:

source leads
→ qualify
→ choose best channel
→ send/prepare message
→ capture replies
→ classify intent

→ learn which channel/source/message converts

But now we need a proper channel layer.

1. Core correction: not all channels behave the same

Treat the four channels differently.

Channel	Best use	Cold outbound?	Automation level
Email	Scalable cold outreach	Yes, with compliance	High
WhatsApp	High-intent business contact	Limited / careful	Medium
Instagram DM	Inbound, replies, ads, warm social leads	Not ideal for cold automation	Medium-low
Messenger	Inbound, Facebook Page, ads, warm leads	Not ideal for cold automation	Medium-low

The main rule:

Email = scalable outbound.
WhatsApp = high-quality assisted or template-based outbound.
Instagram/Messenger = inbound + warm conversation capture, not cold DM blasting.

WhatsApp Business policy says you may contact people only if they gave you their number and opted in, and WhatsApp Business Platform conversations must be initiated with approved templates; replies inside the 24-hour customer-service window can use non-template messages.
WhatsApp for Business

Messenger and Instagram Messaging also operate around a 24-hour response window after a user message, and Meta’s Instagram Messaging API is for Instagram Professional accounts at scale.
Facebook Developers
+2
Facebook Developers
+2

So the system should not assume all channels are equal.

2. New architecture: Omnichannel Growth Engine

Add one major internal layer:

Channel Execution Layer

Full structure:

Lead Source Layer
  Apify, Outscraper, manual CSV, website crawl, referrals, ads

Lead Intelligence Layer
  AI fit scoring, need detection, duplicate detection, contactability

Channel Identity Layer
  email, WhatsApp number, Instagram username/thread, Messenger PSID/thread

Channel Policy Layer
  opt-in, 24-hour windows, templates, suppression, caps

Message Strategy Layer
  offer angle, channel choice, flow routing, AI message generation

Unified Inbox Layer
  inbound replies from WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, email

AI Reply Layer
  classify replies, detect intent, draft response, update lead state

Routing Layer
  send interested leads into existing MenuList onboarding flow

Learning Layer
  attribution, conversion by source/channel/message/flow

This becomes the long-term acquisition system.

6. Channel strategy by channel
6.1 Email

Email should be the most automated outbound channel.

Use it for:

follow-ups
retargeting clicked-but-not-started leads
formal businesses
fallback when WhatsApp not usable

Recommended provider path:

Start: Resend for speed/dev experience
Scale: Amazon SES for cost

Amazon SES lists outbound email at $0.10 per 1,000 emails, with additional costs for data, inbound mail, validation, dedicated IPs, and deliverability tools.
Amazon Web Services, Inc.

6.2 WhatsApp

WhatsApp should be high-trust, not high-blast.

Use it for:

A leads with phone
businesses likely to use WhatsApp
warm follow-up after click/reply
high-value leads
owner replies

Two modes:

Mode A — Assisted WhatsApp
AI drafts message
→ operator clicks “Open WhatsApp”
→ WhatsApp opens with prefilled message
→ human sends
→ system logs sent

This is the safest first mode.

Mode B — WhatsApp Business Platform API

Use only with:

approved templates
clear opt-in/compliant basis
rate limits
quality monitoring
DNC suppression

WhatsApp requires approved templates to initiate conversations on the Business Platform and allows non-template replies inside the 24-hour customer service window.
WhatsApp for Business

WhatsApp features needed:

template library
template approval status
conversation window tracking
message quality tracking
opt-out handling
DNC suppression
assisted-send fallback
AI reply classification
handoff to human

Important: WhatsApp should not be treated like email.

6.3 Instagram DM

Instagram DM should be treated as a warm/inbound channel.

Use it for:

businesses that message MenuList
click-to-Instagram ad conversations
Instagram profile CTA
comments that become DMs where allowed
manual warm outreach tracking
social proof conversations

Do not build automated cold Instagram DM blasting.

Meta’s Instagram Messaging API is for Instagram Professional accounts, and Meta’s docs indicate messaging apps generally have 24 hours to respond after a user message.

Your thinking is correct, with one important refinement:

The pipeline should not only find leads.
It should decide the best channel, best message, best timing, and best MenuList onboarding route for each lead.

So the system should become:

AI Omnichannel Growth Engine

Its job:

lead found
→ AI qualifies
→ AI chooses best channel
→ AI chooses message angle
→ system sends/prepares message
→ inbox captures replies
→ AI classifies intent
→ interested lead is routed into existing MenuList onboarding
→ outcome feeds back into future channel decisions

This is the correct direction.

My decision

Build a Channel Recommendation Engine at the center of the lead-gen system.

Do not hardcode:

if phone → WhatsApp
if email → email
if Instagram → DM

That is too crude.

Instead, for every lead, the AI should output:

JSON
{
  "primaryChannel": "whatsapp",
  "backupChannel": "email",
  "sendMode": "assisted",
  "messageAngle": "menu_link_qr",
  "onboardingFlowId": "restaurant_quick_start",
  "reason": "A-score local cafe, phone available, likely WhatsApp-reachable, no clean menu link detected.",
  "confidence": 0.87
}

The system should tell you:

who to contact
where to contact them
what to say
what flow to send them to
what to do next if they reply/click/ignore
1. The channel decision model

The system should score each channel per lead.

For every lead, compute:

WhatsApp score
Email score
Instagram DM score
Messenger score
Call score, optional
Hold score

Then pick:

primary channel
backup channel
send mode
follow-up path

The channel score should use six factors.

Channel Score =
  Contact Availability
+ Policy Eligibility
+ Lead-Channel Fit
+ Intent / History
+ Cost / Risk
+ Experiment Priority
- Suppression / Negative Signals
1. Contact availability
Does the lead have this channel identity?

Examples:

phone exists → WhatsApp possible
email exists → email possible
Instagram handle exists → Instagram possible
Messenger PSID exists → Messenger possible

But availability does not mean “send immediately.”

2. Policy eligibility

This is the gatekeeper.

WhatsApp, Instagram, and Messenger are not the same as email.

WhatsApp Business Platform requires business-initiated messages outside the customer-service window to use approved templates; Meta’s WhatsApp template documentation says template messages are the type used outside the customer-service window.
Facebook Developers

Messenger and Instagram Messaging use a standard 24-hour response window after a user message; Meta’s Messenger/IG messaging policy states businesses have up to 24 hours to respond to a user.
Facebook Developers

Meta’s Instagram Messaging API is built for Instagram Professional accounts at scale, and webhooks are used to receive real-time Instagram messaging events.
Facebook Developers
+1

So the system must first ask:

Are we allowed to send on this channel right now?

Before it asks:

Will this channel convert?
3. Lead-channel fit

Some leads are naturally better for certain channels.

Examples:

small cafe with public phone → WhatsApp likely strong
formal restaurant with website/email → email likely acceptable
Instagram-active cafe → Instagram can be useful, especially if conversation is warm
Facebook-active business → Messenger useful if they engage through Facebook/Page/ads
high-value lead → WhatsApp + manual call
low-confidence lead → email or hold
4. Intent / history

Past behavior should dominate future messaging.

Examples:

opened email but did not start onboarding → email follow-up
clicked WhatsApp link → WhatsApp follow-up
replied on Instagram → continue Instagram within allowed window
started onboarding but dropped → send help message
asked price → send pricing/value response
said not interested → suppress/hold

Do not treat old leads as new leads.

5. Cost / risk

Each channel has different risk.

Email: low cost, scalable, but deliverability risk
WhatsApp: high response potential, but policy/account-quality risk
Instagram: useful for warm/social leads, risky for cold automation
Messenger: useful for Page/ad-driven inbound, not ideal as cold channel

In India, commercial communication also has a regulatory context. TRAI maintains an Unsolicited Commercial Communication framework, and recent amendments strengthened commercial-message traceability and anti-spam controls.
TRAI
+1

So the system needs suppression, opt-out handling, daily caps, and channel eligibility rules.

6. Experiment priority

Sometimes the AI should choose a channel because you need learning.

Example:

For Bangalore cafes, test:
- WhatsApp assisted
- email
- Instagram warm DM

But experiments should be controlled.

Do not let the system “test” by blasting every platform.

2. Recommended default channel strategy

This is how I would set the default logic.

Email

Use email for:

cold scalable outreach
lower-risk lead batches
backup after WhatsApp not sent/replied
formal businesses
retargeting clicked-but-not-started leads

Automation level:

high

Email can be AI-drafted and system-sent, with unsubscribe/bounce/suppression handling.

WhatsApp

Use WhatsApp for:

A-score leads with phone
small/local restaurants and cafes
high-intent or high-value leads
follow-up after reply/click
manual founder/operator outreach

Automation level:

medium

Start with:

AI drafts → operator approves/sends

Later:

approved WhatsApp templates → API send where compliant

WhatsApp should not be treated as a bulk cold-blast channel.

Instagram DM

Use Instagram for:

businesses whose Instagram is their main public presence
inbound DMs
click-to-Instagram ads
comment-to-DM campaigns
warm social conversations

Automation level:

medium-low

The system should manage and respond to DMs, but I would not make cold Instagram DM the default lead-outreach channel. Use Instagram mainly when the lead has interacted or when the campaign is designed to generate inbound DM intent.

Messenger

Use Messenger for:

Facebook Page messages
click-to-Messenger ads
inbound conversations
warm retargeting through Page interactions

Automation level:

medium-low

Messenger is useful as an inbound and ad-driven conversation channel, not as the default cold outbound channel.

3. Final channel rules

Use this as the baseline.

Lead condition	Primary channel	Backup	Send mode
A lead + phone + local SMB	WhatsApp	Email	Assisted/template
A lead + email only	Email	Hold/manual research	Auto
A lead + active Instagram + no email	Instagram	WhatsApp if phone exists	Warm/manual/inbound
A lead from Instagram ad/DM	Instagram	Email/WhatsApp if shared	Reply-window automation
A lead from Facebook/Messenger	Messenger	Email/WhatsApp if shared	Reply-window automation
B lead + phone	WhatsApp or email	Email	Assisted
B lead + email only	Email	Hold	Auto
C lead	Hold	None	No outreach
DNC/negative	None	None	Blocked
Already converted	None	None	Suppress acquisition

8. Recommended decision tree

Use this simplified logic.

1. Is lead suppressed?
   → Do nothing.

2. Has lead already completed onboarding?
   → Suppress acquisition outreach.

3. Did lead message us on Instagram/Messenger/WhatsApp recently?
   → Reply on same channel within allowed window.

4. Is lead A-score with phone?
   → WhatsApp assisted or approved template.

5. Is lead A/B-score with email?
   → Email.

6. Is lead Instagram-active but no email/phone?
   → Hold for social/inbound campaign, or manual DM only if appropriate.

7. Did lead click but not start onboarding?
   → Follow up on same channel or email.

8. Did lead start onboarding but drop?
   → Send help-oriented message.

9. Low score / unclear / no channel?
   → Hold or enrich.

That is the correct practical behavior.

Your thinking is right:

Lead gen must be intelligent enough to decide where to message each lead.

But the system should not simply choose the channel with available contact info.

It should choose using:

````text
Spec 1 — System Charter and Boundaries
1.1 System name

Use this working name:

MenuList AI Omnichannel Growth Engine

Short internal name:

Growth Engine

The name matters because this is not an onboarding system, not a menu system, and not a product module. It is an acquisition machine.

1.2 One-line charter
The Growth Engine finds, qualifies, contacts, manages, and routes business leads into existing MenuList onboarding flows using AI-driven source intelligence, channel selection, messaging, and reply handling.

More simply:

Find the right businesses.
Decide where to message them.
Say the right thing.
Manage the conversation.
Route interested leads into MenuList.
Learn what converts.
1.3 What the Growth Engine owns

The Growth Engine owns the full marketing and lead acquisition layer.

It owns:

lead discovery
lead enrichment
lead deduplication
lead scoring
lead prioritization
channel selection
promotion campaigns
message generation
message sending/preparation
DM/email inbox management
reply classification
objection handling
follow-up logic
retargeting logic
existing onboarding-flow routing
suppression / do-not-contact management
campaign attribution
channel performance analytics
AI campaign optimization

This is the system’s territory.

1.4 What the Growth Engine does not own

The Growth Engine must not own MenuList product workflows.

It does not own:

MenuList onboarding UX
menu upload flow
menu extraction
menu editing
menu publishing
business verification
business profile management
QR generation
owner dashboard
pricing/payments
customer-facing business pages
freshness confirmations
restaurant account management

Those belong to existing MenuList systems.

The Growth Engine can send leads into those systems and receive feedback events back, but it does not manage the product workflow itself.

1.5 The clean boundary

The clean boundary is:

Growth Engine → routes lead into existing MenuList onboarding flow
MenuList Product → handles onboarding, activation, and product value creation
Growth Engine ← receives outcome events for learning and attribution

The Growth Engine’s terminal job is:

lead routed to correct onboarding flow

Then it waits for feedback:

clicked
started onboarding
completed onboarding
converted
dropped

It should not care how the onboarding flow internally works.

1.6 Primary objective

The objective is not:

scrape maximum leads
send maximum messages
increase DM volume
get replies
book calls
generate previews

The objective is:

increase qualified business leads entering and completing existing MenuList onboarding flows at the lowest sustainable cost and lowest channel risk.

This is the central optimization target.

1.7 Core output

The Growth Engine produces these outputs:

qualified lead
recommended channel
recommended message
recommended onboarding flow
conversation state
next-best action
conversion attribution
campaign recommendations

Example output for one lead:

JSON
{
  "leadId": "lead_123",
  "segment": "A",
  "primaryChannel": "whatsapp",
  "backupChannel": "email",
  "sendMode": "assisted",
  "messageAngle": "menu_link_qr",
  "onboardingFlowId": "restaurant_quick_start",
  "nextBestAction": "prepare_whatsapp_message",
  "reason": "High-fit local cafe with phone available and likely need for a clean customer-facing menu link."
}

That is what the system should produce repeatedly.

1.8 Core users

There are three internal users.

Founder / admin

Can:

create campaigns
approve channel strategy
change scoring rules
review AI recommendations
pause channels
override AI decisions
view economics
manage integrations
Growth operator

Can:

review lead queues
approve messages
handle inbox exceptions
mark replies
suppress leads
route interested leads
monitor daily work queue
AI worker

Can:

score leads
recommend channels
draft messages
classify replies
recommend next actions
summarize campaigns
detect anomalies

AI is treated as an internal worker with limited permissions, not as an unrestricted agent.

1.9 Core principle: AI recommends, policy gates

The system should be AI-driven, but not AI-unbounded.

The order of decision-making should be:

1. Suppression / safety rules
2. Channel policy eligibility
3. Lead quality score
4. AI channel recommendation
5. AI message generation
6. Human approval or auto-send depending on permission level

AI must never override:

do-not-contact
suppression
channel policy
daily caps
blocked template status
invalid contact
human stop decision

The AI can recommend. The policy layer has veto power.

1.10 Channel responsibility

The Growth Engine owns messaging across:

email
WhatsApp
Instagram DM
Messenger

But each channel has a different role.

Email

Role:

scalable outbound and retargeting channel

The system can automate email more aggressively because it is structurally suited to outbound, assuming unsubscribe, bounce, and suppression handling are implemented.

WhatsApp

Role:

high-quality direct outreach and reply channel

WhatsApp should be controlled. WhatsApp Business policy says outside the 24-hour customer-service window, businesses may only send approved message templates; user messages can be replied to without templates inside the 24-hour window.
WhatsApp for Business

Instagram DM

Role:

warm/inbound/social acquisition channel

Instagram DM should primarily manage conversations from inbound DMs, social campaigns, profile CTAs, comment-to-DM flows, and warm interactions. Meta’s Instagram Messaging API is for Instagram Professional accounts at scale, and Instagram messaging webhooks can deliver real-time notifications.
Facebook Developers
+1

Messenger

Role:

Facebook Page / ad-driven / inbound conversation channel

Messenger and Instagram messaging policies use a standard 24-hour response window after user interaction, so the Growth Engine must track whether a conversation is inside or outside the allowed response window.
Facebook Developers

1.11 The key system brain

The most important internal module is:

AI Channel Router

It answers:

Where should we message this lead?

But in full, it decides:

Should we message this lead?
Which channel should we use?
Should it be automated or assisted?
What should we say?
Which onboarding flow should we route to?
When should we follow up?
When should we stop?

This is more important than the scraper itself.

Apify finds raw supply. The Channel Router decides how to turn that supply into qualified demand.

1.12 Growth Engine owned states

The Growth Engine owns these lead states:

new
enriched
scored
qualified
ready_to_contact
contacted
clicked
replied
interested
routed_to_onboarding
onboarding_started
onboarding_completed
converted
not_interested
do_not_contact
suppressed

It does not own internal product states like:

menu_uploaded
menu_extracted
menu_published
business_verified
owner_dashboard_created

Those can be sent back as feedback events, but they are not Growth Engine states.

1.13 Feedback events from MenuList product

Existing MenuList onboarding flows should emit events back to the Growth Engine.

Minimum events:

TypeScript
type OnboardingFeedbackEvent =
  | "flow_link_clicked"
  | "onboarding_started"
  | "onboarding_step_completed"
  | "onboarding_dropped"
  | "onboarding_completed"
  | "converted";

Suggested event payload:

TypeScript
type GrowthFeedbackEvent = {
  eventId: string;

  leadId: string;
  campaignId?: string;
  channel?: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger";
  messageId?: string;
  onboardingFlowId: string;

  eventType:
    | "flow_link_clicked"
    | "onboarding_started"
    | "onboarding_step_completed"
    | "onboarding_dropped"
    | "onboarding_completed"
    | "converted";

  metadata?: Record<string, unknown>;

  occurredAt: Date;
};

The Growth Engine uses this to learn:

which sources work
which channels work
which messages work
which onboarding flow works for which lead type
1.14 Interface from Growth Engine to onboarding

The handoff should be explicit.

TypeScript
type RouteLeadToOnboardingInput = {
  leadId: string;

  onboardingFlowId: string;

  campaignId?: string;
  channel: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger";

  offerAngle:
    | "menu_link_qr"
    | "instagram_bio_menu"
    | "whatsapp_menu_link"
    | "google_profile_menu_link"
    | "simple_setup"
    | "local_restaurant_setup";

  tracking: {
    sourceRunId?: string;
    messageId?: string;
    experimentId?: string;
    variantId?: string;
  };
};

Output:

TypeScript
type RouteLeadToOnboardingOutput = {
  flowUrl: string;
  trackingUrl: string;
};

The Growth Engine should not create a new onboarding flow. It should select and route into an existing one.

1.15 What the AI is allowed to do

AI can:

classify business type
detect likely fit
detect likely need
score lead quality
recommend channel
recommend message angle
choose onboarding flow
draft messages
classify replies
draft replies
recommend follow-ups
summarize campaign performance
recommend campaign changes
detect risk and anomalies

AI can act automatically only when:

confidence is high
policy allows it
suppression checks pass
channel caps allow it
the action is low-risk
1.16 What AI is not allowed to do

AI must not:

override do-not-contact
message suppressed leads
send WhatsApp/Instagram/Messenger outside policy windows
invent claims about the business
say we scraped them
mention Google Maps/reviews/ratings in outreach
claim their website/menu is bad without verified basis
create fake urgency
promise guaranteed results
route leads into non-existing flows
change MenuList onboarding behavior
change pricing
publish product-facing content

This is a hard boundary.

1.17 Messaging boundary

The Growth Engine can say:

MenuList helps restaurants create a clean customer-facing menu link + QR.
You can start here.

It should not say:

Your current menu is missing.
Your website is bad.
You are losing customers.
We scraped your profile.
We generated this for you.
We guarantee more customers.

The message should be useful, direct, and low-friction.

The system should optimize for:

clear CTA
low cognitive load
high trust
low creepiness
1.18 Promotion boundary

The system can run promotions.

A promotion is:

a controlled campaign to a defined segment using defined channels, templates, caps, and onboarding routes.

It is not:

unrestricted broadcasting

Promotion campaign inputs:

audience
channel mix
message angle
onboarding flow
template variants
daily caps
suppression rules
stop conditions

Example:

Bangalore cafe QR-menu campaign

Audience:
A-score cafes in Koramangala and Indiranagar

Channels:
WhatsApp assisted + email fallback

Offer:
clean menu link + QR

Onboarding flow:
restaurant_quick_start

Caps:
100 contacts/day
pause if negative response > 3%

This is how promotions should run.

1.19 Safety and reputation boundary

The system must protect:

MenuList domain reputation
WhatsApp account quality
Instagram account quality
Messenger/Page quality
sender identity
brand trust
legal/compliance posture

Therefore every outbound action must pass:

suppression check
channel eligibility check
daily cap check
campaign cap check
message safety check
template status check, if applicable

A lead saying “don’t contact” on one channel must suppress acquisition contact across all channels unless an admin explicitly narrows scope.

1.20 Core objects owned by Growth Engine

The Growth Engine should own these objects:

growthLeads
growthCampaigns
growthSourceRuns
growthConversations
growthMessages
growthTemplates
growthSuppressions
growthExperiments
growthEvents
aiRuns
aiPolicies
channelIdentities

It should not own:

menus
business profiles
owner accounts
onboarding screens
product subscriptions
product usage state beyond feedback events
1.21 Data boundary

The Growth Engine can store:

lead identity
business name
category
location
contact details
source attribution
channel identities
message history
reply classifications
campaign performance
onboarding feedback events
suppression records
AI decisions

It should avoid storing unnecessary third-party content such as:

reviews
photos
scraped menu content
scraped long descriptions
irrelevant profile data

The system is for marketing and lead acquisition, not building a copied business database.

1.22 Human control model

Use five AI autonomy levels.

Level 0 — AI suggests only

Human must act.

Use for:

new channels
risky campaigns
large send-volume changes
policy-sensitive actions
Level 1 — AI drafts

Human approves or edits.

Use for:

first WhatsApp outreach
Instagram/Messenger replies
negative/unclear replies
Level 2 — AI queues

AI prepares action in a queue.

Use for:

email sends
follow-ups
channel recommendations
lead routing
Level 3 — AI acts with guardrails

AI acts automatically if confidence and policy checks pass.

Use for:

email follow-ups
low-risk reply answers
lead scoring
suppression on clear DNC
campaign summaries
Level 4 — AI optimizes

AI recommends or applies campaign-level changes within admin-defined caps.

Use later for:

source allocation
message variant selection
channel budget distribution

The system should start conservative per channel but be designed to support higher autonomy.

1.23 Channel automation posture

Default automation posture:

Email:
AI-drafted, auto-send allowed with caps.

WhatsApp:
AI-drafted, assisted-send by default.
API-template send only when eligible and approved.

Instagram:
AI-drafted replies for inbound/warm conversations.
No cold DM blasting by default.

Messenger:
AI-drafted replies for inbound/Page/ad conversations.
No cold blasting by default.

This is the right long-term posture.

1.24 What “intelligent lead gen” means here

For MenuList, intelligent lead gen means the system can answer:

Is this business worth contacting?
Why?
Which channel should we use?
What message angle should we use?
Which existing onboarding flow should we route them to?
What should we do if they do not reply?
What should we do if they click but do not start?
What should we do if they start but drop?
Which campaigns are producing real conversions?
Which channels are becoming risky or inefficient?

It is not just:

scrape leads and send messages.

The intelligence is in the routing, channel choice, and learning loop.

1.25 Non-negotiable principles
Principle 1 — Product boundary stays clean
Growth Engine handles acquisition.
MenuList handles product/onboarding.
Principle 2 — AI is constrained
AI works through typed flows, policies, and audit logs.
Principle 3 — Channel policy gates everything
No AI recommendation can bypass channel eligibility.
Principle 4 — Every message is attributed
Every outbound message must connect to source, campaign, channel, template, variant, and onboarding flow.
Principle 5 — Every reply becomes structured state
Replies should not stay as random inbox messages.
AI classifies and routes them.
Principle 6 — Suppression is global by default
DNC on one channel should protect all channels.
Principle 7 — Optimize for onboarding outcomes
The system should learn from onboarding starts, completions, and conversions — not just replies.
1.26 Final charter statement
The MenuList AI Omnichannel Growth Engine is an internal acquisition system that finds and qualifies business leads, selects the best messaging channel, manages outreach and conversations across email, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Messenger, routes interested leads into existing MenuList onboarding flows, and continuously improves source, channel, message, and routing decisions based on actual onboarding outcomes.

It does not own onboarding, menu creation, business verification, or product activation. It owns the marketing path up to and including lead routing, conversation management, attribution, and growth optimization.

That is the boundary.

Next spec item: North-star metrics and conversion definitions.

````text
Spec 2 — North-Star Metrics and Conversion Definitions
2.1 Core decision

The Growth Engine should not optimize for:

leads scraped
messages sent
reply rate
DM volume
email open rate
click rate

Those are useful diagnostics, but they are not the goal.

The system should optimize for:

qualified businesses entering and completing existing MenuList onboarding flows from growth-sourced channels.

Recommended north-star metric:

Growth-sourced completed onboardings per week

More exact:

Number of qualified leads sourced, contacted, and routed by the Growth Engine that complete a MenuList onboarding flow within the attribution window.

This keeps the system focused on real acquisition, not activity.

2.2 Why “completed onboarding” is the right north star

A scraped lead is not valuable.

A contacted lead is not valuable.

A reply is not necessarily valuable.

A click is not necessarily valuable.

An onboarding start is better, but still incomplete.

The strongest Growth Engine-owned result is:

lead completed an existing MenuList onboarding flow

That means the Growth Engine found the right business, reached it through a workable channel, used a good message, routed it to the right flow, and produced a real acquisition outcome.

If MenuList later has a stronger product event like:

business activated
business published
business verified
business paid
business retained

then the Growth Engine should use those as downstream quality feedback, but its core operating metric should remain:

completed onboardings from growth-sourced leads
2.3 Metric hierarchy

Use a three-layer metric model.

Layer 1: North-star metric
Layer 2: Funnel metrics
Layer 3: Diagnostic metrics
Layer 1 — North-star
Growth-sourced completed onboardings per week
Layer 2 — Funnel metrics
raw leads imported
qualified leads
contact-ready leads
messages sent/prepared
replies
clicks
interested leads
routed leads
onboarding starts
onboarding completions
converted businesses
Layer 3 — Diagnostic metrics
source quality
channel health
message performance
AI confidence
human override rate
negative response rate
suppression rate
cost per step
time-to-conversion

Do not let Layer 3 metrics dominate decisions unless they explain Layer 1.

2.4 Core funnel definitions

The Growth Engine needs strict definitions. Otherwise the dashboard will lie.

1. Raw lead

A business candidate imported from a source.

Examples:

Apify result
manual CSV row
Instagram inbound profile
Messenger inbound business
referral
website form lead

Definition:

A raw business/contact record that has not yet passed normalization, dedupe, and qualification.

Status:

raw_imported

Not counted as a real lead yet.

2. Normalized lead

A raw lead that has been cleaned into a standard format.

Required normalized fields:

business name
category
city
source
at least one identity or contact field if available

Status:

normalized

Purpose:

ready for dedupe and scoring
3. Unique lead

A normalized lead that is not a duplicate.

Deduped against:

phone
email
website/domain
Instagram identity
Messenger identity
business name + area + city
existing Growth Engine leads
existing converted businesses
suppression records

Status:

unique

This is where the system starts avoiding spam and repetition.

4. Qualified lead

A unique lead that passes fit, need, contactability, and risk thresholds.

Minimum conditions:

relevant business category
target geography or target segment
not suppressed
not obviously wrong vertical
not clearly closed
not a duplicate
has at least one usable channel or can be enriched
AI/rule score above threshold

Status:

qualified

This is the first important acquisition metric.

Formula:

qualified_lead_rate = qualified_leads / unique_leads
5. Contact-ready lead

A qualified lead with at least one eligible channel.

Eligible channel means:

email can be sent
or WhatsApp assisted/API send is allowed
or Instagram/Messenger reply is allowed
or human call/manual action is appropriate

Status:

ready_to_contact

Formula:

contact_ready_rate = contact_ready_leads / qualified_leads

This tells you whether your sources are producing reachable businesses.

6. Contacted lead

A contact-ready lead that received or was manually sent an outbound message.

For each channel:

Email: provider confirms sent
WhatsApp assisted: operator confirms sent
WhatsApp API: provider confirms accepted/sent
Instagram/Messenger: reply or allowed outbound sent

Status:

contacted

Important distinction:

WhatsApp opened ≠ contacted
WhatsApp sent/manual confirmed = contacted

Formula:

contact_rate = contacted_leads / contact_ready_leads
7. Engaged lead

A contacted lead that shows measurable interaction.

Engagement can be:

reply received
onboarding link clicked
email clicked
Instagram/Messenger response
WhatsApp response
requested details
asked question

Status:

engaged

Formula:

engagement_rate = engaged_leads / contacted_leads

Do not overvalue engagement. It is useful, but not enough.

8. Interested lead

An engaged lead whose reply or behavior indicates possible intent.

Examples:

asks for details
asks price
asks how to start
says yes
requests link
clicks setup link multiple times
starts onboarding

Status:

interested

AI should classify this.

Formula:

interest_rate = interested_leads / contacted_leads
9. Routed lead

A lead that was sent into a specific existing MenuList onboarding flow.

Required fields:

leadId
onboardingFlowId
channel
campaignId
messageId
offerAngle
trackingUrl
routedAt

Status:

routed_to_onboarding

Formula:

routing_rate = routed_leads / contacted_leads

or:

routing_rate_from_interested = routed_leads / interested_leads

This is one of the most important Growth Engine-owned actions.

10. Onboarding started

A routed lead that starts the existing MenuList onboarding flow.

This event comes from MenuList product/onboarding.

Event:

onboarding_started

Status:

onboarding_started

Formula:

onboarding_start_rate = onboarding_started / routed_leads

This measures landing/flow-message fit.

11. Onboarding completed

A routed lead that completes the existing MenuList onboarding flow.

This event comes from MenuList product/onboarding.

Event:

onboarding_completed

Status:

onboarding_completed

Formula:

onboarding_completion_rate = onboarding_completed / routed_leads

and:

start_to_completion_rate = onboarding_completed / onboarding_started

This is the Growth Engine’s north-star event.

12. Converted business

A lead that completes the outcome MenuList considers conversion.

This may be one of:

business activated
business published
business verified
business paid
business retained past threshold

This is product-defined, not Growth Engine-defined.

Event:

converted

Formula:

growth_sourced_conversion_rate = converted / routed_leads

Use conversion as downstream quality feedback.

2.5 Recommended status model

Use these statuses in the Growth Engine:

TypeScript
type GrowthLeadStatus =
  | "raw_imported"
  | "normalized"
  | "duplicate"
  | "suppressed"
  | "rejected"
  | "qualified"
  | "ready_to_contact"
  | "contacted"
  | "engaged"
  | "interested"
  | "routed_to_onboarding"
  | "onboarding_started"
  | "onboarding_completed"
  | "converted"
  | "not_interested"
  | "do_not_contact";

Avoid product-specific states like:

menu_uploaded
menu_created
business_verified

Those belong outside the Growth Engine.

2.6 Attribution window

Every Growth Engine campaign needs an attribution window.

Recommended default:

14 days from first message
30 days from first routed onboarding link

Use two windows:

Contact attribution window
A lead reply/click/start is attributed to a message if it happens within 14 days of outbound contact.
Onboarding attribution window
A completed onboarding is attributed to the Growth Engine if it happens within 30 days of routed link click or onboarding start.

Why two windows?

Replies happen quickly.
Onboarding completion may take longer.

Store both.

2.7 Attribution levels

Attribution should be tracked at five levels.

source
campaign
channel
message/template
onboarding flow

For every routed lead, store:

TypeScript
type GrowthAttribution = {
  leadId: string;

  sourceProvider?: "apify" | "outscraper" | "manual" | "instagram" | "messenger" | "referral" | "ads";
  sourceRunId?: string;

  campaignId: string;

  channel: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger";

  conversationId?: string;
  messageId?: string;

  templateId?: string;
  experimentId?: string;
  variantId?: string;

  offerAngle: string;
  onboardingFlowId: string;

  firstContactedAt?: Date;
  firstClickedAt?: Date;
  onboardingStartedAt?: Date;
  onboardingCompletedAt?: Date;
  convertedAt?: Date;
};

This lets the system answer:

Which source + channel + message + flow combination works best?
2.8 North-star metric formula

Primary:

Growth-sourced completed onboardings per week

Formula:

NSM = count(onboarding_completed events where source = Growth Engine and occurredAt within week)

More useful operating version:

Qualified growth-sourced completed onboardings per week

Formula:

Qualified NSM =
count(onboarding_completed events where:
  lead.segment in ["A", "B"]
  lead.source = Growth Engine
  attribution is valid
  occurredAt within week
)

This prevents the system from optimizing toward junk completions.

2.9 Efficiency metric

North-star volume alone can become expensive. Pair it with efficiency.

Primary efficiency metric:

Cost per completed onboarding

Formula:

cost_per_completed_onboarding =
total_growth_engine_cost / onboarding_completed_count

Include costs:

source costs
AI costs
email costs
WhatsApp costs
tool/provider costs
operator time cost, if tracked

Exclude:

core product/onboarding costs
general engineering salary
unrelated brand/marketing spend

unless you intentionally want full CAC.

2.10 Quality metric

You need a quality metric so the system does not push low-value businesses.

Recommended:

Qualified completion rate

Formula:

qualified_completion_rate =
onboarding_completed / qualified_leads

Also track:

converted_business_rate = converted / onboarding_completed

If available.

If lots of leads complete onboarding but do not activate/convert, the Growth Engine is sending the wrong leads or wrong promise.

2.11 Risk metric

The Growth Engine must monitor channel and brand risk.

Primary risk metric:

Negative response rate

Formula:

negative_response_rate =
(not_interested + do_not_contact + complaints + angry replies) / contacted_leads

Break it into:

not_interested_rate
do_not_contact_rate
complaint_rate
wrong_contact_rate
unsubscribe_rate
bounce_rate

Stop conditions should be based on these.

Example:

pause campaign if DNC/complaint rate crosses threshold
2.12 Channel-specific metrics
Email

Track:

sent
delivered
bounced
opened
clicked
replied
unsubscribed
complaints
onboarding started
onboarding completed

Core email metrics:

email_reply_rate = email_replies / email_sent
email_click_rate = email_clicks / email_delivered
email_completion_rate = onboarding_completed_from_email / email_sent
email_cost_per_completion = email_cost / onboarding_completed_from_email

Open rate is secondary because it can be unreliable and is not the business outcome.

WhatsApp

Track:

messages prepared
messages manually sent
API messages sent
delivered
read, if available
replied
DNC
negative replies
onboarding started
onboarding completed

Core WhatsApp metrics:

whatsapp_reply_rate = whatsapp_replies / whatsapp_sent
whatsapp_completion_rate = onboarding_completed_from_whatsapp / whatsapp_sent
whatsapp_negative_rate = negative_whatsapp_replies / whatsapp_sent

Also track:

template approval status
quality warnings
conversation window expiry
assisted-send completion rate
Instagram DM

Track:

inbound DMs
outbound replies
reply-window active
flow links sent
flow links clicked
onboarding started
onboarding completed
unmatched inbound users

Core Instagram metrics:

instagram_flow_start_rate = onboarding_started_from_instagram / flow_links_sent_on_instagram
instagram_completion_rate = onboarding_completed_from_instagram / flow_links_sent_on_instagram

Do not measure Instagram like cold email. It is mostly warm/inbound/social.

Messenger

Track:

inbound conversations
outbound replies
flow links sent
clicks
onboarding starts
onboarding completions
window expirations

Core Messenger metric:

messenger_completion_rate = onboarding_completed_from_messenger / flow_links_sent_on_messenger
2.13 Source quality metrics

Every source should be judged by output quality, not volume.

For each source/provider:

raw leads imported
unique leads
qualified leads
contact-ready leads
contacted leads
interested leads
onboarding starts
onboarding completions
converted businesses

Key formulas:

unique_rate = unique_leads / raw_leads

qualified_rate = qualified_leads / unique_leads

contact_ready_rate = contact_ready_leads / qualified_leads

source_completion_rate = onboarding_completed / raw_leads

cost_per_qualified_lead = source_cost / qualified_leads

cost_per_completed_onboarding = source_cost / onboarding_completed

This tells you whether Apify, manual lists, Instagram inbound, ads, or referrals are actually working.

2.14 AI performance metrics

Since AI is part of the Growth Engine, track AI quality.

For each AI worker:

runs
success rate
failure rate
average confidence
human review rate
human override rate
auto-action rate
cost per run
latency
downstream conversion impact

Core AI metric:

human_override_rate =
human_overrides / AI_decisions_reviewed

If override rate is high:

AI prompt/model/schema needs improvement

For channel router specifically:

channel_recommendation_win_rate =
onboarding_completed for AI-recommended primary channel / contacted via AI-recommended primary channel

Compare against human/manual routing.

2.15 Message performance metrics

Each template and message variant should be judged by downstream outcome.

Track:

sent
replied
clicked
interested
onboarding started
onboarding completed
negative replies
DNC

Important formulas:

template_completion_rate =
onboarding_completed / messages_sent_with_template

template_negative_rate =
negative_replies / messages_sent_with_template

template_efficiency =
onboarding_completed / total_template_cost

Do not select winning messages based on reply rate alone.

A message that gets many replies but few onboarding completions is not necessarily good.

2.16 Onboarding flow routing metrics

Since Growth Engine routes leads into existing flows, it must measure flow fit.

For each onboarding flow:

routed leads
starts
completions
drop-offs
conversions
completion rate by channel
completion rate by lead segment
completion rate by offer angle

Core formula:

flow_completion_rate =
onboarding_completed / leads_routed_to_flow

Also:

flow_start_rate =
onboarding_started / leads_routed_to_flow

flow_drop_rate =
onboarding_dropped / onboarding_started

The Growth Engine should learn:

which flow works for cafes
which flow works for Instagram leads
which flow works for WhatsApp leads
which flow works for high-score vs low-score leads
2.17 Conversion quality tiers

Use three tiers.

Tier 1 — Soft conversion
lead replied or clicked

Useful for diagnosing message/channel performance.

Tier 2 — Acquisition conversion
lead started onboarding

Useful for measuring routing and CTA quality.

Tier 3 — Core conversion
lead completed onboarding

This is the Growth Engine north-star.

Tier 4 — Business conversion
business activated / verified / paid / retained

This belongs to MenuList product/business metrics but should feed back into Growth Engine quality scoring.

2.18 Dashboard hierarchy

The main dashboard should show:

Top line
Growth-sourced completed onboardings this week
Cost per completed onboarding
Qualified completion rate
Negative response rate
Funnel
raw leads
unique leads
qualified leads
contact-ready leads
contacted
engaged
interested
routed
onboarding started
onboarding completed
converted
Breakdown
by source
by campaign
by channel
by message/template
by offer angle
by onboarding flow
by area/category
Alerts
high negative rate
email bounce spike
WhatsApp risk spike
low flow completion
high AI override rate
source duplicate spike
campaign cost spike

This dashboard tells you what to scale and what to stop.

2.19 Weekly operating report

AI should generate a weekly growth report.

Structure:

1. North-star performance
2. Best source
3. Best channel
4. Best message angle
5. Best onboarding flow
6. Worst-performing source/channel/message
7. Cost per completion
8. Negative response risks
9. AI mistakes / high override areas
10. Recommended actions

Example output:

This week, Growth Engine generated 42 completed onboardings at ₹X per completion.

Best segment:
Koramangala cafes via WhatsApp assisted, menu_link_qr angle.

Weak segment:
HSR cloud kitchens via email. Low qualified rate and low onboarding start rate.

Recommendation:
Increase Koramangala cafe volume by 30%.
Pause HSR cloud kitchen campaign.
Route Instagram-inbound leads to quick-start flow instead of generic flow.

This prevents you from becoming the analyst.

2.20 Stop and scale rules

Every campaign should have stop/scale rules.

Scale if
qualified rate is high
contact-ready rate is high
completion rate is above target
negative rate is low
cost per completion is acceptable
channel health is stable
Pause if
DNC/complaint rate is high
wrong-contact rate is high
cost per completion is too high
qualified rate is too low
channel bounce/failure rate is high
source duplicate rate is high
onboarding completion rate is poor

Example rules:

Scale campaign if:
onboarding_completion_rate_from_contacted >= target
and negative_response_rate < threshold
and cost_per_completion < target
Pause campaign if:
negative_response_rate > threshold
or contact_ready_rate < threshold
or source_duplicate_rate > threshold

Exact thresholds should be configurable.

2.21 Anti-metrics

These numbers can mislead you if treated as goals.

Do not optimize for:

raw leads scraped
messages sent
email open rate
social DM volume
WhatsApp read rate
reply rate alone
click rate alone
AI automation rate
low cost per raw lead

A cheap raw lead that never completes onboarding is noise.

A high reply rate with low onboarding completion is weak messaging.

A high automation rate with high negative response is dangerous.

The system should optimize for:

completed onboarding volume
cost efficiency
lead quality
channel safety
long-term learnings
2.22 Recommended metric names

Use consistent names in the product/admin.

Raw Leads
Unique Leads
Qualified Leads
Contact-Ready Leads
Contacted Leads
Engaged Leads
Interested Leads
Routed Leads
Onboarding Starts
Onboarding Completions
Growth Conversions
Cost per Qualified Lead
Cost per Onboarding Start
Cost per Onboarding Completion
Negative Response Rate
DNC Rate
Suppression Rate
Channel Completion Rate
Source Completion Rate
AI Override Rate

Avoid vague names like:

hot leads
won leads
sales
deals
pipeline

This is not a CRM.

2.23 Final metric system

The Growth Engine should optimize this equation:

More completed MenuList onboardings
÷ lower acquisition cost
÷ lower channel risk
× higher lead quality

Operationally:

North-star:
Growth-sourced completed onboardings per week

Efficiency:
Cost per completed onboarding

Quality:
Qualified completion rate
Downstream conversion rate, if available

Risk:
Negative response rate
DNC/complaint rate
Channel health

Learning:
Performance by source, channel, message, offer angle, onboarding flow

That is the metric foundation.

2.24 Final definition
A successful Growth Engine lead is a qualified business lead that the system sourced or captured, selected the right channel for, contacted or replied to, routed into an existing MenuList onboarding flow, and that completed the onboarding flow within the attribution window.

That is what the system should be built to produce repeatedly.

Spec 3 — Lead Data Model
3.1 Core decision

The Growth Engine’s central object is:

Growth Lead

A Growth Lead represents a business the system may contact, nurture, route into an existing MenuList onboarding flow, and learn from.

It is not a MenuList business record.

It is not a customer account.

It is not an onboarding session.

It is an acquisition object.

Clean boundary:

Growth Lead = marketing/acquisition identity
MenuList Business = product/business identity
Onboarding Session = product onboarding identity

The Growth Engine may reference MenuList product records, but it should not own them.

3.2 What one lead means

A lead is one real-world business acquisition target.

Example:

ABC Cafe, Koramangala, Bangalore

That business may have multiple contact identities:

email
phone / WhatsApp
Instagram profile
Messenger / Facebook Page identity
website
source URL

But these should map to one lead.

The system must avoid creating separate leads like:

ABC Cafe from Apify
ABC Cafe from Instagram
ABC Cafe from email reply
ABC Cafe from Messenger

Those are not separate leads. They are separate identities or conversations attached to one lead.

3.3 Lead model responsibilities

The lead record should answer:

Who is this business?
Where did we find it?
Is it relevant?
How reachable is it?
Which channels do we know?
Which channel should we use?
What should we say?
Which existing MenuList onboarding flow should we route to?
What happened after contact?
Should we follow up, suppress, or stop?
What did AI decide and why?

The lead record should not answer:

What menu did they upload?
What is their published MenuList page?
What is their owner dashboard state?
What product plan are they on?

Those are outside this system.

3.4 Primary collections

For the lead data model, use these collections:

growthLeads
growthLeadIdentities
growthLeadDedupeKeys
growthSuppressions
growthEvents
aiRuns

Related collections covered later:

growthConversations
growthMessages
growthCampaigns
growthSourceRuns
growthTemplates
growthExperiments

The primary document is:

growthLeads/{leadId}

Everything else should reference leadId.

3.5 Growth lead schema

This is the canonical lead object.

TypeScript
type GrowthLead = {
  id: string;

  status: GrowthLeadStatus;

  business: GrowthLeadBusiness;

  source: GrowthLeadSource;

  identities: GrowthLeadIdentitySummary;

  intelligence: GrowthLeadIntelligence;

  routing: GrowthLeadRouting;

  outreach: GrowthLeadOutreach;

  onboardingFeedback: GrowthLeadOnboardingFeedback;

  suppression: GrowthLeadSuppressionSummary;

  ai: GrowthLeadAiSummary;

  ownership: GrowthLeadOwnership;

  timestamps: GrowthLeadTimestamps;
};

This document should stay relatively compact. Message history, AI run details, and conversations live in separate collections.

3.6 Lead status

Use one primary status field.

TypeScript
type GrowthLeadStatus =
  | "raw_imported"
  | "normalized"
  | "duplicate"
  | "rejected"
  | "suppressed"
  | "qualified"
  | "ready_to_contact"
  | "contacted"
  | "engaged"
  | "interested"
  | "routed_to_onboarding"
  | "onboarding_started"
  | "onboarding_completed"
  | "converted"
  | "not_interested"
  | "do_not_contact";

Status rules:

raw_imported → normalized
normalized → duplicate / rejected / qualified
qualified → ready_to_contact
ready_to_contact → contacted
contacted → engaged / interested / not_interested / do_not_contact
interested → routed_to_onboarding
routed_to_onboarding → onboarding_started
onboarding_started → onboarding_completed
onboarding_completed → converted

Terminal states:

duplicate
rejected
do_not_contact
converted

not_interested is semi-terminal. It can be retried later only if policy allows and cooldown expires.

3.7 Business object
TypeScript
type GrowthLeadBusiness = {
  name: string;
  normalizedName: string;

  category: {
    raw?: string;
    normalized:
      | "restaurant"
      | "cafe"
      | "bakery"
      | "dessert_shop"
      | "cloud_kitchen"
      | "juice_shop"
      | "tea_shop"
      | "bar_restaurant"
      | "hotel_restaurant"
      | "other_food"
      | "non_food"
      | "unknown";

    confidence: number;
  };

  scale: {
    type:
      | "single_location_smb"
      | "small_local_chain"
      | "large_chain"
      | "franchise"
      | "unknown";

    confidence: number;
    reason?: string;
  };

  location: {
    country: "IN" | string;
    city: string;
    normalizedCity: string;
    area?: string;
    normalizedArea?: string;
    addressText?: string;
    lat?: number;
    lng?: number;
  };

  website?: {
    url: string;
    normalizedDomain: string;
    status:
      | "unknown"
      | "not_found"
      | "loads"
      | "down"
      | "blocked"
      | "invalid";
  };

  publicPresence?: {
    instagramUrl?: string;
    facebookUrl?: string;
    googleMapsUrl?: string;
    otherUrls?: string[];
  };
};

Important rules:

business.name is the display name.
business.normalizedName is for dedupe/search.
category.normalized is AI/rule-normalized.
scale.type helps avoid wasting outbound on large chains.
website.status helps route messaging angle.

Do not store scraped reviews, ratings, photos, descriptions, or menus inside the lead object. If source data contains those, treat them as temporary source intelligence, not lead truth.

3.8 Source object

A lead can come from multiple sources over time. The lead document should store the primary source plus a compact source history summary.

TypeScript
type GrowthLeadSource = {
  primary: {
    provider:
      | "apify"
      | "outscraper"
      | "manual_csv"
      | "website"
      | "instagram"
      | "messenger"
      | "facebook"
      | "email_inbound"
      | "referral"
      | "ads"
      | "existing_menulist_signal"
      | "unknown";

    sourceType:
      | "google_maps"
      | "manual_import"
      | "website_crawl"
      | "social_inbound"
      | "ad_inbound"
      | "referral"
      | "customer_demand_signal"
      | "unknown";

    campaignId?: string;
    sourceRunId?: string;
    sourceUrl?: string;

    importedAt: Date;
  };

  seenInSources: {
    provider: string;
    sourceRunId?: string;
    sourceUrl?: string;
    seenAt: Date;
  }[];

  sourceQuality?: {
    providerScore?: number;
    sourceConfidence?: number;
    riskLevel: "low" | "medium" | "high";
  };
};

Purpose:

primary source = attribution
seenInSources = enrichment + dedupe memory
sourceQuality = AI/campaign intelligence

Do not let seenInSources grow forever. Keep only useful source references.

3.9 Identity summary

The lead document should keep a compact summary of known channel identities.

Detailed identities should live in growthLeadIdentities.

TypeScript
type GrowthLeadIdentitySummary = {
  email?: {
    value: string;
    normalized: string;
    status:
      | "unknown"
      | "valid"
      | "invalid"
      | "bounced"
      | "unsubscribed"
      | "suppressed";

    confidence: number;
    lastVerifiedAt?: Date;
  };

  phone?: {
    raw: string;
    e164: string;
    countryCode?: string;

    status:
      | "unknown"
      | "valid"
      | "invalid"
      | "wrong_number"
      | "suppressed";

    whatsappLikely?: boolean;
    confidence: number;
    lastVerifiedAt?: Date;
  };

  whatsapp?: {
    phoneE164: string;

    status:
      | "unknown"
      | "available"
      | "opt_in_unknown"
      | "template_required"
      | "active_window"
      | "invalid"
      | "suppressed";

    lastConversationId?: string;
    customerWindowExpiresAt?: Date;
  };

  instagram?: {
    username?: string;
    userId?: string;

    status:
      | "unknown"
      | "known"
      | "inbound_only"
      | "active_window"
      | "invalid"
      | "suppressed";

    lastConversationId?: string;
    customerWindowExpiresAt?: Date;
    confidence: number;
  };

  messenger?: {
    psid?: string;
    pageId?: string;

    status:
      | "unknown"
      | "known"
      | "inbound_only"
      | "active_window"
      | "invalid"
      | "suppressed";

    lastConversationId?: string;
    customerWindowExpiresAt?: Date;
    confidence: number;
  };

  preferredChannel?: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger" | "call";
};

This object is for fast dashboard queries and channel routing.

Full identity records should be separate so that the system can store multiple emails, multiple phones, and multiple social identities.

3.10 Detailed identity collection

Use:

growthLeadIdentities/{identityId}

Schema:

TypeScript
type GrowthLeadIdentity = {
  id: string;
  leadId: string;

  type:
    | "email"
    | "phone"
    | "whatsapp"
    | "instagram_username"
    | "instagram_user_id"
    | "messenger_psid"
    | "facebook_page"
    | "website_domain"
    | "source_url";

  value: string;
  normalizedValue: string;
  valueHash: string;

  status:
    | "unknown"
    | "valid"
    | "invalid"
    | "bounced"
    | "wrong_number"
    | "suppressed"
    | "unsubscribed"
    | "active"
    | "inactive";

  source: {
    provider:
      | "apify"
      | "outscraper"
      | "manual"
      | "website_crawl"
      | "inbound_message"
      | "onboarding_event"
      | "ai_inference";

    sourceRunId?: string;
    confidence: number;
    foundAt: Date;
  };

  channelPolicy?: {
    canUseForOutbound: boolean;
    reasonIfBlocked?: string;
    optInStatus?: "unknown" | "not_required" | "required" | "confirmed" | "blocked";
    customerWindowExpiresAt?: Date;
  };

  lastUsedAt?: Date;
  lastInboundAt?: Date;
  lastVerifiedAt?: Date;

  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
};

Use this collection to avoid stuffing too many identity details into the lead doc.

3.11 Intelligence object

This is where the AI/rules summarize lead quality.

TypeScript
type GrowthLeadIntelligence = {
  fit: {
    isRelevant: boolean;
    score: number; // 0-100
    reason: string[];
    confidence: number;
  };

  need: {
    score: number; // 0-100

    primaryNeed:
      | "menu_link_qr"
      | "instagram_bio_menu"
      | "whatsapp_menu_link"
      | "google_profile_menu_link"
      | "simple_digital_presence"
      | "unknown";

    evidence: {
      type:
        | "no_website"
        | "weak_website"
        | "pdf_menu"
        | "image_menu"
        | "instagram_only"
        | "no_clear_menu_link"
        | "manual_signal"
        | "customer_demand_signal"
        | "unknown";

      description: string;
      confidence: number;
      sourceUrl?: string;
    }[];

    confidence: number;
  };

  contactability: {
    score: number; // 0-100

    availableChannels: ("email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger" | "call")[];

    bestReachChannel?: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger" | "call";

    riskFlags: string[];

    confidence: number;
  };

  intent: {
    score: number; // 0-100

    signals: {
      type:
        | "reply"
        | "click"
        | "onboarding_started"
        | "asked_question"
        | "asked_price"
        | "customer_demand"
        | "inbound_dm"
        | "manual";

      weight: number;
      occurredAt: Date;
    }[];

    lastIntentAt?: Date;
  };

  risk: {
    score: number; // 0-100. Higher = more risky.

    flags: {
      type:
        | "possible_duplicate"
        | "large_chain"
        | "wrong_vertical"
        | "low_confidence_identity"
        | "channel_policy_risk"
        | "high_negative_risk"
        | "source_risk"
        | "already_suppressed"
        | "unknown";

      severity: "low" | "medium" | "high";
      reason: string;
    }[];
  };

  totalScore: number; // 0-100

  segment: "A" | "B" | "C" | "REJECT";

  recommendedAction:
    | "contact"
    | "enrich"
    | "hold"
    | "human_review"
    | "reject"
    | "suppress";

  explanation: string[];

  lastScoredAt?: Date;
  scoringVersion: string;
};

This object is the lead-quality brain.

Recommended scoring meaning:

A = high-priority contact
B = contact or enrich depending on channel availability
C = hold / low priority
REJECT = do not contact

This is where the Growth Engine stores the recommended acquisition route.

3.15 Suppression summary

Detailed suppressions live in growthSuppressions.

The lead record keeps a summary for fast checks.

TypeScript
type GrowthLeadSuppressionSummary = {
  isSuppressed: boolean;

  scope?: "global" | "campaign" | "channel" | "identity";

    | "do_not_contact"

  suppressionIds?: string[];

  canRetryAfter?: Date;
};

Default rule:

do_not_contact = global suppression
wrong_number = phone/WhatsApp suppression
unsubscribe = email suppression
not_interested = campaign cooldown or global depending severity
converted = suppress acquisition outreach

3.19 Dedupe keys

Use:

growthLeadDedupeKeys/{keyHash}

Schema:

TypeScript
type GrowthLeadDedupeKey = {
  id: string; // hash of key

  key: string;

  keyType:
    | "phone"
    | "email"
    | "domain"
    | "instagram_username"
    | "instagram_user_id"
    | "messenger_psid"
    | "facebook_page"
    | "source_url"
    | "name_area_city";

  leadId: string;

  confidence: number;

  source: "system" | "ai" | "manual";

  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
};

Example keys:

phone:+919876543210
email:owner@abccafe.com
domain:abccafe.com
instagram_username:abccafe.blr
messenger_psid:123456789
name_area_city:abc-cafe:koramangala:bangalore

Priority:

phone / email / domain / social IDs = strong
name + area + city = weak

AI can recommend fuzzy dedupe, but deterministic keys should remain the foundation.

3.23 Required lead queries

The model must support these fast queries:

Ready to contact
status = ready_to_contact
segment = A
primaryChannel = whatsapp/email/etc.
not suppressed
sort by totalScore desc
Channel queue
routing.channelRecommendation.primaryChannel = whatsapp
routing.channelRecommendation.sendMode = assisted_send
status = ready_to_contact
Follow-up due
outreach.followUp.nextFollowUpAt <= now
status in contacted / engaged / interested
suppression.isSuppressed = false
Interested leads
status = interested
routing.onboarding.routedFlowId missing
Routed but not started
status = routed_to_onboarding
onboardingFeedback.currentState = routed
older than X hours/days
Started but not completed
onboardingFeedback.currentState = started
drop missing
completedAt missing
Suppressed
suppression.isSuppressed = true
3.24 Suggested indexes

For Firestore-like storage, prepare indexes around actual work queues.

growthLeads:
- status ASC, intelligence.segment ASC, intelligence.totalScore DESC
- status ASC, routing.channelRecommendation.primaryChannel ASC, intelligence.totalScore DESC
- status ASC, routing.channelRecommendation.sendMode ASC, intelligence.totalScore DESC
- outreach.followUp.nextFollowUpAt ASC, status ASC
- onboardingFeedback.currentState ASC, timestamps.updatedAt DESC
- source.primary.campaignId ASC, status ASC, intelligence.totalScore DESC
- suppression.isSuppressed ASC, status ASC
- business.location.normalizedCity ASC, business.location.normalizedArea ASC, intelligence.segment ASC

For dedupe:

growthLeadDedupeKeys:
- keyHash unique document ID
- leadId ASC

For identities:

growthLeadIdentities:
- valueHash unique-ish lookup
- leadId ASC, type ASC
- type ASC, status ASC

For events:

growthEvents:
- leadId ASC, createdAt DESC
- campaignId ASC, createdAt DESC
- type ASC, createdAt DESC
3.25 Validation rules

Before a lead can become qualified, it must have:

business.name
business.normalizedName
business.category.normalized
business.location.city
source.primary.provider
intelligence.totalScore
intelligence.segment
suppression.isSuppressed = false

Before a lead can become ready_to_contact, it must have:

status = qualified
at least one usable channel identity
routing.channelRecommendation.primaryChannel
routing.channelRecommendation.sendMode not blocked
routing.onboarding.recommendedFlowId

Before a lead can become routed_to_onboarding, it must have:

trackingUrl
onboardingFlowId
campaignId or source attribution
channel
messageId or inbound conversation reference

Before a lead can become converted, it must receive a valid product/onboarding feedback event.

3.26 What not to store in the lead object

Do not store:

full message history
full AI prompt/response bodies
scraped reviews
scraped photos
scraped menu content
large raw source payloads
full onboarding payloads
product account details
menu data
payment data
sensitive personal notes

Store summaries and references only.

Detailed data belongs in:

growthMessages
aiRuns
growthEvents
existing MenuList product collections
3.27 Final lead data model principle

The lead record should be:

small enough to query fast
rich enough to route intelligently
clean enough to avoid channel chaos
separate enough to protect MenuList product boundaries
auditable enough to trust AI decisions

The Growth Lead is the acquisition brain’s memory.

It should unify:

source
business identity
channel identities
AI intelligence
routing decision
outreach state
onboarding feedback
suppression state

But it must never become:

a product business profile
a menu object
a customer account
a CRM deal record

Next spec item: Lead source strategy.

Spec 4 — Lead Source Strategy
4.1 Core decision

The Growth Engine should not depend on one source.

It should use a source portfolio:

Cold outbound sources
+ warm/inbound sources
+ paid acquisition sources
+ existing MenuList behavioral signals
+ manual/referral sources

But the system should not integrate every source immediately with equal weight. It should rank every source by one question:

Does this source produce qualified leads that complete existing MenuList onboarding?

Not:

Does this source produce many raw leads?

The source strategy should optimize for:

cost per completed onboarding

not:

cost per scraped lead
4.2 Source strategy principle

The source layer should do four jobs:

1. Find businesses likely to be relevant.
2. Extract enough contact/channel identity to reach them.
3. Feed AI enough context to score and route them.
4. Learn which source/channel/segment combinations convert.

It should not try to become:

a public business database
a copied Google Maps directory
a restaurant data warehouse
a MenuList product data source

This distinction matters.

External data should support acquisition. It should not become MenuList product truth.

4.3 Source categories

Use five major source categories.

1. Cold local business discovery
2. Contact and channel enrichment
3. Warm/inbound social sources
4. Paid lead sources
5. Owned/MenuList behavioral sources

Each category plays a different role.

4.4 Source category 1 — Cold local business discovery

This is where Apify fits.

Purpose:

Find restaurants/cafes/food businesses in target areas.

Primary candidates:

Apify Google Maps actors
Outscraper
Scrap.io
manual CSV imports
local directories, if useful

Recommended first primary source:

Apify Google Maps scraper

Reason:

It supports local business extraction, API workflows, exports, scheduling, and enough fields for lead qualification.

Apify’s Google Maps scraper listings describe extraction of local place data such as addresses, contact details, websites, coordinates, reviews, prices, menus, and lead/contact enrichment fields; the exact cost depends on the actor and enrichment settings, with marketplace listings showing low per-1,000-place pricing.
Apify
+2
Apify
+2

Backup benchmark:

Outscraper

Outscraper positions itself as a pay-as-you-go Google Maps/business data provider with no monthly fee, a monthly free tier, and pricing/enrichment options that vary by service used.
outscraper.com
+2
outscraper.com
+2

Secondary benchmark:

Scrap.io

Scrap.io markets extraction across Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Bing Maps, including business names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, websites, social links, reviews, and other business data from many countries.
Scrap.io

My recommendation:

Use Apify as the first cold-discovery source.
Benchmark Outscraper after enough data.
Keep Scrap.io as a later comparison, not first integration.

Do not start by integrating three vendors. Start with one, measure source quality, then compare.

4.5 Google Maps data boundary

This is important.

If using Google Maps-derived scraping tools, treat the result as:

temporary lead intelligence

not:

MenuList product data

Google Maps Platform terms state that customers must not export, extract, or scrape Google Maps Content for use outside the services, and examples include pre-fetching, indexing, storing, resharing, rehosting, and copying/saving business names, addresses, or user reviews. Google’s Business Profile GoogleLocations API guide also says its endpoints are for merchants with an existing business relationship and using them for lead generation or competitive analysis is against policy.
Google Cloud
+1

Operational rule:

Allowed for Growth Engine:
- discover candidate businesses
- decide whether they are worth contacting
- locate possible contact/channel paths
- store minimal acquisition records
- attribute source and campaign

Not allowed as MenuList product truth:
- scraped reviews
- scraped photos
- copied menu content
- scraped descriptions
- public pages created from source data
- long-term rehosting of third-party business content

The Growth Engine can use external data to decide who to contact. Existing MenuList onboarding/product flows decide what becomes MenuList data.

4.6 Source category 2 — Contact and channel enrichment

Discovery gives you candidates. Enrichment gives you reachability.

Purpose:

Find better contact/channel identities for already-promising leads.

Enrichment sources:

business website crawl
contact page extraction
email extraction
phone normalization
Instagram/Facebook link detection
WhatsApp link detection
secondary provider lookup
manual operator enrichment

Important rule:

Only enrich leads that pass basic fit.

Do not spend enrichment budget on junk.

Use enrichment waterfall:

Lead discovered
→ basic fit check
→ dedupe
→ if relevant but contact weak:
    website crawl
→ if website has contact page:
    extract email / phone / social links
→ if still promising:
    secondary provider
→ if still weak:
    hold or reject

Enrichment should be selective.

Example:

1,000 raw leads
→ 400 relevant food businesses
→ 220 unique + contactable
→ 80 promising but missing best channel
→ enrich only those 80

Do not enrich all 1,000.

4.7 Source category 3 — Warm/inbound social sources

These are not cold scraping sources. They are conversation sources.

Include:

Instagram DMs
Messenger conversations
comments/private replies where allowed
profile CTA responses
social campaign replies

Purpose:

Capture businesses that show intent through Meta channels.

Meta’s Instagram Messaging API is for Instagram Professional accounts at scale, Instagram Messaging Webhooks provide real-time notifications, and Meta’s Messenger/Instagram policy states businesses generally have up to 24 hours to respond to a user message.
Facebook Developers
+2
Facebook Developers
+2

Operational rule:

Instagram/Messenger are primarily warm/inbound acquisition sources.

Do not treat them as default cold DM blasting channels.

Good use:

Instagram post CTA: “DM MENU for setup”
Click-to-Instagram ad
Facebook Page message
Messenger lead conversation
Comment-to-DM flow where allowed

Bad use:

scrape 5,000 Instagram handles and auto-DM all of them

For Growth Engine, Instagram/Messenger leads should be high-quality because they start with user/business interaction.

4.8 Source category 4 — Paid lead sources

Paid sources should feed the same Growth Engine.

Sources:

Meta Lead Ads
Click-to-WhatsApp ads
Click-to-Instagram ads
Click-to-Messenger ads
Google Search Ads to MenuList setup flow
retargeting ads

Meta provides Lead Ads webhook integration for CRM-style capture, so lead forms can push submitted leads into the Growth Engine rather than CSV exports.
Facebook Developers

The Growth Engine should normalize paid leads the same way as scraped/imported leads:

lead created
→ source = meta_lead_ad / google_ad / etc.
→ AI scores
→ channel router decides next action
→ existing onboarding flow router selects flow
→ events feed back

Paid sources should be measured by:

cost per onboarding start
cost per completed onboarding
cost per converted business

not just:

cost per form submit
4.9 Source category 5 — Owned/MenuList behavioral sources

These may become the best source over time.

Examples:

business visited existing MenuList page
business started but abandoned onboarding
customer requested a menu/business
business clicked a setup link
business came from referral link
business replied previously but did not complete
old lead became active again

These are high-signal because they involve actual MenuList behavior.

Owned sources should get priority over cold sources.

Reason:

A lead that already clicked or started onboarding is usually better than a cold scraped business.

The source planner should always check owned signals before spending money on more scraping.

4.10 Source priority model

Rank sources by strategic value.

Tier 1 — Highest quality
existing MenuList behavioral signals
referrals
inbound Instagram/Messenger/WhatsApp conversations
completed/abandoned onboarding feedback
customer demand signals

Why:

warm intent or product-adjacent behavior
Tier 2 — Strong scalable acquisition
Apify Google Maps discovery
Outscraper benchmark
Meta Lead Ads
Click-to-WhatsApp / Instagram / Messenger ads
manual high-quality lists

Why:

scalable, but quality varies
Tier 3 — Enrichment sources
website crawl
contact extraction
social link extraction
secondary data providers

Why:

useful only after lead passes fit
Tier 4 — Experimental
local directories
industry directories
Instagram profile discovery
Facebook Page discovery
event/vendor lists

Why:

may work, but needs measurement
Avoid or restrict
Zomato/Swiggy scraping
review scraping
photo scraping
large platform content reuse
mass social handle scraping
Google Business Profile APIs for lead gen

Reason:

policy risk, low strategic fit, or product-boundary confusion

A source run is not a campaign. A campaign can contain many source runs.

Example:

Source run 2: Apify Indiranagar cafes
