````text
21.6 Experiment types
1. Source experiment

Question:

Which source produces better completed onboardings?

Example:

Apify Google Maps vs Outscraper for Bangalore cafes.

Primary metric:

cost_per_completed_onboarding

Secondary:

qualified_rate
contact_ready_rate
onboarding_start_rate
negative_response_rate
2. Channel experiment

Question:

Which channel works best for this lead segment?

Example:

A-score cafes: WhatsApp assisted vs email.

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate

Guardrail:

negative_response_rate
DNC rate
channel health
3. Offer angle experiment

Question:

Which acquisition angle creates the most completed onboardings?

Example:

menu_link_qr vs whatsapp_menu_link for local cafes.

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate

Secondary:

reply_rate
click_rate
negative_rate
4. Template experiment

Question:

Which message copy works best inside a given offer angle?

Example:

Short WhatsApp copy vs slightly explanatory WhatsApp copy.

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate

Guardrail:

negative_response_rate
5. Onboarding flow experiment

Question:

Which existing MenuList onboarding flow should this lead type enter?

Example:

restaurant_quick_start vs mobile_quick_start for WhatsApp leads.

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate

Secondary:

flow_start_rate
drop_rate
6. Send-time experiment

Question:

When should we message this audience?

Example:

Morning vs afternoon vs evening for restaurant owners.

Primary metric:

onboarding_start_rate or completion_rate

Secondary:

reply_rate
negative_rate
7. Follow-up experiment

Question:

Which follow-up timing or channel recovers more leads?

Example:

clicked-not-started: follow up after 24h vs 48h.

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate

Guardrail:

negative/DNC rate
8. AI router experiment

Question:

Does AI channel routing outperform fixed channel rules?

Example:

AI chooses channel vs WhatsApp-first vs email-first.

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate

Secondary:

human_override_rate
negative_response_rate
cost_per_completion
9. Multi-factor experiment

Use sparingly.

Example:

channel + offer angle combination.

Only run when you have enough volume. Otherwise results will be noisy.

21.7 Default experiment rule

Run one main variable at a time unless volume is high.

Bad:

Variant A: WhatsApp + short template + quick-start flow
Variant B: Email + long template + different flow

You will not know what caused the difference.

Better:

Same audience
Same offer angle
Same onboarding flow
Different channel only

or:

Same audience
Same channel
Same flow
Different template only
21.8 Experiment unit

Choose assignment unit carefully.

Lead-level assignment

Use for:

channel
offer angle
onboarding flow
template

One lead gets one variant.

Conversation-level assignment

Use for:

reply handling
retargeting
inbound responses

One conversation gets one variant.

Message-level assignment

Use for:

template copy
send-time tests

Useful but can get messy if one lead sees multiple variants.

Campaign-level assignment

Use for:

source strategy
geographic expansion
large-scale tests
21.9 Deterministic assignment

Use deterministic hashing for lead assignment.

Reason:

same lead should always stay in same variant
reruns should be stable
attribution stays clean

Example:

TypeScript
function assignVariant({
  experimentId,
  leadId,
  variants,
}: {
  experimentId: string;
  leadId: string;
  variants: { id: string; allocationPercent: number }[];
}) {
  const hash = stableHash(`${experimentId}:${leadId}`);
  const bucket = hash % 100;

  let cumulative = 0;
  for (const variant of variants) {
    cumulative += variant.allocationPercent;
    if (bucket < cumulative) return variant.id;
  }

  return variants[variants.length - 1].id;
}

This prevents random reassignment.

21.10 Holdout group

Some experiments need a holdout.

Example:

Retargeting clicked-not-started leads.

Variants:

A: follow-up after 24h
B: follow-up after 48h
C: no follow-up holdout

Holdout helps answer:

Did follow-up actually improve completion, or would they have completed anyway?

Use holdout carefully when the opportunity cost is acceptable.

21.11 Experiment eligibility

Before assigning a lead to an experiment, check:

lead is in audience
lead not suppressed
lead status eligible
channel eligible, if experiment is channel-specific
template active/approved
onboarding flow active
campaign caps allow it
lead not already assigned to conflicting experiment

If a variant is ineligible for a lead:

exclude lead from experiment
or assign to fallback variant

Do not force an ineligible channel/flow just to preserve experiment purity.

Safety > experiment.

21.12 Experiment conflicts

A lead should not be in conflicting experiments at the same time.

Examples of conflict:

two channel experiments
two template experiments on same message
two onboarding flow experiments
retargeting experiment conflicts with campaign experiment

Use conflict groups.

TypeScript
type ExperimentConflictGroup =
  | "source"
  | "channel"
  | "offer_angle"
  | "template"
  | "onboarding_flow"
  | "follow_up"
  | "send_time";

Rule:

one active experiment per conflict group per lead/conversation
21.13 Experiment assignment object

Collection:

growthExperimentAssignments

Schema:

TypeScript
type GrowthExperimentAssignment = {
  id: string;

  experimentId: string;
  variantId: string;

  unitType:
    | "lead"
    | "conversation"
    | "message"
    | "campaign"
    | "source_run";

  unitId: string;

  leadId?: string;
  conversationId?: string;
  messageId?: string;
  campaignId?: string;

  assignedAt: Date;

  assignmentMethod:
    | "random"
    | "weighted_random"
    | "deterministic_hash"

    | "assigned"
    | "exposed"
    | "completed"
    | "excluded"

This lets every outcome trace back to variant.

21.14 Exposure event

Assignment is not exposure.

A lead is assigned when the system decides the variant.

A lead is exposed when they actually receive or encounter the variant.

Examples:

channel experiment exposure = message sent/prepared on assigned channel
template experiment exposure = message sent with template
flow experiment exposure = flow link sent or clicked
source experiment exposure = lead imported from source run

Use event:

experiment_exposed

Schema:

TypeScript
type GrowthExperimentExposureEvent = {
  id: string;

  experimentId: string;
  variantId: string;

  assignmentId: string;

  leadId?: string;
  conversationId?: string;
  messageId?: string;
  routeId?: string;

  exposureType:
    | "source_imported"
    | "message_sent"
    | "message_prepared"
    | "flow_link_sent"
    | "flow_link_clicked"
    | "follow_up_sent";

  occurredAt: Date;
};

This prevents counting assigned-but-never-contacted leads as exposed.

21.15 Outcome events

Outcomes are standard Growth Engine events.

Relevant outcomes:

message_replied
flow_link_clicked
onboarding_started
onboarding_completed
converted
negative_reply
do_not_contact
email_bounced
unsubscribe
complaint

The Experiment Engine joins outcomes to exposure via:

leadId
messageId
routeId
assignmentId
time window
21.16 Attribution window for experiments

Each experiment should define an attribution window.

Defaults:

reply attribution: 14 days after message exposure
click attribution: 14 days after message exposure
onboarding start: 30 days after flow link exposure
onboarding completion: 30 days after onboarding start or 45 days after exposure
negative/DNC: 14 days after exposure

Schema:

TypeScript
type ExperimentAttributionWindow = {
  replyDays: number;
  clickDays: number;
  onboardingStartDays: number;
  onboardingCompletionDays: number;
  negativeDays: number;
};

Do not use infinite attribution. It pollutes results.

    };

    };

21.18 Winning criteria

A variant wins only if:

primary metric improves materially
guardrails are not violated
sample size is adequate
downstream quality is not worse

Example:

Template B has 30% higher reply rate but 20% lower onboarding completion.
Template B does not win.

Example:

WhatsApp has 2x completion rate but 5x DNC rate.
Do not scale until risk is resolved.

Recommended winner logic:

winner = highest onboarding_completion_rate
subject to:
  negative_rate <= threshold
  dnc_rate <= threshold
  cost_per_completion <= threshold
  sample_size adequate
21.19 Guardrail metrics

Every experiment must have guardrails.

Minimum guardrails:

negative response rate
DNC rate
complaint rate
bounce/failure rate
cost per completion

Channel-specific:

Email
bounce rate
unsubscribe rate
complaint rate
WhatsApp
negative response rate
DNC rate
quality/account warning
manual-send burden
Instagram/Messenger
window expiry rate
negative response rate
reply failure rate

If guardrail breaches:

pause variant or experiment
21.20 Experiment stop rules

Stop experiment if:

guardrail breach
channel account risk
template safety issue
campaign stopped
variant clearly harmful
admin stops manually
minimum sample reached and winner selected
max duration reached

Pause, not delete.

Retain data.

21.23 Experiment examples
Example 1 — Channel experiment

Hypothesis:

A-score cafes with phone will complete onboarding at higher rate through WhatsApp-assisted than email.

Audience:

A-score cafes
Bangalore
phone + email available
not contacted last 30 days

Variants:

A: WhatsApp assisted
B: Email

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate

Guardrails:

WhatsApp negative rate < 3%
DNC rate < 1%
Example 2 — Offer angle experiment

Hypothesis:

WhatsApp menu link angle converts better than generic menu link + QR for phone-first leads.

Audience:

A/B food businesses
WhatsApp eligible

Variants:

A: menu_link_qr
B: whatsapp_menu_link

Same channel, same flow, same send timing.

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate
Example 3 — Onboarding flow experiment

Hypothesis:

Instagram inbound leads complete better in instagram_quick_start than restaurant_quick_start.

Audience:

Instagram inbound leads
intent = interested/send_link

Variants:

A: instagram_quick_start
B: restaurant_quick_start

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate

Secondary:

drop_rate
Example 4 — Follow-up timing experiment

Hypothesis:

Clicked-not-started leads respond better to 48h follow-up than 24h follow-up.

Audience:

clicked_not_started bucket
A/B leads

Variants:

A: follow-up after 24h
B: follow-up after 48h
C: no follow-up holdout

Primary metric:

onboarding_completion_rate

Guardrail:

negative response rate
21.24 AI and experiments

AI should support experiments in three ways.

1. Suggest experiments

AI can analyze data and say:

WhatsApp is outperforming email for A-score cafes, but sample is small. Run channel experiment.
2. Respect assignments

AI Channel Router, Message Generator, and Flow Router must respect experiment variant assignment unless blocked by eligibility/safety.

3. Analyze results

AI can summarize:

Variant B has lower reply rate but higher onboarding completion. Recommend scaling B.

AI must not silently change variant assignment.

21.25 Experiment assistant output
TypeScript
type ExperimentAssistantOutput = {
  recommendedExperiment?: {
    hypothesis: string;
    type: GrowthExperiment["type"];
    audience: GrowthCampaignAudience;
    variants: GrowthExperimentVariant[];
    primaryMetric: GrowthExperiment["metrics"]["primary"];
    guardrails: GrowthExperiment["metrics"]["guardrails"];
  };

  reason: string[];

  expectedLearning: string;

  risks: string[];

  priority: "low" | "normal" | "high";
};
21.26 Bandit optimization later

Long-term, you may use adaptive allocation.

But initially, use fixed allocation.

Adaptive/bandit can be useful when:

volume is high
outcome signal is fast
guardrails are stable
sample bias is controlled

Use cases:

email template variants
send-time optimization
offer angle allocation

Avoid bandit initially for:

WhatsApp
DNC-sensitive channels
low-volume onboarding flow tests
high-risk experiments

Do not add complexity before enough volume.

21.27 Statistical rigor without overkill

You do not need academic-grade experimentation at the beginning, but you do need discipline.

Minimum rules:

define hypothesis before launch
define primary metric before launch
define guardrails before launch
assign variants deterministically
track exposure separately from assignment
do not call winner too early
do not change variants mid-run without versioning

This alone avoids most bad conclusions.

21.28 Common experiment mistakes
Mistake 1 — Testing too many things at once

Fix:

one main variable per experiment
Mistake 2 — Picking winner by reply rate

Fix:

use onboarding completion as primary when possible
Mistake 3 — Ignoring negative rate

Fix:

guardrails required
Mistake 4 — No exposure tracking

Fix:

assignment ≠ exposure
Mistake 5 — Changing campaign mid-test

Fix:

campaign/experiment versioning
Mistake 6 — Running tiny tests and trusting them too much

Fix:

sample-size adequacy flag
confidence label
21.29 Experiment integration with campaign builder

Campaign builder should allow:

No experiment
Use existing experiment
Create new experiment
AI suggested experiment

If experiment enabled, campaign review page must show:

hypothesis
variants
allocation
primary metric
guardrails
sample size target
expected risk

Campaign cannot launch an experiment without:

primary metric
variant definitions
guardrails
assignment unit
21.30 Experiment integration with router systems
Channel Router

If experiment dimension = channel:

router receives forced channel variant
router checks eligibility
if eligible, uses it
if blocked, excludes or fallback
Offer Angle Selector

If dimension = offer angle:

selector uses assigned angle
Template Selector

If dimension = template:

selector uses assigned template
Onboarding Flow Router

If dimension = onboarding flow:

flow router uses assigned flow if eligible and active
Follow-up Logic

If dimension = follow-up timing:

follow-up scheduler uses assigned delay/policy
21.31 Experiment invalidation

Mark assignment/outcome invalid if:

lead was suppressed before exposure
lead was already converted
message was never sent/prepared
wrong channel was used due to manual override
template was edited outside variant
flow URL was manually changed
channel eligibility blocked variant
operator deviated from assigned path

Invalidated assignments should not count as exposed outcomes.

Store reason.

21.32 Manual override handling

If operator changes the assigned message/channel/flow:

mark experiment_deviation = true

Schema:

TypeScript
type ExperimentDeviation = {
  assignmentId: string;
  leadId: string;

  originalVariantId: string;

  deviationType:
    | "channel_changed"
    | "template_changed"
    | "flow_changed"
    | "message_edited"
    | "manual_skip"
    | "manual_send_different";

  reason?: string;
  operatorId: string;

  occurredAt: Date;
};

This keeps experiment results honest.

21.33 Experiment result interpretation

Classify results:

clear winner
likely winner
inconclusive
harmful variant
needs more data
guardrail failed

Recommended result logic:

TypeScript
type ExperimentConclusion =
  | "clear_winner"
  | "likely_winner"
  | "inconclusive"
  | "guardrail_failed"
  | "harmful_variant"
  | "needs_more_data";

Do not force a winner.

“Inconclusive” is a valid result.

21.34 AI experiment review

After experiment reaches sample or duration threshold, AI generates:

hypothesis
result summary
variant comparison
primary metric result
guardrail result
confidence
recommended action
what to test next

Example:

Result: likely winner.
Variant B, whatsapp_menu_link, had 1.6x onboarding completion rate vs menu_link_qr, with similar negative rate.
Recommendation: scale B for A-score WhatsApp-eligible cafes, but continue collecting data for bakeries.
21.35 What not to experiment with casually

Avoid casual experimentation on:

DNC handling
unsubscribe handling
angry replies
pricing claims
compliance language
channel policy bypasses
unsupported customer demand claims

These should be policy-controlled, not growth-tested.

21.36 Experiment metrics by channel
Email

Experiment safely across:

subject
body length
offer angle
CTA wording
send time
follow-up timing

Guardrails:

unsubscribe
bounce
complaint
negative replies
WhatsApp

Experiment cautiously across:

assisted message copy
offer angle
send timing
whether to include link immediately or ask first

Guardrails:

DNC
negative rate
manual workload
account quality
Instagram/Messenger

Experiment mainly on:

reply wording
flow routing
CTA wording
content/ad-driven inbound prompt

Guardrails:

response-window expiry
negative replies
unmatched leads
21.37 Experiment lifecycle
draft
→ review
→ running
→ paused
→ completed
→ winner selected / inconclusive
→ archived
Draft

Experiment config editable.

Review

Validation checks.

Running

Assignment/exposure active.

Paused

No new exposures. Existing outcomes still tracked.

Completed

No new exposures. Outcome window may still be open.

Winner selected

Result applied to campaign/router/template policy.

Archived

Read-only.

21.38 Experiment validation

Before running:

hypothesis exists
variants sum to 100%
primary metric selected
guardrails selected
audience exists
sample size target exists
templates/flows/channels active
eligibility can support variants
no conflicting experiment
tracking exists

If any critical item fails, block launch.

21.39 Experiment-to-policy promotion

When a variant wins, do not just note it. Promote it into policy.

Examples:

winning channel → update channel router weights for that segment
winning template → make default template for that offer/channel
winning flow → update flow router performance preference
winning source → increase source planner priority
winning follow-up timing → update follow-up policy

Promotion should be:

admin-approved or AI-recommended with approval

Record policy change event.

21.40 Final experiment contract

Every active experiment must have:

TypeScript
type FinalExperimentContract = {
  experimentId: string;

  hypothesis: string;

  type:
    | "source"
    | "channel"
    | "offer_angle"
    | "template"
    | "onboarding_flow"
    | "send_time"
    | "follow_up"
    | "ai_router"
    | "multi_factor";

  audienceSnapshotId?: string;

  assignment: {
    unit: "lead" | "conversation" | "message" | "campaign" | "source_run";
    method: "random" | "weighted_random" | "deterministic_hash" | "manual";
  };

  variants: {
    variantId: string;
    allocationPercent: number;
    config: Record<string, unknown>;
  }[];

  primaryMetric:
    | "onboarding_completion_rate"
    | "onboarding_start_rate"
    | "cost_per_completed_onboarding"
    | "negative_response_rate";

  guardrails: {
    maxNegativeRate?: number;
    maxDncRate?: number;
    maxBounceRate?: number;
    maxComplaintRate?: number;
    maxCostPerCompletion?: number;
  };

  attributionWindow: ExperimentAttributionWindow;

  status: "review" | "running" | "paused" | "completed" | "stopped";

  createdAt: Date;
};

No experiment should run without this contract.

21.41 Final principle

The Experiment Engine makes the Growth Engine smarter over time.

Without it, you will make decisions based on:

vibes
reply screenshots
one-off wins
manual intuition

With it, the system learns:

which source finds the best leads
which channel converts each segment
which message angle creates real onboarding
which template avoids negative replies
which existing onboarding flow completes best
which follow-up recovers intent

The goal is not to test everything.

The goal is to create a controlled learning machine where every campaign makes the next campaign sharper.

Next spec item: Attribution and feedback loop.
````

````text
Spec 22 — Attribution and Feedback Loop
22.1 Purpose

The Attribution and Feedback Loop connects Growth Engine activity to real MenuList onboarding outcomes.

It answers:

Which lead source worked?
Which channel worked?
Which message worked?
Which offer angle worked?
Which onboarding flow worked?
Which campaign created completed onboardings?
Which AI decision improved or hurt conversion?
What should the system do differently next time?

Without attribution, the Growth Engine becomes a messaging machine.

With attribution, it becomes a learning acquisition system.

22.2 Core principle

Every growth action must be traceable to downstream outcomes.

The system should be able to trace:

source run
→ lead
→ campaign
→ channel route
→ message
→ template
→ offer angle
→ onboarding flow route
→ click
→ onboarding start
→ onboarding completion
→ conversion

The Growth Engine should optimize using actual MenuList outcomes, not activity metrics.

Primary learning signal:

completed onboarding

Secondary learning signals:

onboarding started
interested reply
flow link clicked
negative reply
DNC
bounce/failure
22.3 Boundary

The Growth Engine owns attribution and feedback ingestion.

It does not own the product/onboarding state itself.

Clean boundary:

Growth Engine sends tracked route into existing MenuList onboarding.
MenuList onboarding emits feedback events.
Growth Engine records those events and updates acquisition intelligence.

Growth Engine should not know how the onboarding flow internally works beyond:

started
step completed
dropped
completed
converted
22.4 Attribution hierarchy

Use multiple attribution levels.

1. Lead source attribution
2. Campaign attribution
3. Channel attribution
4. Message/template attribution
5. Offer angle attribution
6. Onboarding flow attribution
7. Experiment attribution
8. AI decision attribution

Each level answers a different question.

Source attribution
Did Apify / manual / Instagram inbound / Meta Lead Ads produce good leads?
Campaign attribution
Did this campaign generate completed onboardings?
Channel attribution
Did email, WhatsApp, Instagram, or Messenger work best for this lead segment?
Message attribution
Which template or message created the outcome?
Offer angle attribution
Which positioning made leads act?
Onboarding flow attribution
Which existing flow completed best for this segment?
Experiment attribution
Which variant won?
AI decision attribution
Did AI routing/scoring/message decisions improve outcomes?
22.5 Core attribution object

Use a central object for attribution snapshots.

Collection:

growthAttributions

Schema:

TypeScript
type GrowthAttribution = {
  id: string;

  leadId: string;

  source?: {
    provider?: string;
    sourceType?: string;
    sourceRunId?: string;
    firstSeenAt?: Date;
  };

  campaign?: {
    campaignId?: string;
    campaignType?: string;
    campaignVersion?: number;
  };

  channel?: {
    channel: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger" | "call";
    channelAccountId?: string;
    conversationId?: string;
  };

  message?: {
    messageId?: string;
    templateId?: string;
    templateVersion?: number;
    templateFamily?: string;
    offerAngle?: OfferAngle;
  };

  route?: {
    routeId?: string;
    onboardingFlowId?: string;
    trackingUrl?: string;
  };

  experiment?: {
    experimentId?: string;
    variantId?: string;
    assignmentId?: string;
  };

  ai?: {
    leadScorerRunId?: string;
    channelRouterRunId?: string;
    offerSelectorRunId?: string;
    flowRouterRunId?: string;
    messageGeneratorRunId?: string;
    nextBestActionRunId?: string;
  };

  touchType:
    | "first_touch"
    | "last_touch"
    | "assisted_touch"
    | "primary_route";

  outcome?: {
    flowClickedAt?: Date;
    onboardingStartedAt?: Date;
    onboardingCompletedAt?: Date;
    convertedAt?: Date;
    negativeAt?: Date;
    dncAt?: Date;
  };

  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
};

This object can be generated at key moments and updated as outcomes arrive.

22.6 Route ID as the attribution anchor

Every Growth Engine onboarding link must use a route ID.

Example:

https://menulist.com/g/r/route_abc123

The route redirects to the actual existing MenuList onboarding flow.

Why route ID matters:

It captures click before redirect.
It links message → route → flow → onboarding events.
It lets onboarding fetch lead/context safely.
It avoids exposing raw lead IDs or contact data.
It lets flow URL change without breaking attribution.

Never send raw onboarding links in growth campaigns.

Always send tracked route links.

Collection:

growthLeadRoutes

Schema:

This is the main bridge between acquisition and onboarding.

22.8 Product feedback event contract

Existing MenuList onboarding/product flows should emit events back to the Growth Engine.

Collection:

growthFeedbackEvents

Schema:

TypeScript
type GrowthFeedbackEvent = {
  id: string;

  routeId?: string;
  leadId?: string;

  onboardingFlowId: string;

  product?: {
    onboardingSessionId?: string;
    businessId?: string;
    userId?: string;
    accountId?: string;
  };

  eventType:
    | "flow_link_clicked"
    | "onboarding_started"
    | "onboarding_step_completed"
    | "onboarding_dropped"
    | "onboarding_completed"
    | "converted";

  step?: {
    stepId?: string;
    stepName?: string;
    stepIndex?: number;
  };

  drop?: {
    reason?: string;
    userFacingReason?: string;
    technicalReason?: string;
  };

  attribution?: {
    campaignId?: string;
    sourceRunId?: string;
    channel?: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger" | "call";
    messageId?: string;
    templateId?: string;
    offerAngle?: OfferAngle;
    experimentId?: string;
    variantId?: string;
  };

  metadata?: Record<string, unknown>;

  occurredAt: Date;
  receivedAt: Date;
};

The product/onboarding system should send only the event context needed for attribution, not full product state.

22.9 Required feedback events

Minimum required events:

flow_link_clicked
onboarding_started
onboarding_completed
converted

Recommended additional events:

onboarding_step_completed
onboarding_dropped

These extra events help retargeting and flow-quality analysis.

22.10 Event handling rules
flow_link_clicked

When route link is clicked:

route.status = clicked
route.stats.clickCount += 1
route.stats.firstClickedAt / lastClickedAt
lead.status = engaged, if earlier state
conversation/message marked clicked
growthEvent = flow_link_clicked

This event comes from the tracking redirect, not necessarily product onboarding.

onboarding_started

When existing flow starts:

route.status = started
route.stats.startedAt = occurredAt
lead.status = onboarding_started
lead.onboardingFeedback.currentState = started
campaign stats increment
message/template/channel attribution updated
growthEvent = onboarding_started
onboarding_step_completed

When product emits step progress:

append feedback event
update route/product session summary
use for drop-off analysis
do not change lead status unless first start

This is diagnostic, not primary conversion.

onboarding_dropped

When product detects drop:

route.status = dropped
route.stats.droppedAt = occurredAt
lead.onboardingFeedback.currentState = dropped
create retargeting bucket = started_not_completed / onboarding_dropped
trigger Next-Best-Action
growthEvent = onboarding_dropped

Growth Engine should not fix the product issue. It should decide retargeting or human review.

onboarding_completed

When flow completes:

route.status = completed
route.stats.completedAt = occurredAt
lead.status = onboarding_completed
campaign/template/channel/source/flow stats updated
pending acquisition follow-ups cancelled
growthEvent = onboarding_completed

This is the Growth Engine’s primary success event.

converted

When MenuList product/business logic says converted:

route.status = converted
route.stats.convertedAt = occurredAt
lead.status = converted
suppress acquisition outreach
close active acquisition conversations
update downstream quality metrics
growthEvent = lead_converted

Conversion definition belongs to MenuList product/business logic, not the Growth Engine.

22.11 Feedback ingestion API

Create internal endpoint:

POST /api/internal/growth/feedback

Input:

TypeScript
type RecordGrowthFeedbackInput = {
  routeId?: string;
  leadId?: string;
  onboardingFlowId: string;

  eventType:
    | "onboarding_started"
    | "onboarding_step_completed"
    | "onboarding_dropped"
    | "onboarding_completed"
    | "converted";

  product?: {
    onboardingSessionId?: string;
    businessId?: string;
    userId?: string;
    accountId?: string;
  };

  step?: {
    stepId?: string;
    stepName?: string;
    stepIndex?: number;
  };

  drop?: {
    reason?: string;
    technicalReason?: string;
  };

  occurredAt: Date;

  metadata?: Record<string, unknown>;
};

Output:

TypeScript
type RecordGrowthFeedbackOutput = {
  ok: boolean;
  feedbackEventId?: string;
  leadId?: string;
  routeId?: string;
  actionsTriggered?: string[];
};

The endpoint should authenticate internal callers only.

22.12 Feedback event idempotency

Product systems may send duplicate events.

Use idempotency key:

eventType + routeId + onboardingSessionId + stepId + occurredAt

or product-provided event ID.

Schema addition:

TypeScript
idempotencyKey: string;

Before processing:

if key exists → ignore/return success
else process

Do not double-count onboarding starts or completions.

22.13 Attribution windows

Define attribution windows so old activity does not over-credit campaigns.

Recommended defaults:

TypeScript
type AttributionWindows = {
  replyDays: number;               // default 14
  clickDays: number;               // default 14
  onboardingStartDays: number;     // default 30
  onboardingCompletionDays: number;// default 45
  conversionDays: number;          // default 60
};

Suggested defaults:

reply: 14 days after message
click: 14 days after message
onboarding start: 30 days after route sent/clicked
onboarding completion: 45 days after route sent or 30 days after start
conversion: 60 days after route

Attribution should be configurable by campaign.

22.14 Attribution models

Support at least three attribution models.

Last-touch attribution

Credit the last message/route before onboarding start/completion.

Use for:

simple operational decisions
template/channel decisions
First-touch attribution

Credit the first Growth Engine source/campaign touch.

Use for:

source quality
top-of-funnel acquisition
Assisted attribution

Credit all meaningful touches before conversion.

Use for:

multi-channel learning
follow-up value
retargeting analysis

Default dashboard can start with last-touch and first-touch.

Data model should support assisted attribution.

Use event-driven updates plus periodic reconciliation.

Update offer angle performance.

sent

The Flow Router should use these stats to route future leads.

22.23 Feedback updates to AI decisions

Every AI decision should be linked to downstream outcomes.

Examples:

leadScorerRunId → did A leads complete more often?
channelRouterRunId → did recommended channel convert?
offerSelectorRunId → did selected angle work?
flowRouterRunId → did selected flow complete?
messageGeneratorRunId → did message produce negative replies?
nextBestActionRunId → did action lead to start/completion?

Use an AI outcome summary.

Collection:

aiDecisionOutcomes

Schema:

TypeScript
type AiDecisionOutcome = {
  id: string;

  aiRunId: string;

    | "lead_score"

  };

This makes AI measurable.

22.24 Feedback updates to lead scoring

Lead scoring should improve based on outcomes.

Examples:

A-score leads complete at 12%
B-score leads complete at 3%
C-score leads complete at 0.5%

If A-score does not outperform B/C, scoring is weak.

Track:

completion rate by lead score band
negative rate by lead score band
DNC rate by lead score band
cost per completion by score band

Use this to adjust:

fit weights
need weights
contactability weights
risk penalties
segment thresholds

For follow-up/retargeting:

follow-up sent
clicked

By bucket:

22.26 Feedback reconciliation

Event-driven updates can fail or arrive out of order.

Run:

22.27 Attribution conflict handling

Sometimes multiple touches claim credit.

Example:

Email sent
WhatsApp sent
Instagram inbound
Onboarding completed

Use ordered attribution logic.

Route-based attribution first

If onboarding uses route ID:

credit route’s attribution
Message-based attribution second

If route missing but message link known:

credit message containing link
Conversation-based attribution third

If message missing:

credit latest active conversation before start
Lead-level fallback

If no specific route/message:

credit first/last campaign touch based on attribution model

Route ID should solve most ambiguity.

22.28 Attribution invalidation

Invalidate attribution if:

lead was already converted before exposure
message was never sent
route was manually shared outside Growth Engine
operator changed flow without logging
experiment assignment was violated
suppression existed before message
event arrived outside attribution window

Invalidated events can still be stored, but not counted in experiment/campaign metrics.

Matching order:

route ID

If route ID is missing but match is strong:

attach feedback to lead with confidence score

    | "route_id"

    | "manual";

Default:

low-confidence matches go to human review

22.35 Feedback loop into suppression and safety

Feedback should update risk controls.

Examples:

template causes high DNC → pause template

source causes wrong-contact replies → lower source quality score
segment causes negative replies → tighten qualification

This should happen automatically or through AI recommendation.

Stop-rule triggers should use feedback events.

source duplicate rate

Increase Apify Koramangala cafes.

Benchmark Outscraper for bakeries because Apify contactability is low.

Without feedback, source strategy is guesswork.

22.37 Feedback loop into Channel Router

Channel Router uses:

completion rate by channel + segment

DNC rate by channel
fallback success rate
channel health

Example:

WhatsApp assisted completion rate 2.3x email, negative rate acceptable.
Prefer WhatsApp assisted.

B-score restaurants:
Email has lower negative rate and similar completion.

Example:

or:

Stop second follow-up for this segment.
22.41 Unmatched feedback queue

Some product events will not match a route/lead.

/admin/growth/unmatched-feedback

22.42 Feedback confidence

Every feedback attribution should have confidence.

TypeScript
type FeedbackAttributionConfidence =
  | "exact"
  | "high"
  | "medium"
  | "low"
  | "unmatched";

Examples:

route ID match → exact
email match + same campaign window → high
business name + area match → medium
fuzzy name only → low
no match → unmatched

Only exact/high should count in core metrics by default.

Medium can be reviewed.

Low should not affect experiment results.

22.43 Feedback event integrity

Every feedback event should be:

authenticated
idempotent
timestamped
schema-validated
attribution-linked
append-only

Do not let product frontend send arbitrary untrusted feedback without server validation.

Recommended:

onboarding backend emits feedback events
not client-only tracking

Client click tracking is useful, but completion/conversion should come from server-side product events.

22.44 Feedback and privacy

Feedback events should avoid unnecessary product data.

Avoid storing:

Growth Engine needs outcome signals, not product internals.

Example:

Attribution should still work if within window.

Campaign dashboards should show:

Do not judge a campaign too early if completion window is still open.

Operator capacity supports 50/day.

Increase WhatsApp-assisted allocation for A-score cafes.

Do not use WhatsApp for B/C leads yet.

This is the kind of learning the Growth Engine should produce.

22.53 Failure modes
Failure mode 1 — No route ID

Outcome cannot be attributed.

Fix:

all growth links must use route ID
Failure mode 2 — Product events missing

Dashboard undercounts completions.

Fix:

backend feedback events required
reconciliation jobs
unmatched feedback queue
Failure mode 3 — Duplicate feedback events

Campaign overcounts.

Fix:

idempotency keys
event dedupe
Failure mode 4 — Attribution window too long

Old campaigns get false credit.

Fix:

configurable attribution windows
matured metrics
Failure mode 5 — Attribution optimized for clicks

Wrong winner selected.

Fix:

primary metric = onboarding completion
Failure mode 6 — Manual shares not tracked

Operator sends raw onboarding link.

Fix:

UI should only expose tracked route links
raw links hidden/disabled in Growth Engine
Failure mode 7 — Low-confidence fuzzy matches pollute metrics

Fix:

exact/high confidence only for core metrics
human review for medium
exclude low
````

````text
Spec 23 — Suppression, Safety, and Reputation Controls
23.1 Purpose

The Suppression, Safety, and Reputation Controls layer protects MenuList from bad outreach.

It answers:

Who must never be contacted?
Which identity/channel is blocked?
When should a campaign pause?
When should a channel slow down or stop?
When should pending actions be cancelled?
When should AI be blocked from acting?
How do we protect email, WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, and brand reputation?

This is the hard safety layer of the Growth Engine.

No AI worker, campaign, operator, or automation path should bypass it.

23.2 Core principle

Growth should be aggressive in intelligence, but conservative in execution.

The system can be aggressive about:

finding leads
scoring leads
choosing channels
drafting messages
testing campaigns
learning from outcomes

But it must be conservative about:

sending messages
respecting opt-outs
handling DNCs
avoiding duplicate outreach
protecting sender accounts
stopping bad campaigns
using WhatsApp/Instagram/Messenger safely

The safety layer has veto power.

AI recommends.
Campaigns request.
Execution prepares.
Safety decides whether action is allowed.
23.3 What this layer owns

It owns:

global suppression
identity suppression
channel suppression
campaign cooldowns
DNC handling
unsubscribe handling
wrong-contact handling
bounce/complaint handling
negative-reply handling
duplicate-outreach prevention
contact-frequency limits
channel health monitoring
campaign stop rules
reputation thresholds
pending-action cancellation
human override rules
safety incidents
audit logs

It does not own:

lead scoring
channel routing logic
message copywriting
onboarding flow UX
product onboarding
pricing policy
business verification

It is an enforcement and protection layer.

23.4 Safety hierarchy

Use this order of authority:

1. Global suppression
2. Identity/channel suppression
3. Legal/channel policy constraints
4. Campaign stop rules
5. Channel account health
6. Contact-frequency limits
7. Message safety guardrails
8. Human approval rules
9. AI/campaign/operator request

If a higher layer blocks something, lower layers do not matter.

Example:

Lead is do_not_contact.
AI says “send follow-up.”
Result: blocked.
23.5 Suppression scopes

Suppression must support different scopes.

TypeScript
type SuppressionScope =
  | "global"
  | "lead"
  | "identity"
  | "channel"
  | "campaign"
  | "domain"
  | "business_cluster";
global

Blocks all acquisition outreach to the lead/business across all channels.

Use for:

do_not_contact
complaint
manual global block
lead

Blocks outreach to one Growth Lead.

Use for:

bad fit
rejected lead
converted lead
manual stop
identity

Blocks one identity.

Examples:

one phone number
one email address
one Instagram user ID
one Messenger PSID

Use for:

wrong number
bounced email
invalid email
wrong Instagram identity
channel

Blocks one channel for a lead.

Use for:

email unsubscribe
WhatsApp wrong number
Instagram block
Messenger unavailable
campaign

Blocks a lead from one campaign only.

Use for:

not interested in current campaign
cooldown
already contacted in this campaign
domain

Blocks a domain.

Use for:

company asked not to contact
email domain complaint
agency/domain-wide suppression
business_cluster

Blocks related records.

Use for:

large chain/franchise not targeted
duplicate branch group
manually blocked brand
23.6 Suppression reasons

Use fixed suppression reasons.

TypeScript
type SuppressionReason =
  | "do_not_contact"
  | "unsubscribe"
  | "wrong_number"
  | "wrong_business"
  | "invalid_email"
  | "email_bounce"
  | "email_complaint"
  | "spam_complaint"
  | "not_interested"
  | "converted"
  | "duplicate"
  | "bad_fit"
  | "manual_block"
  | "policy_block"
  | "channel_health"
  | "campaign_cooldown";

These reasons drive behavior.

Do not store arbitrary freeform suppression states only as notes.

Collection:

    | "email_complaint"
    | "spam_complaint"
    | "not_interested"
    | "converted"
    | "duplicate"
    | "bad_fit"
    | "manual_block"
    | "policy_block"
    | "channel_health"
    | "campaign_cooldown";

  target: {
    leadId?: string;
    identityId?: string;
    channel?: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger" | "call";
    emailHash?: string;
    phoneHash?: string;

    instagramUserIdHash?: string;
    instagramUsernameHash?: string;
    messengerPsidHash?: string;
    businessNameAreaHash?: string;

    businessClusterId?: string;
  };

  source:
    | "operator"
    | "ai_reply_classifier"
    | "unsubscribe_link"
    | "email_bounce"
    | "email_complaint"
    | "provider_event"
    | "channel_policy"
    | "system_stop_rule"
    | "admin";

  evidence: {
    messageId?: string;

  };

Suppression records should be auditable and hard to remove accidentally.

23.8 Suppression lookup contract

Before any action, call:

TypeScript
checkSuppression(input)

Input:

TypeScript
type SuppressionCheckInput = {
  leadId: string;

  channel?: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger" | "call";

  identityIds?: string[];

  email?: string;
  phoneE164?: string;
  domain?: string;
  instagramUserId?: string;
  instagramUsername?: string;
  messengerPsid?: string;

  campaignId?: string;

  action:
    | "send_initial_message"
    | "send_follow_up"
    | "reply_to_inbound"
    | "send_onboarding_flow"
    | "retarget"
    | "reactivate"
    | "manual_contact";
};

Output:

TypeScript
type SuppressionCheckResult = {
  allowed: boolean;

  blockLevel?:
    | "global"
    | "lead"
    | "identity"
    | "channel"
    | "campaign"
    | "domain"
    | "business_cluster";

  reason?: SuppressionReason;

  suppressionIds: string[];

  canRetryAfter?: Date;

  recommendedAction:
    | "allow"
    | "block"
    | "hold_until_cooldown"
    | "use_different_channel"
    | "human_review";

  explanation: string;
};

This function must be called before:

message generation
message execution
follow-up creation
campaign enrollment

manual send confirmation
23.9 Channel policy constraints

The safety system must encode channel-specific constraints.

WhatsApp

WhatsApp Business policy states that businesses may reply to a user message within the 24-hour customer service window without a message template, but outside that window, messages must use approved message templates. This makes WhatsApp unsuitable as a blind bulk cold-outbound channel in the same way email is used.
WhatsApp for Business

Default controls:

cold WhatsApp = assisted send or approved template only
API send outside active window = approved template required
reply inside active window = allowed if policy and safety pass
DNC/wrong number = immediate suppression
quality warning = pause or reduce send volume
Instagram DM and Messenger

Meta’s Messenger/Instagram messaging policy says businesses generally have up to 24 hours to respond to a user, so the Growth Engine should treat Instagram and Messenger primarily as inbound/warm channels unless a compliant campaign mechanism exists.
Facebook Developers

Default controls:

cold Instagram/Messenger outbound = blocked by default
inbound DM/reply = allowed inside active window
expired window = block or switch channel
DNC/negative = suppress
Email

Commercial email needs unsubscribe/opt-out handling, accurate sender/header information, and non-deceptive subject lines under CAN-SPAM’s business guidance. The Growth Engine should enforce these at template/render time, not rely on AI to remember them.
Federal Trade Commission

Default controls:

unsubscribe link or reply-opt-out required
bounced email = suppress email identity
complaint = suppress and investigate
deceptive subject = block
sender domain health = monitored
India commercial communication context

TRAI’s TCCCPR framework is specifically aimed at unsolicited commercial communications, and TRAI’s official TCCCPR page describes the framework as protecting customers from UCC while allowing commercial communication to customers who have opted in or set preferences. The Growth Engine should therefore treat opt-out handling, contact caps, suppression, and channel discipline as core infrastructure rather than optional hygiene.
Telecom Regulatory Authority of India

23.10 Global hard blocks

These block every channel.

do_not_contact
complaint
spam_complaint
manual global block
converted lead, for acquisition outreach
duplicate of suppressed lead
known wrong business with no clean match
policy block

If global block exists:

no message generation
no send job
no follow-up
no retargeting
no reactivation

The only allowed action is:

internal review or suppression confirmation
23.11 Identity-level blocks

These block one identity.

Email identity

Block if:

unsubscribed
hard bounced
complaint
invalid format
manual block

Amazon SES supports an account-level suppression list to prevent sending to addresses that produced bounces or complaints, and SES can configure suppression reasons such as BOUNCE and COMPLAINT. If SES is used, Growth Engine suppressions should sync or mirror SES bounce/complaint outcomes.
AWS Documentation

Phone / WhatsApp identity

Block if:

wrong number
DNC on that number
invalid phone
manual phone block
Instagram identity

Block if:

user asked not to be contacted
identity mismatch
blocked/reported
invalid username/user ID
manual block
Messenger identity

Block if:

user asked not to be contacted
wrong identity
PSID invalid
Page context unavailable
manual block
23.12 Channel-level blocks

These block one channel for a lead.

Examples:

email unsubscribed, but WhatsApp may remain usable if no global DNC
WhatsApp wrong number, but email may remain usable
Instagram window expired, but email may be usable
Messenger conversation closed, but email may be usable

But if the user says:

do not contact us again
stop messaging us
remove us

default should be global suppression.

23.13 Campaign-level cooldowns

Not every negative response is global DNC.

Use campaign-level cooldown for:

not interested
not now
already have solution
no reply after max follow-ups
low intent

Example:

Lead says “not now.”
→ campaign cooldown 60 days.
→ no more messages in this campaign.
→ reactivation possible later if policy allows.

But if they say:

don’t contact again

that is global DNC.

23.14 DNC handling

DNC is the highest-priority safety event.

Trigger phrases include:

stop
do not contact
don’t message
remove my number
unsubscribe
don’t email
don’t call
mat bhejo
message mat karo

DNC workflow:

1. Detect via deterministic rule and/or AI classifier.
2. Create suppression.
3. Cancel pending actions and send jobs.
4. Close active conversations.
5. Send exact confirmation only if appropriate.
6. Do not include any promotional CTA.
7. Mark lead do_not_contact if global.
8. Log event.

Approved response:

Understood. We won’t contact you again.

No link. No pitch. No objection handling.

23.15 Unsubscribe handling

Email unsubscribe can come from:

unsubscribe link
reply “unsubscribe”
provider complaint/unsubscribe event
manual operator action

Workflow:

1. Create email/channel suppression.
2. Mark email identity unsubscribed.
3. Cancel pending email actions.
4. Keep non-email channels eligible only if language was email-specific.
5. If wording is broad, create global DNC.

Example:

“Unsubscribe from emails” → email suppression.
“Do not contact us again” → global suppression.
23.16 Wrong-number handling

Wrong number should suppress the phone/WhatsApp identity.

Workflow:

1. Mark phone identity wrong_contact.
2. Suppress phone/WhatsApp identity.
3. Cancel WhatsApp/call actions.
4. Do not suppress entire lead by default.
5. Return lead to enrichment if still valuable.
6. If they also say stop/contact complaint, global suppress.

Approved response:

Sorry about that. We won’t contact this number again.
23.17 Wrong-business handling

Wrong business means identity/lead matching may be wrong.

Workflow:

1. Move to human review.
2. Mark identity conflict.
3. Pause all outreach to lead until resolved.
4. If confirmed wrong, suppress identity or reject lead.
5. If duplicate/merge issue, resolve dedupe.

Approved response:

Sorry about that. We’ll correct this on our side.

No further pitch.

23.18 Complaint handling

Complaint examples:

This is spam.
How did you get my number?
I will report this.
Stop contacting us.

Workflow:

1. Immediately pause pending outreach to lead.
2. Create global suppression unless human review decides narrower scope.
3. Move to Human Review / Safety Incident.
4. Send DNC confirmation only if appropriate.
5. Check campaign-level negative/complaint rate.
6. If pattern exists, pause campaign.

Complaint is not a normal objection. It is a safety signal.

23.19 Negative response handling

Negative replies include:

not interested
no need
already have solution
not now

Workflow depends on severity:

soft negative → not_interested + campaign cooldown
hard negative → suppression
angry/complaint → global suppression + review

Soft negative approved response:

Understood. Thanks.

No link unless the wording is clearly “not now, maybe later” and the campaign policy allows a soft link.

Default: do not pitch after negative.

23.20 Converted lead suppression

Once a lead completes onboarding or converts:

stop acquisition outreach
cancel pending follow-ups
close acquisition conversations
mark acquisition_suppressed reason = converted

This does not mean MenuList product cannot message them later.

It means:

Growth acquisition campaigns should stop treating them as a prospect.

Future lifecycle/product messaging belongs to another system or a different campaign class with separate rules.

23.21 Duplicate suppression

If a lead is merged or marked duplicate:

duplicate lead should be suppressed/rejected
canonical lead retains history
pending actions on duplicate are cancelled
conversations are re-linked if appropriate

Do not let duplicates remain contactable.

Duplicate outreach creates brand damage.

23.22 Contact frequency limits

Set frequency limits at multiple levels.

TypeScript
type ContactFrequencyPolicy = {
  maxMessagesPerLeadPerCampaign: number;
  maxMessagesPerLeadPer30Days: number;

  maxInitialOutreachPerLead: number;

  maxFollowUpsPerConversation: number;

  minHoursBetweenMessagesSameChannel: number;
  minHoursBetweenMessagesAnyChannel: number;

  maxChannelsPerLeadPerCampaign: number;

  cooldownAfterNoReplyDays: number;
  cooldownAfterNotInterestedDays: number;
};

Recommended defaults:

max follow-ups: 2
min same-channel gap: 48–72h
max channels per campaign: 2
no-reply cooldown: 30–60d
not-interested cooldown: 60–90d
DNC: permanent/global
23.23 Cross-channel safety rule

Do not harass leads across channels.

Bad:

Email no reply
→ WhatsApp same day
→ Instagram next day
→ Messenger next day

Good:

Primary channel
→ one follow-up or backup channel if justified
→ stop/cooldown

The safety layer should track:

total touches per lead
channels used
time between touches
negative signals

Then block over-contacting.

23.24 Campaign safety thresholds

Each campaign must define stop thresholds.

TypeScript
type CampaignSafetyThresholds = {
  maxNegativeRate: number;
  maxDncRate: number;
  maxComplaintRate: number;
  maxWrongContactRate: number;
  maxBounceRate: number;
  maxUnsubscribeRate: number;
  maxDeliveryFailureRate: number;
  maxHumanReviewBacklog?: number;
};

Recommended starting thresholds should be conservative and adjusted with data.

Example:

DNC spike → pause campaign
complaint > threshold → stop campaign and review
bounce spike → pause email sends
wrong-contact spike → review source quality

Exact thresholds should be configurable by channel and campaign type.

23.25 Channel account health controls

Track health per sending account.

TypeScript
type ChannelAccountHealth = {
  channelAccountId: string;
  channel: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger";

  status:
    | "healthy"
    | "warning"
    | "restricted"
    | "disabled"
    | "unknown";

  metrics: {
    sent24h?: number;
    failureRate24h?: number;
    bounceRate24h?: number;
    complaintRate24h?: number;
    unsubscribeRate24h?: number;
    negativeReplyRate24h?: number;
    dncRate24h?: number;
    wrongContactRate24h?: number;
  };

  limits: {
    maxDailySends?: number;
    currentDailySends?: number;
  };

  canSend: boolean;
  reasonIfBlocked?: string;

  updatedAt: Date;
};

If health becomes:

warning → reduce volume / require human review
restricted → pause sends
disabled → block sends
23.26 Email reputation controls

Email safety controls:

SPF/DKIM/DMARC configured
unsubscribe handling
bounce handling
complaint handling
sender domain monitoring
daily send caps
new-domain ramping
reply-to inbox active
suppression sync

Block email sends if:

recipient unsubscribed
recipient bounced
domain suppressed
sender account paused
bounce/complaint threshold exceeded
template missing unsubscribe
subject deceptive

If SES is used, mirror SES hard-bounce/complaint suppression into Growth Engine and avoid continuing to send to addresses that have bounced or complained.
AWS Documentation

23.27 WhatsApp reputation controls

WhatsApp safety controls:

assisted-send default for cold leads
approved templates required for API cold/initiated sends
daily caps
quality/account health monitoring
DNC detection
wrong-number suppression
negative-rate monitoring
no multi-message cold sequences by default

Block WhatsApp if:

phone invalid/wrong
DNC
template required but not approved
account quality warning/restriction
daily cap reached
campaign negative threshold hit

WhatsApp Business policy explicitly warns that policy violations can result in limitations or loss of access to WhatsApp Business services, so account-quality protection should be treated as infrastructure.
WhatsApp for Business

23.28 Instagram/Messenger reputation controls

Instagram and Messenger safety controls:

inbound/warm-first usage
24-hour response window tracking
no cold mass DM by default
identity confidence checks
window-expiry blocking
account/webhook health
negative/DNC suppression

Block Instagram/Messenger if:

no active user-initiated conversation
response window expired
identity suppressed
account disconnected
campaign attempts cold DM blasting
message safety risk

The standard Meta messaging policy gives businesses up to 24 hours to respond to a user, so the Growth Engine should surface response-window expiry as both a safety and urgency signal.
Facebook Developers

23.29 Source safety controls

Source quality can create safety risk.

Track source risk metrics:

wrong-contact rate
DNC rate
negative rate
duplicate rate
bad-category rate
invalid-contact rate
bounce rate

If a source produces high risk:

pause source segment
lower source score
require enrichment/verification
require human review before outreach
stop using source

Example:

Apify cloud-kitchen query produces high wrong-number rate.
→ pause source run pattern.

Source safety is part of reputation safety.

23.30 AI safety controls

AI can recommend unsafe actions if not constrained.

Controls:

structured outputs only
fixed action taxonomies
banned claims
message safety checker
eligibility contract required
suppression check required
confidence thresholds
human review below threshold
AI cannot execute suppression removal
AI cannot override DNC
AI cannot change pricing
AI cannot invent channel availability

If AI output conflicts with policy:

policy wins
AI event logged as blocked/invalid
23.31 Message safety controls

Before sending:

message safety check
banned claim scan
channel-specific validator
template approval check
conditional claim evidence check
unsubscribe footer check for email
WhatsApp template exact-match check

Block message if:

banned claim
unsupported customer-request claim
missing unsubscribe
template mismatch
DNC response includes promotion
channel-inappropriate tone
deceptive subject

This prevents “AI creativity” from becoming liability.

23.32 Pending-action cancellation

When a suppression or stop event occurs, cancel pending actions.

Events that cancel pending actions:

do_not_contact
unsubscribe
wrong_number
complaint
converted
campaign_paused
campaign_stopped
channel_account_restricted
identity_invalidated
lead_rejected
lead_merged_duplicate

Cancel:

send jobs
follow-ups
retargeting actions
campaign queue items
assisted-send cards
scheduled emails

Cancellation should be event-driven and auditable.

23.33 Safety incident object

Create a safety incident record for serious issues.

Collection:

growthSafetyIncidents

Schema:

TypeScript
type GrowthSafetyIncident = {
  id: string;

  severity:
    | "low"
    | "medium"
    | "high"
    | "critical";

  type:
    | "complaint"
    | "dnc_missed"
    | "wrong_contact_spike"
    | "high_bounce_rate"
    | "high_dnc_rate"
    | "channel_account_warning"
    | "unsafe_message_sent"
    | "template_policy_issue"
    | "duplicate_outreach"
    | "source_quality_issue"
    | "ai_guardrail_failure";

  leadId?: string;
  campaignId?: string;
  messageId?: string;
  conversationId?: string;
  channelAccountId?: string;
  sourceRunId?: string;
  aiRunId?: string;

    | "open"
    | "investigating"
    | "resolved"
    | "false_positive";

  actionsTaken: string[];

  createdAt: Date;
  resolvedAt?: Date;
  resolvedBy?: string;
};

Examples of critical incidents:

message sent after DNC
unsafe pricing claim sent
complaint spike
WhatsApp account restricted
email complaint spike
23.34 Safety incident response

Define response levels.

Low

Example:

single soft negative
single invalid email

Action:

log and continue
Medium

Example:

wrong-number cluster
template mild safety warning

Action:

review source/template
adjust routing
High

Example:

DNC rate spike
email bounce spike
WhatsApp negative spike

Action:

pause campaign/channel segment
admin review
Critical

Example:

message after DNC
formal complaint
channel account restricted
unsafe promise sent at scale

Action:

stop campaign
cancel pending actions
admin incident review
fix root cause

This dashboard should be checked before scaling campaigns.

Per channel show:

23.37 Suppression dashboard

Route:

/admin/growth/suppressions

Filters:

channel

Actions:

view evidence

Suppression removal must require:

admin role

No silent unsuppression.

23.38 Human override rules

Human override is allowed for some blocks, not all.

Override allowed
hold
cooldown, with admin/operator reason
human_review
campaign-level not-interested cooldown
source-risk hold
Override not allowed except admin/safety review
do_not_contact
complaint
unsubscribe for email
wrong number for same phone
channel account disabled
template rejected for API send
global suppression

Every override creates:

human_override event
reason
operator/admin ID
before/after state
23.39 Safety config

Central config:

23.40 Safety enforcement points

Safety checks happen at multiple points.

campaign enrollment
lead routing
message generation
message safety check
send job creation
execution preflight
follow-up scheduling
retargeting scheduling
manual send confirmation
channel switch
AI auto-action

Safety is not one function. It is a system-wide gate.

But all checks should use the same suppression/policy records.

23.41 Pre-send safety contract

Every send must pass:

TypeScript
type PreSendSafetyResult = {

No execution without this.

Create events:

23.43 Reconciliation jobs

Safety state can drift. Add reconciliation jobs.

cancelPendingActionsForSuppressedLeads
findMessagesSentAfterSuppression
findDuplicateOutreach
recalculateCampaignRisk
recalculateChannelHealth

findExpiredCooldowns
findInvalidIdentityStillContactable

This prevents silent safety bugs.

23.44 Safety metrics

Track:

DNC rate
unsubscribe rate
complaint rate
wrong-number rate
negative response rate
bounce rate
duplicate outreach rate
blocked-send count
human override count
unsafe-message block count
campaign auto-pauses
channel health warnings
suppression creation rate
suppression removal rate
message-after-suppression incidents

Break down by:

source
campaign
channel
template
offer angle
lead segment
operator
AI worker

This identifies the root cause of risk.

23.45 Risk diagnosis examples
High wrong-number rate

Likely cause:

bad source
bad phone normalization
old data
shared/central numbers

Action:

pause source segment
raise contactability threshold
require enrichment
High DNC rate

Likely cause:

bad targeting
wrong channel
message too aggressive
too many follow-ups

Action:

pause campaign
review template
reduce volume
change audience
High email bounce rate

Likely cause:

bad email source
old emails
invalid extraction

Action:

pause email sends
suppress bounced identities
improve verification
High WhatsApp negative rate

Likely cause:

using WhatsApp too cold
bad message timing
bad audience

Action:

switch to assisted/manual only
reduce daily cap
tighten A-lead threshold
High AI guardrail failures

Likely cause:

template too loose
prompt too open
offer angle risky
bad variables

Action:

tighten templates
reduce AI personalization level
improve banned-claim checks
23.46 Default safety posture

Use these defaults.

DNC = global suppression
Complaint = global suppression + safety incident
Wrong number = identity/channel suppression
Email unsubscribe = email suppression
Hard bounce = email identity suppression
Converted = suppress acquisition outreach
Not interested = campaign cooldown
No reply after max follow-ups = cooldown
Cold WhatsApp = assisted or approved-template only
Instagram/Messenger = inbound/reply-window only
Email = auto-send allowed with unsubscribe/bounce handling

This is the correct baseline.

23.47 Safety and AI autonomy

AI autonomy should decrease as risk increases.

Low risk:
A/B lead, valid email, safe template, no suppression → auto-send email allowed.

Medium risk:
Cold WhatsApp, high-value lead, medium confidence → assisted/human approval.

High risk:
pricing, complaint, DNC ambiguity, identity conflict → human review.

Critical risk:
DNC, complaint, global suppression → block/suppress.

AI should never get Level 4 autonomy on:

DNC ambiguity
pricing without policy
complaints
cold WhatsApp at scale
Instagram/Messenger cold outreach
suppression removal
23.48 Final safety contract

Before any action, the Growth Engine should be able to produce:

TypeScript
type FinalSafetyDecision = {
  leadId: string;

  action:
    | "send_message"
    | "prepare_assisted_send"
    | "reply"
    | "follow_up"
    | "retarget"
    | "reactivate"
    | "route_to_onboarding"
    | "manual_contact";

  channel?: "email" | "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "messenger" | "call";

  allowed: boolean;

  decision:
    | "allow"
    | "allow_with_human_approval"
    | "hold"
    | "block"
    | "suppress"
    | "pause_campaign"
    | "pause_channel";

  blockers: {
    type: string;
    severity: "low" | "medium" | "high" | "critical";
    message: string;
  }[];

  suppressionsApplied?: {
    suppressionId: string;
    scope: SuppressionScope;
    reason: SuppressionReason;
  }[];

  pendingActionsCancelled?: string[];

  requiredHumanApproval: boolean;

  auditEventId: string;

  checkedAt: Date;
};

No outbound action should proceed without a positive safety decision.

23.49 Final principle

The Growth Engine is allowed to scale only if it can stop itself.

This layer makes sure the system can:

respect DNC immediately
avoid duplicate outreach
stop bad campaigns
protect channel accounts
protect sender domains
avoid creepy messages
cancel unsafe pending actions
learn from negative signals
preserve brand trust

The rule is:

Growth speed is useful only if reputation survives.

For MenuList, that matters more than squeezing a few extra replies out of aggressive outreach.
````

````text
Spec 24 — Channel Health Dashboard
24.1 Purpose

The Channel Health Dashboard monitors whether MenuList’s acquisition channels are safe, usable, scalable, and converting.

It covers:

email
WhatsApp
Instagram DM
Messenger

Its job is not just to show volume. Its job is to answer:

Can we safely send more?
Which channel is healthy?
Which channel is risky?
Which account/template/campaign is causing problems?
Where are messages failing?
Where are replies converting?
Where should we pause, throttle, or scale?

This dashboard protects growth from becoming channel damage.

24.2 Core principle

The dashboard should optimize for:

safe completed onboardings

not:

more messages sent

A channel is not healthy just because it sends many messages.

A healthy acquisition channel has:

stable delivery
low failure rate
low bounce/complaint/DNC rate
manageable inbox load
acceptable cost
clear attribution to onboarding starts/completions
no platform/account warnings

If a channel produces replies but high complaints, DNCs, or wrong contacts, it is not healthy.

24.3 What this dashboard owns

The Channel Health Dashboard owns:

channel health visibility
channel account status
campaign/channel risk visibility
delivery health
reply health
conversion health
queue health
webhook health
template health
suppression/DNC monitoring
channel capacity monitoring
alerting
pause/throttle recommendations

It does not own:

channel routing decisions
message writing
lead scoring
campaign creation
onboarding product state
business activation
provider credential management

It observes, alerts, and recommends. Other systems act.

24.4 Core views

The dashboard should have these views:

1. Channel Overview
2. Email Health
3. WhatsApp Health
4. Instagram Health
5. Messenger Health
6. Account / Provider Health
7. Campaign Risk by Channel
8. Template Health
9. Webhook and Queue Health
10. Alerts and Incidents

The default view should be Channel Overview.

24.5 Channel health status model

Use one common status model across all channels.

TypeScript
type ChannelHealthStatus =
  | "healthy"
  | "watch"
  | "warning"
  | "throttled"
  | "paused"
  | "restricted"
  | "disabled"
  | "unknown";
Status meanings
healthy:
channel is operating normally

watch:
minor issue or metric moving in wrong direction

warning:
risk rising; volume should not increase

throttled:
system is intentionally reducing volume

paused:
system has stopped new sends temporarily

restricted:
provider/account/platform limitation exists

disabled:
channel is unavailable

unknown:
data missing, webhook down, or provider status unknown

The Growth Engine should treat:

healthy/watch → usable
warning → usable with caution
throttled → limited sending
paused/restricted/disabled → block or require admin review
unknown → conservative behavior
24.6 Channel Health Score

Each channel gets a score from 0–100.

Channel Health Score =
  Delivery Health
+ Reputation/Safety Health
+ Conversation Health
+ Conversion Health
+ Provider/Integration Health
- Risk Penalty

Suggested weights:

Delivery health:             20
Reputation/safety health:    25
Conversation health:         15
Conversion health:           25
Provider/integration health: 15
Risk penalty:               -40 max

Interpretation:

85–100: healthy
70–84: watch
55–69: warning
40–54: throttled
<40: paused/restricted review

This score is not a vanity metric. It should directly affect campaign caps and eligibility.

24.7 Channel overview screen

Top-level screen should show:

Channel
Status
Health Score
Sent / Prepared Today
Replies Today
Onboarding Starts
Onboarding Completions
Negative Rate
DNC Rate
Failure Rate
Open Queue
Open Alerts
Recommended Action

Example:

Email      Healthy   91   320 sent   18 replies   11 starts   4 completions   0.8% negative   0.2% DNC   1.1% failure   Scale cautiously
WhatsApp   Watch     78   42 sent    14 replies   8 starts    3 completions   2.1% negative   0.7% DNC   0.5% failure   Keep assisted only
Instagram  Healthy   87   26 replies 13 starts   5 completions   low risk   Reply window active
Messenger  Unknown   48   webhook delay detected   Pause new replies until fixed

The dashboard should make the decision obvious:

scale
hold
throttle
pause
investigate
24.8 Common metrics across all channels

Every channel should track:

outbound prepared
outbound sent
provider accepted
delivered, if available
read/opened, if available
clicked
inbound replies
interested replies
onboarding starts
onboarding completions
converted leads
negative replies
DNCs
wrong contacts
failed sends
blocked sends
pending queue
human review queue
cost
cost per onboarding start
cost per completed onboarding

Core common formulas:

reply_rate = replies / sent

interested_rate = interested_replies / sent

start_rate = onboarding_starts / sent

completion_rate = onboarding_completions / sent

negative_rate = negative_replies / sent

dnc_rate = dnc / sent

failure_rate = failed_sends / attempted_sends

cost_per_completion = channel_cost / onboarding_completions

Use sent carefully. For assisted WhatsApp, count only manually confirmed sends, not opened send cards.

24.9 Email Health

Email health should monitor:

sender account status
domain status
bounce rate
complaint rate
unsubscribe rate
delivery failure rate
open/click/reply
reply quality
onboarding starts/completions
template performance
sender volume
suppression list growth

Amazon SES includes a reputation metrics page for bounce and complaint rates, and AWS states these metrics are important to account health. AWS also notes that a bounce rate of 5% or more may put an SES account under review, and 10% or more may lead to paused sending. Use those as hard reference points if SES is the provider, while keeping internal thresholds more conservative.
AWS Documentation
+1

Email health object
TypeScript
type EmailHealth = {
  channel: "email";

  status: ChannelHealthStatus;
  healthScore: number;

  account: {
    provider: "ses" | "resend" | "postmark" | "sendgrid" | "other";
    accountId: string;
    fromDomain: string;
    fromAddress: string;

    spfConfigured?: boolean;
    dkimConfigured?: boolean;
    dmarcConfigured?: boolean;
  };

  metrics24h: {
    sent: number;
    delivered?: number;
    bounced: number;
    complaints: number;
    unsubscribes: number;
    opened?: number;
    clicked: number;

24.16 Health score formulas
Email health score
Email Health =
  25 × delivery score
+ 25 × bounce/complaint safety score
+ 15 × unsubscribe safety score
+ 15 × engagement/conversion score
+ 10 × domain/account config score
+ 10 × queue/webhook score
- risk penalties
WhatsApp health score
WhatsApp Health =
  20 × delivery/API success score
+ 25 × DNC/negative/wrong-number safety score
+ 20 × account/template quality score
+ 15 × reply/conversion score
+ 10 × assisted queue health
+ 10 × cap/utilization score
- risk penalties
Instagram/Messenger health score
Social DM Health =
  20 × webhook/account health
+ 20 × reply-window health
+ 20 × inbound matching health
+ 20 × reply/conversion score
+ 10 × negative/DNC safety score
+ 10 × queue health
- risk penalties

24.23 Alert routing

Alerts should go to different owners.

email bounce/complaint → growth admin
WhatsApp quality/template → growth admin/operator
webhook failure → engineering/admin
human review backlog → operator/admin
campaign negative spike → admin
source wrong-number spike → source/campaign owner

Notifications can go to:

dashboard
email
Slack/Telegram optional

Do not over-notify. Only notify for actionable risk.

24.24 Health-driven campaign control

Channel health should directly affect campaigns.

If channel health degrades:

pause new sends
reduce caps
require human approval
switch to backup channel
stop campaign

Example rules:

TypeScript
if email.status === "warning" {
  reduce email daily cap by 50%;
}

if email.status === "paused" {
  block all new email sends;
}

if whatsapp.status === "warning" {
  disable API sends and keep assisted only;
}

if instagram.webhookHealth === "failed" {
  block Instagram replies until fixed;
}

The Campaign Builder and Channel Eligibility Engine must consume channel health.

24.25 Health-driven AI routing

AI Channel Router should receive channel health as input.

Example:

JSON
{
  "email": { "status": "healthy", "score": 91 },
  "whatsapp": { "status": "warning", "score": 62 },
  "instagram": { "status": "healthy", "score": 87 }
}

Router behavior:

healthy → can prefer
watch → usable
warning → use cautiously
throttled → lower priority
paused/restricted/disabled → do not use
unknown → conservative

This prevents the AI from recommending a channel that is technically eligible but operationally risky.

24.26 Health-driven Next-Best-Action

NBA should use health.

Examples:

Email bounced spike → stop email follow-ups and try WhatsApp for A leads
WhatsApp wrong-number spike → pause WhatsApp for that source segment
Instagram reply window backlog → prioritize Instagram replies
Messenger webhook failure → queue human/system alert, do not auto-reply

Channel health should affect priority and action type.

24.27 Health-driven source review

If a source causes channel health problems, surface it.

Examples:

Source run produces high wrong-number rate.
Email list produces high bounce rate.
Apify category query produces high DNC rate.
Manual CSV has duplicate outreach.

Dashboard should show:

risk by source provider
risk by source run
risk by area/category
risk by campaign

This links channel health back to lead quality.

24.33 Health status transitions

Define status transitions.

healthy → watch
watch → warning
warning → throttled
throttled → paused
paused → healthy/watch after recovery

Do not jump straight from critical to healthy without observation.

Recovery rule:

channel must remain below risk thresholds for N hours/days before status improves

Example:

Email bounce spike resolved.
Keep status = watch for 48h before healthy.
24.34 Automatic pause rules

The system should auto-pause in serious cases.

Auto-pause if:

DNC/complaint rate exceeds critical threshold
email complaint rate exceeds critical threshold
channel account restricted
WhatsApp quality critical
template rejected/paused
webhook failure prevents inbound processing
message-after-DNC incident detected

Auto-pause scope:

template
campaign
channel account
entire channel

Default:

pause smallest safe scope first

Example:

One template causing DNC spike → pause template.
Entire channel quality warning → pause channel/API sends.

24.42 Failure modes
Failure mode 1 — Dashboard optimizes for volume

Fix:

primary health view includes completion, negative, DNC, and cost metrics.
Failure mode 2 — Account health warnings missed

Fix:

provider sync + alerts + auto-pause rules.
Failure mode 3 — Webhook failure invisible

Fix:

webhook freshness metrics and queue health.
Failure mode 4 — Bad template damages channel

Fix:

template-level health and auto-pause.
Failure mode 5 — Source quality creates channel risk

Fix:

risk by source run and area/category.
Failure mode 6 — Assisted WhatsApp queue overload

Fix:

queue backlog affects health and campaign pacing.
Failure mode 7 — Unknown status treated as healthy

Fix:

unknown = conservative / hold / investigate.
24.43 Final dashboard contract

Every channel health dashboard view should answer:

1. Is this channel usable right now?
2. How much can we safely send?
3. What is the current risk?
4. What is the current conversion quality?
5. Which campaign/template/source is causing risk?
6. What should we pause, throttle, or scale?
7. Are webhooks and queues working?
8. Are pending messages safe to continue?

If the dashboard does not support these decisions, it is just reporting noise.

24.44 Final principle

The Channel Health Dashboard is the Growth Engine’s speed limiter.

It lets MenuList scale acquisition without losing control of:

email reputation
WhatsApp account quality
Instagram/Messenger responsiveness
operator capacity
campaign risk
lead trust

The rule:

Scale only channels that are healthy, converting, and safe.
Throttle or pause everything else.

Next spec item: AI Campaign Optimizer.
````
